questions.title: Lambda vs. Kappa for a Fraud Platform That Also Needs Retraining
questions.prompt: Explain Lambda and Kappa architecture at the mechanism level, then say which you would choose for an enterprise fraud-detection platform that needs sub-second scoring and also needs nightly historical reprocessing for model retraining, and why.
questions.modelAnswer:
Lambda architecture runs two independent code paths against the same source data: a batch layer that recomputes exact, complete views on a schedule, and a speed layer that produces approximate, low-latency views from the live stream, merged at serving time to reconcile the two. The appeal is that you get to use mature, well-understood batch engines for anything too complex or stateful to express cheaply in a streaming job, but the cost is real: two codebases implementing the same business logic independently drift out of sync, and someone has to own the reconciliation between them. Kappa architecture collapses this to one code path: everything, including historical reprocessing, runs as a stream, and reprocessing means replaying the stream from an earlier offset through the same logic rather than running a separate batch job. The requirement for Kappa to work is a durable, replayable log that retains enough history to replay from.

For a fraud-detection platform that needs sub-second scoring and nightly retraining, I would lean Kappa, but implemented in a way that doesn't force Kafka itself to retain unbounded history. Land raw events into a Bronze Delta table via Structured Streaming — Delta's transaction log and time travel make the table itself the durable, replayable source of truth, so Kafka only needs a modest retention window and Delta carries the rest. The same streaming job powers real-time scoring off the Silver layer, and nightly retraining reads the identical Bronze/Silver tables in batch mode, which guarantees training and serving see exactly the same transformation logic because it is the same code, not a parallel reimplementation. This gets Kappa's single-codebase guarantee without the usual Kappa objection that infinite log retention is expensive.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start by being precise about the mechanism, because people often use 'Lambda' loosely to mean 'has a batch job somewhere.' Lambda is specifically two separate code paths — batch and speed — merged at serving time, and the real cost isn't infrastructure, it's that the two implementations of the same business logic inevitably drift. Kappa is one code path where reprocessing is just replaying the stream. For this fraud use case, I'd go Kappa, but I wouldn't rely on Kafka alone to be the infinite log — I'd land everything into Delta Lake first, let Delta's transaction log and time travel be the durable, replayable history, and have both the real-time scorer and the nightly retraining job read off the same Delta tables. That way I'm not maintaining two versions of the feature logic, which in fraud is exactly where subtle drift causes a model to behave differently in production than it did in training.
questions.example: A specific failure mode this avoids: a Lambda-style batch feature pipeline computes 'transactions in the last 10 minutes' slightly differently from the speed-layer streaming version (different window boundary handling), so the model sees different feature values live than it was trained on — a silent accuracy regression that's hard to detect because both pipelines 'work.'
commonMistakes: Conflates Lambda with simply 'having a batch job' rather than two independently implemented code paths
Assumes Kappa strictly requires Kafka to retain unlimited history instead of using a durable table format as the log
Ignores the reconciliation-drift risk that is Lambda's core weakness
Recommends streaming everywhere regardless of whether the latency requirement justifies the added complexity

Correctly defines Kappa's single-path, replay-from-log mechanism
Identifies Delta Lake's transaction log/time travel as a practical durable log for Kappa
Ties the recommendation to the specific scenario (sub-second scoring + nightly retraining)

questions.title: Applying CAP Theorem to a Real Multi-Region Order Platform
questions.prompt: A retailer runs order-entry systems in two regions and wants both regions to stay writable during a cross-region network partition, with eventual reconciliation. Explain CAP theorem in concrete terms for this system, state which guarantee they are giving up, and describe how you would design the reconciliation so the business can live with the trade-off.
questions.modelAnswer:
CAP theorem says that during an actual network partition, a distributed system can preserve either consistency (every node sees the same data) or availability (every node keeps serving reads and writes), but not both; outside of a partition, the real engineering trade-off most systems actually live with day to day is between consistency and latency, not consistency and availability. Wanting both regions writable during a partition is explicitly choosing AP: availability over consistency. The direct consequence is that the two regions can accept conflicting writes on the same order or the same inventory count during the partition, and there is no way to prevent that while keeping both sides live — the only choice is how you resolve the conflict once connectivity returns.

The design response is to make conflicts resolvable by construction rather than by luck. Use a conflict resolution strategy appropriate to the data: last-writer-wins with a reliable vector clock or HLC (hybrid logical clock) for fields where overwrite is acceptable, but for anything with business meaning — like decrementing inventory — model the operation as a commutative, order-independent delta (an increment/decrement event) rather than an absolute value write, so merging two regions' events doesn't require picking a winner, it just replays both deltas. For orders specifically, assign a region-scoped ID prefix so two regions can never generate colliding primary keys, and run a reconciliation job after the partition heals that detects genuine business conflicts (e.g., the same inventory oversold across regions) and surfaces them for a human or compensating workflow, rather than silently picking one write and discarding the other.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd first correct the framing slightly: CAP is really about behavior during an actual partition, and what the client is describing — wanting both regions writable no matter what — means they've already chosen availability over consistency, whether they've said it explicitly or not. I'd make sure they understand what that costs: during a partition, the two regions can and will accept conflicting writes on the same record, full stop, there's no way around that while both stay live. My job as the architect is making sure that when conflicts happen, they're recoverable rather than silently wrong. For inventory specifically, I'd push hard to model writes as deltas — increments and decrements — instead of absolute values, because deltas from two regions merge cleanly without a human needing to pick a winner. For orders, I'd use region-prefixed IDs so there's never a key collision, and I'd build an explicit reconciliation job that runs after the partition heals and flags real business conflicts, like oversold inventory, instead of quietly discarding one side's write.
commonMistakes: States CAP theorem as 'pick two of three' without clarifying it only strictly applies during an actual partition
Doesn't recognize that wanting both regions writable is an explicit AP choice with a real cost
Proposes last-writer-wins for all data types, including ones (like inventory) where that silently loses information
Has no concrete reconciliation mechanism once the partition heals
keyPoints: States CAP theorem precisely (behavior during a partition, not a permanent three-way tradeoff)
Identifies this scenario as an explicit availability-over-consistency (AP) choice
Proposes delta/commutative writes for conflict-prone numeric state
Proposes collision-proof ID design across regions
Includes a concrete post-partition reconciliation mechanism

evaluationCriteria.criterion: States CAP theorem accurately and concretely

questions.title: Exactly-Once Semantics in a Delta Lake Streaming Pipeline
questions.prompt: A Structured Streaming job writes payment events into a Delta table, and the business requires that no payment is ever double-counted even if the job restarts mid-batch. Explain what 'exactly-once' really means in this context, where the guarantee actually comes from, and where it can still break.
questions.modelAnswer:
Exactly-once in Structured Streaming writing to Delta does not mean the event is read exactly once from the source — a job restart after a failure will almost always re-read events it already processed, because checkpointing commits offsets after a batch succeeds, not before. What it actually means is exactly-once effect: the sink is designed so that reprocessing the same batch produces the same end state as processing it once, which Delta achieves through idempotent writes keyed by the combination of the streaming query's checkpoint location and a deterministic batch/epoch ID that Delta records in the transaction log and refuses to apply twice. The guarantee holds as long as three conditions are true: the source offsets are replayable (Kafka, Event Hubs, Auto Loader with checkpointing), the transformation logic is deterministic given the same input batch, and the checkpoint location is never shared or reused across two different streaming queries writing to the same table.

Where it actually breaks in practice: if the transformation includes a non-deterministic element (a call to an external service, a random UUID generated per row, or a timestamp captured inside the transform rather than from the source event), the retried batch produces different rows than the original attempt, and Delta's idempotent-write check — which matches on batch identity, not row content — will not catch the duplication. It also breaks if someone manually deletes and recreates the checkpoint directory after a failure, because that erases the record of which batches already committed, or if the sink table is written to by more than one streaming query sharing app IDs. For payment data specifically, I would add a belt-and-suspenders application-level dedup key (payment ID) with a MERGE on write, so correctness doesn't depend solely on checkpoint hygiene.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain this carefully because 'exactly-once' is one of the most misunderstood terms in streaming — it doesn't mean the event is only read once, it means reprocessing the same micro-batch produces the same result as processing it once. That guarantee comes from Delta tracking which checkpoint-and-batch-ID combinations have already been committed to the table and refusing to commit the same one twice. Where I've seen it actually break is when the transformation itself isn't deterministic — if you're calling an external API inside the transform, or generating a UUID per row instead of using one from the source event, a retried batch produces different data, and Delta's dedup check won't catch that because it's matching on batch identity, not row content. For something as sensitive as payments, I wouldn't rely on checkpoint semantics alone — I'd add an application-level MERGE keyed on the actual payment ID as a second layer of defense, because that protects correctness even if someone fumbles the checkpoint location during an operational fix.
commonMistakes: Believes exactly-once means the source event is read exactly one time
Doesn't connect the guarantee to checkpoint-location plus batch-ID tracking in the Delta transaction log
Misses that non-deterministic transforms silently break the guarantee
Relies solely on the streaming engine's guarantee with no application-level idempotency key for high-value data

Explains the checkpoint + batch-ID mechanism behind Delta's idempotent writes
Lists the preconditions (replayable source, deterministic transform, dedicated checkpoint)
Identifies non-determinism as the real-world break case
Recommends a belt-and-suspenders application-level dedup for high-stakes data

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines exactly-once effect vs. exactly-once delivery

questions.title: SCD Type 2 at Enterprise Scale in a Lakehouse
questions.prompt: Walk through how you would implement a Type 2 slowly changing dimension for a customer table with hundreds of millions of rows and frequent attribute changes, in a Delta Lake lakehouse that also feeds a Power BI semantic model and a dbt-managed mart, and explain the specific performance and correctness traps at that scale.
questions.modelAnswer:
At enterprise scale, the core mechanics of SCD2 don't change — you still track effective_from, effective_to, and is_current, and you still close out the prior row and insert a new one when a tracked attribute changes — but the implementation has to avoid two things that are cheap to ignore at small scale and expensive at hundreds of millions of rows: full-table rewrites and uncontrolled file fragmentation. I would implement the merge using Delta's MERGE INTO with the match condition scoped to the natural key and is_current = true, so Delta only rewrites the files containing current rows, not the entire table's history — this is the single biggest lever at this scale, because a naive implementation that recomputes the whole dimension nightly turns a few-minute job into an hours-long one as history accumulates. I would also partition or Z-order on the natural key's hash and on is_current, so both the merge's lookup and downstream point-in-time joins can skip irrelevant files.

The correctness traps that show up specifically at scale: dbt's snapshot feature implements SCD2 well for moderate volumes but its default full-table comparison strategy doesn't scale gracefully to hundreds of millions of rows without an explicit, well-chosen check_cols strategy and an incremental source query — you want dbt comparing against only recently-changed source rows, not scanning the entire upstream table every run. On the Power BI side, a Type 2 dimension with high change frequency can balloon far beyond what you'd expect from customer count alone, and if the semantic model's relationships aren't built against a conformed, filtered 'current row' view, you get fan-out and double-counted facts in measures. The other classic trap is clock skew between the source system's change-capture timestamp and the pipeline's processing time — using processing time as effective_from instead of the actual business-event time silently corrupts point-in-time history during any backfill or reprocessing.
questions.professionalAnswer: The mechanics of Type 2 don't change at scale, but I'd be upfront that a naive implementation falls over well before you hit hundreds of millions of rows. My first move is making sure the MERGE INTO only touches is_current rows for the matching keys, not the whole table — that's the difference between a merge that finishes in minutes versus hours once history piles up. I'd also Z-order on the natural key and is_current so both the merge and any downstream point-in-time query can skip files instead of scanning everything. On the dbt side, I've seen teams use the default snapshot strategy and just let it do a full comparison against the entire upstream source every run — that's fine on day one and brutal eighteen months later, so I'd insist on an incremental source query scoped to recently changed rows plus explicit check_cols. And I'd flag early that a high-churn Type 2 dimension can quietly make the Power BI model's cardinality much bigger than the raw customer count suggests, so the semantic layer needs to filter to current rows for standard reporting and only expose full history through a separate, clearly-labeled historical path.

Uses pipeline processing time instead of business-event time for effective_from, corrupting backfills
Lets dbt snapshot scan the full upstream source table instead of an incremental source query
Builds the Power BI model against full dimension history instead of a current-row-filtered view, causing fan-out
No partitioning/Z-order strategy, so merges and point-in-time joins scan far more data than necessary

Scopes the MERGE to avoid full-table rewrites at scale

Identifies event-time vs. processing-time as a correctness trap for backfills
Proposes a concrete partitioning/Z-order strategy

questions.title: Data Mesh vs. Centralized Platform: What Actually Changes
questions.prompt: A VP of Engineering wants to move from a centralized data platform team to a 'data mesh' because they read it reduces bottlenecks. Explain what data mesh actually changes structurally and technically versus a well-run centralized platform, and the conditions under which it genuinely helps rather than just distributing the same problems.
questions.modelAnswer:
Data mesh is primarily an organizational and ownership model wearing a technical costume. The actual change is that domain teams — not a central platform team — own the production, quality, and SLA of the data products from their own business domain, and a central team's job shifts from building and operating every pipeline to building the self-serve infrastructure platform (provisioning, cataloging, governance guardrails) that lets domain teams do that ownership well. Technically, this usually manifests as each domain publishing governed, discoverable 'data products' (often Delta or Iceberg tables with defined schemas, SLAs, and ownership metadata registered in a catalog like Unity Catalog or Purview) rather than a central team owning every ETL job end to end. Federated computational governance — a shared, platform-enforced set of standards for things like PII handling, naming, and interoperability — is what keeps this from degenerating into every domain doing its own incompatible thing.

The condition under which it genuinely helps: the organization is large enough and domain-diverse enough that a single central team has become a real bottleneck because it doesn't understand each domain's business logic well enough to model it correctly, and the business is willing to invest in making domain teams capable of owning data engineering quality (which usually means embedding data engineers in domain teams, not just handing SQL access to analysts). Where it just redistributes the same problems: a mid-sized org adopts the label without the org design change, domain teams get told they 'own' data products but have no engineering capacity or incentive to maintain SLAs, and you end up with the same quality and bottleneck problems, just now inconsistent across a dozen uncoordinated teams instead of centralized in one accountable one. I would tell this VP that the platform work (self-serve infra, governance) has to come first and be funded as its own initiative, or 'mesh' just becomes an excuse to defund the central team without replacing its function.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd push back gently on the premise, because 'data mesh' gets reached for as a technology fix when the actual problem is almost always organizational. The real shift isn't a new tool, it's that domain teams take ownership of their own data product's quality and SLA, and the central team's job changes from building every pipeline to building the self-serve platform and the governance guardrails that make distributed ownership safe. I'd ask this VP directly: are you willing to fund domain teams having real data engineering capacity, and are you willing to invest in the platform and governance layer first? Because if the answer is 'no, we just want to stop being a bottleneck,' what actually happens is you get the same quality and coordination problems, just scattered across more teams with less accountability. I've seen mesh work well exactly once the org was big enough that a central team genuinely couldn't understand every domain's business logic — and I've seen it fail just as often when it was used as cover to defund a central team without replacing its function.
commonMistakes: Treats data mesh as primarily a technology choice rather than an organizational/ownership model
Assumes adopting mesh automatically reduces bottlenecks without funding domain-level engineering capacity
Ignores federated computational governance, leading to incompatible domain-level standards
Recommends mesh for organizations too small or too centralized in business logic to benefit

questions.title: ACID Internals: Delta Lake's Transaction Log vs. Snowflake's MVCC
questions.prompt: Explain, at the mechanism level, how Delta Lake provides ACID guarantees through its transaction log and how Snowflake provides them through its own metadata and versioning model, and explain one practical consequence of the difference for an architect choosing between them for a highly concurrent write workload.
questions.modelAnswer:
Delta Lake provides ACID guarantees through the _delta_log: every write produces a new JSON (and periodically consolidated Parquet checkpoint) commit file describing exactly which data files were added and removed, and the table's state at any version is the deterministic replay of that log. Concurrent writers use optimistic concurrency control — each writer reads the table version it started from, prepares its change, and on commit checks whether any conflicting commit landed in between; if a true conflict exists (two writers touching overlapping files/partitions), one fails and must retry, otherwise Delta reconciles non-overlapping concurrent commits automatically. Isolation is effectively snapshot isolation: readers always see a consistent version as of the moment they started, never a partial write.

Snowflake provides ACID guarantees through its own proprietary metadata layer sitting above immutable micro-partitions: every DML statement creates new micro-partitions rather than mutating existing ones, and a transaction's visibility is controlled by Snowflake's internal metadata service, which also underlies Time Travel. Snowflake's concurrency model also uses a form of snapshot isolation but is fully managed — there is no user-visible log to reason about or periodically checkpoint, and conflict handling for concurrent DML against the same table is handled internally with its own retry/locking semantics specific to Snowflake's engine.

The practical consequence for a highly concurrent write workload: Delta's optimistic concurrency means many small, frequently-conflicting concurrent writers against the same table (or the same partitions) will see elevated commit-retry rates and potential throughput degradation unless you deliberately partition writers apart (different tables, different partitions, or a serialization pattern like a dedicated streaming writer); this is a real design constraint you have to account for explicitly in a Databricks/Delta architecture. Snowflake abstracts this concurrency management away from the architect entirely — it's simpler to reason about for highly concurrent OLTP-adjacent write patterns, but you give up visibility into and control over exactly how conflicts are resolved, and you can't tune it with partitioning the way you can with Delta.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through the mechanism difference directly because it actually changes how I'd design around concurrent writes. Delta's guarantees come from the transaction log — every commit is a record of exactly which files were added and removed, and concurrent writers use optimistic concurrency, meaning they only find out at commit time whether they conflicted with someone else, and if they did, they retry. That's powerful because it's an open, inspectable log, but it also means I have to actively design to avoid two writers fighting over the same partitions, or I'll see commit retries pile up under heavy concurrent write load. Snowflake does something conceptually similar — snapshot isolation over immutable micro-partitions — but it's entirely managed inside Snowflake's engine, so as an architect I don't get to see or tune the conflict resolution directly. My practical takeaway for a client choosing between them: if you expect genuinely high-concurrency writes against the same table, Snowflake gives you less to worry about operationally, while Delta gives you more control but requires you to actively architect around write contention — separate streaming writers from batch writers, partition deliberately — rather than assuming it'll just work at scale.

Assumes Snowflake has no concurrency control because the user doesn't see it
Fails to connect the mechanism difference to a concrete architectural consequence
Assumes both platforms behave identically under concurrent write contention

questions.title: Comparing Governance Models: Unity Catalog, Snowflake RBAC, and Purview
questions.prompt: An enterprise runs Databricks, Snowflake, and Power BI side by side. Compare Unity Catalog's governance model, Snowflake's native RBAC and tagging model, and Microsoft Purview's role as a cross-platform catalog, and explain where a single source of governance truth should actually live in this environment.
questions.modelAnswer:
Unity Catalog governs Databricks-native assets (tables, volumes, models, notebooks) with a three-level namespace (catalog.schema.table), grants expressed in standard GRANT/REVOKE SQL, and automatic column-level lineage across every query that runs through Databricks compute, plus row/column-level security via row filters and column masks defined once and enforced consistently regardless of which tool queries the table. Snowflake's native model is also RBAC-based (roles granted to users, privileges granted to roles) with its own object tagging, masking policies, and row access policies, and its own internal lineage captured through ACCESS_HISTORY and object dependencies — technically comparable in capability to Unity Catalog, but scoped entirely to Snowflake's own objects. Purview is different in kind: it is a cross-platform metadata catalog and scanning service that can crawl Databricks, Snowflake, Power BI, and many other sources to build a unified, searchable catalog with lineage stitched across systems, but it is fundamentally a catalog and discovery layer, not an enforcement engine — it does not itself grant or deny query-time access inside Databricks or Snowflake.

In this environment, there cannot be one single system that is simultaneously the enforcement point for both Databricks and Snowflake, because each platform enforces its own access control natively and neither can enforce policy inside the other. The pragmatic answer is to accept two enforcement points (Unity Catalog for everything Databricks-native, Snowflake RBAC for everything Snowflake-native) with consistent policy definitions maintained as code across both — the same PII classification and masking rule implemented once in each platform's own policy language — and use Purview as the single pane of glass for discovery, lineage, and compliance reporting across both, not as the thing that actually blocks a query. Power BI's own row-level security then becomes a third enforcement layer specifically for the semantic model, which should mirror, not reinvent, the underlying platform's access rules to avoid a user seeing different data depending on which layer they hit.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd be direct that there's no single tool here that enforces access across all three platforms — that's just not how any of them work. Unity Catalog enforces access and lineage for everything living in Databricks, Snowflake's RBAC does the same for everything in Snowflake, and neither one can reach into the other. Purview's role is different: it's a catalog and discovery layer that can crawl and stitch lineage across both plus Power BI, but it doesn't actually block a query — so I wouldn't present it to leadership as 'the governance system,' I'd present it as 'the governance visibility system.' My actual recommendation is to accept two real enforcement points, keep the policy definitions — PII classification, masking rules — defined consistently as code so they're implemented the same way in both platforms even though they're technically two separate policy engines, and use Purview as the compliance team's single pane of glass for proving that consistency rather than as the enforcement mechanism itself. And I'd make sure Power BI's row-level security mirrors the underlying data platform's rules rather than inventing its own, because that's the classic way a user ends up seeing different numbers depending on which tool they query.

Treats Unity Catalog and Snowflake RBAC as interchangeable with no platform-boundary limitation

questions.title: One Semantic Layer or Two? dbt Semantic Layer vs. Power BI Models
questions.prompt: The analytics engineering team maintains metric definitions in the dbt Semantic Layer, and the BI team maintains a parallel set of measures inside a large Power BI semantic model. Explain the real risk of running both, and describe the architecture you would recommend to get to one source of truth for metric logic.
questions.modelAnswer:
The risk of running both is not theoretical — it is the single most common cause of 'why do two dashboards show different revenue numbers' escalations in organizations that have both a mature dbt practice and a mature Power BI practice. A metric like 'active customer' or 'net revenue' ends up with two independent implementations of the same business logic: one expressed as a dbt metric/semantic-layer definition compiled to SQL, and one expressed as a DAX measure inside the Power BI model, and the two will drift the moment either team changes a filter condition, a currency conversion step, or an edge-case exclusion without telling the other. Neither team is wrong in isolation; the architecture is wrong for allowing two independent authorities over the same business definition.

The recommended direction is to make the dbt Semantic Layer the single authority for metric definitions and logic, and have Power BI consume those metrics rather than reimplement them — either via the dbt Semantic Layer's supported query interfaces feeding a DirectQuery or import-mode table that Power BI then only visualizes, or at minimum by generating the DAX measure definitions from the dbt metric YAML in CI so they're mechanically kept in sync rather than manually maintained in two places. Where this gets nuanced is performance and modeling flexibility: Power BI's in-memory VertiPaq engine and its relationship model exist for a reason — fast interactive slicing, time intelligence, and row-level security at the visualization layer — so the realistic end state is usually a hybrid: dimensional structure and simple additive aggregations stay as Power BI model relationships for performance, while the actual business-logic-heavy metric calculations (anything with complex filters, exclusions, or multi-step business rules) are defined once in dbt and surfaced into the model as pre-computed columns or synced measures, not reinvented in DAX. I would present this as a multi-quarter migration with the dbt metrics behind a small number of high-visibility, frequently-disputed metrics first — not a rip-and-replace of the entire Power BI model.
questions.professionalAnswer: I've seen this exact situation cause real credibility damage with executives — two teams, two definitions of 'active customer,' two dashboards, and a VP asking in a leadership meeting why they don't match. My answer is always the same: pick one authority for the logic, and I'd argue strongly for that being the dbt Semantic Layer, because it's version-controlled, tested, and already the place where the transformation logic for that metric lives upstream. Power BI shouldn't reinvent that logic in DAX — it should consume it. That said, I wouldn't pretend Power BI's engine is irrelevant; it's genuinely good at fast interactive slicing and row-level security, so I'd keep dimensional relationships and simple aggregations in the model itself and only migrate the metrics that actually cause disputes — the ones leadership has caught in a mismatch — first. I'd frame it as a prioritized migration, not a full rebuild, because trying to move every DAX measure to dbt metrics at once is a multi-quarter project that will stall if I pitch it as all-or-nothing.

questions.title: Batch, Micro-Batch, or True Streaming: Matching Latency to SLA
questions.prompt: Explain the real differences between batch, micro-batch, and continuous (true) streaming processing, and describe a framework for deciding which one a given enterprise use case actually needs instead of defaulting to whichever is most fashionable.
questions.modelAnswer:
Batch processing runs on a schedule against a bounded dataset and optimizes for throughput and simplicity at the cost of latency — the result is only as fresh as the last run. Micro-batch, Structured Streaming's default trigger model, processes the stream in small bounded chunks on a short fixed or available-now interval (seconds to low minutes), giving most of batch's operational simplicity, exactly-once-style guarantees, and mature tooling, with latency in the seconds-to-minutes range. True continuous/streaming processing (Spark's experimental continuous mode, Flink, or a dedicated event-processing engine) processes each record as it arrives with latency in the tens of milliseconds, but at real cost: weaker fault-tolerance guarantees in some engines' continuous modes, more operational complexity, and often a narrower set of supported operations (certain joins or aggregations aren't available in true continuous mode the way they are in micro-batch).

The decision framework is to work backward from the actual business SLA, not the latency the engineering team finds most interesting to build: if the consuming process is a human looking at a dashboard, anything under roughly 5-15 seconds of freshness is imperceptible to the business value and micro-batch is the right default — it is simpler to operate, debug, and reason about, and the tooling (Structured Streaming, Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines) is mature. If the consuming process is a machine making a decision with real financial or safety consequence within a tight window — fraud blocking a transaction, a trading system reacting to a price feed, an industrial safety cutoff — then the latency requirement is intrinsic to the use case and justifies true streaming's added complexity. The two traps I watch for: teams reaching for true continuous streaming because it's technically impressive when a 30-second micro-batch would satisfy the actual SLA and be far easier to operate and debug, and the opposite trap, teams defaulting to nightly batch for something that's actually gating a real-time customer-facing decision just because that's the existing pipeline pattern in the organization.
questions.professionalAnswer: I always start this conversation by asking who or what actually consumes the data and how fast they need it, because that answer should drive the architecture, not the other way around. If it's a person looking at a dashboard, the difference between five seconds and thirty seconds of freshness is invisible to them, so I default to micro-batch — Structured Streaming's standard trigger model — because it's dramatically easier to operate, debug, and reason about than true continuous processing, and the guarantees are stronger. I only reach for true continuous or an engine like Flink when the consumer is a machine making a real-time decision with a tight SLA baked into the use case itself — fraud blocking a transaction before it clears, for example. The trap I actively watch for on my own teams is engineers wanting to build the more sophisticated streaming system because it's more interesting, when the actual business requirement would be satisfied just fine by a boring micro-batch job that's much cheaper to run and maintain.
commonMistakes: Treats 'streaming' as a single category rather than distinguishing micro-batch from true continuous processing
Defaults to the most technically sophisticated option without checking the actual business SLA
Ignores the reduced operational maturity/narrower operation support of true continuous processing engines
Assumes nightly batch is always acceptable for anything not explicitly labeled 'real-time'
keyPoints: Correctly distinguishes batch, micro-batch, and true continuous processing
States realistic latency and tradeoff profiles for each
Proposes a decision framework anchored on actual consumer/SLA, not technical preference
Names the over-engineering trap (continuous streaming where micro-batch suffices)
Names the under-engineering trap (batch where real-time is actually required)

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Accurately distinguishes the three processing models
States realistic tradeoffs for each
Proposes a sound SLA-driven decision framework
Identifies both over- and under-engineering traps

questions.title: Why Data Contracts Matter Once You Have More Than One Producing Team
questions.prompt: Explain what a data contract actually is beyond 'documentation,' why enterprises adopt them once they have multiple teams producing data for shared consumption, and how you would enforce one technically rather than just writing it down in a wiki.
questions.modelAnswer:
A data contract is a versioned, machine-checkable specification of a dataset's schema, semantics, and service-level expectations — field names and types, nullability, valid value ranges, the business meaning of key fields, freshness SLA, and what counts as a breaking versus non-breaking change — agreed between the producing team and its consumers, and enforced at the point the data is published, not discovered after a downstream dashboard breaks. The reason enterprises adopt them once more than one team produces shared data is that without a contract, the only thing binding a producer to a consumer's expectations is informal communication, and informal communication reliably fails at organizational scale: a producing team renames a column, changes an enum's valid values, or starts emitting nulls where there used to be zeros, ships it because it passed their own tests, and a downstream dbt model or Power BI report silently breaks or silently produces wrong numbers days later with no one aware a contract was violated.

Enforcing a contract technically means it has to be checked automatically at a gate the producer cannot bypass: schema and expectation checks run in the producing pipeline's CI (for example, a dbt contract on a model's columns and types, or Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines expectations that fail or quarantine data violating the agreed shape) before the change can be deployed, and ideally the same specification is registered in the catalog (Unity Catalog comments/tags, or a schema registry for streaming sources) so consumers can discover what they're actually bound to rather than trusting tribal knowledge. The critical design decision is what happens on a violation: a hard contract fails the producing pipeline and blocks the bad data from ever landing, which protects correctness but can halt an upstream team's deploy; a soft contract quarantines or flags the violation and lets the pipeline continue, which protects uptime but requires someone to actually look at the quarantine. I generally recommend hard contracts for a small set of genuinely load-bearing enterprise tables (anything executive dashboards or financial reporting depend on) and soft/monitored contracts everywhere else, because treating every dataset as equally critical just trains teams to ignore the alerts.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd define it precisely because 'data contract' gets used loosely: it's a versioned, enforced specification of a dataset's schema and expectations, agreed between whoever produces it and whoever consumes it, and the enforcement part is what separates it from documentation. A wiki page describing a schema doesn't stop someone from quietly renaming a column — it just tells people what was true as of whenever it was last updated. A real contract is checked automatically, in CI, at the point of publish, so a breaking change can't ship without either failing the build or triggering an explicit versioning decision. I push hard for this once an org has more than one team producing data other teams depend on, because informal 'let's just talk about changes' genuinely does not survive past a handful of teams — someone always ships a change without realizing who's downstream. On enforcement strictness, I don't treat every table the same: for the handful of tables that feed executive or financial reporting, I want a hard contract that blocks a bad deploy outright; for everything else, a monitored soft contract that flags violations is usually the right balance, because if everything is a hard stop, teams start finding ways to route around the gate.
questions.example: A real scenario this prevents: a source team changes a status field's valid values from ('active','inactive') to also include 'paused' without telling anyone; a downstream dbt model's CASE statement treats 'paused' as an unhandled default and silently miscategorizes those customers in an executive churn dashboard for three weeks before anyone notices the enum changed.
commonMistakes: Describes a data contract as documentation rather than an enforced, machine-checkable specification
Has no concrete technical enforcement mechanism (CI gate, pipeline expectations)
Treats every dataset as equally deserving of a hard-fail contract, which trains teams to bypass the gate
Ignores versioning/breaking-vs-non-breaking-change definition as part of the contract
keyPoints: Defines a data contract as versioned and machine-enforced, not documentation
Explains why informal communication fails once multiple teams produce shared data
Describes a concrete technical enforcement mechanism (CI gate, pipeline expectations, registry)
Distinguishes hard-fail from soft/quarantine enforcement and when to use each
Addresses breaking vs. non-breaking change versioning

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines a data contract as enforced, not just documented
Explains the organizational failure mode it solves
Proposes a concrete enforcement mechanism
Distinguishes enforcement strictness by criticality

questions.title: Design a Metadata-Driven Pipeline Framework
questions.prompt: Rather than writing a separate pipeline for each of 200 source tables feeding a Fabric lakehouse, design a metadata-driven orchestration framework that can onboard a new source by adding a configuration row instead of writing new pipeline code. Show the control-table shape you'd use and the pipeline logic that reads it.
questions.code:
-- Control table (Lakehouse or Fabric SQL DB)
CREATE TABLE dbo.PipelineConfig (
    SourceId INT IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    SourceSystem VARCHAR(50),
    SourceSchema VARCHAR(100),
    SourceTable VARCHAR(200),
    TargetLakehouse VARCHAR(100),
    TargetTable VARCHAR(200),
    LoadType VARCHAR(20),        -- 'FULL' or 'INCREMENTAL'
    WatermarkColumn VARCHAR(100),
    PrimaryKeyColumns VARCHAR(500),
    IsActive BIT,
    LastWatermarkValue DATETIME2,
    LastRunStatus VARCHAR(20)
);
questions.modelAnswer: The framework is built around a single control table that describes every source's identity, load strategy, and incremental watermark, read at the start of each orchestration run by one generic pipeline (an ADF/Fabric Data Factory 'ForEach' over an active-sources lookup) rather than one pipeline per table. The Lookup activity selects all rows where IsActive = 1, the ForEach iterates with a concurrency limit appropriate to the source system's throughput tolerance, and inside the loop a single parameterized Copy/Dataflow activity receives the source schema, table, load type, and watermark column as parameters rather than having them hardcoded — so onboarding table 201 is an INSERT into the control table, not a new pipeline. For incremental loads, the pipeline reads LastWatermarkValue from the control row, builds a dynamic WHERE clause (or uses CDC/change-tracking metadata where the source supports it) bounded by that watermark and the current run's start time, and on successful completion writes the new high-water mark back to the same control row — critically, inside the same logical unit of work as the load's success, so a failed load never advances the watermark and silently skips data on the next run. LastRunStatus and a separate audit/log table capture row counts and duration per run for operational visibility, and a stored procedure or Fabric notebook step handles schema-drift detection by comparing the source's current schema to a cached prior schema before the load, raising an explicit alert rather than letting a new or renamed column silently fail or get silently dropped.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd build this around one control table that holds everything the pipeline needs to know about a source — load type, watermark column, where it's landing — and one generic orchestration pipeline that loops over the active rows in that table with a parameterized copy activity inside. Onboarding source 201 becomes a row insert, not a deployment. The part I'd be most careful about is the watermark update: I only ever advance LastWatermarkValue after I've confirmed the load actually succeeded, in the same transactional step, because the classic bug in these frameworks is advancing the watermark optimistically and then silently losing data on a retry after a partial failure. I'd also build in explicit schema-drift detection rather than letting an unexpected new column just get silently dropped by the copy activity — I want that to raise an alert I can see, not fail quietly three weeks later when someone asks why a new field isn't showing up downstream.
questions.example: Onboarding a new Salesforce object into the framework: one INSERT into PipelineConfig with SourceSystem='Salesforce', LoadType='INCREMENTAL', WatermarkColumn='LastModifiedDate' — no pipeline code change, the next scheduled run picks it up automatically via the ForEach's Lookup.
commonMistakes: Advances the watermark before confirming the load actually succeeded, risking silent data loss on retry
Hardcodes source-specific logic inside the generic pipeline instead of passing it as parameters from the control table
No concurrency limit on the ForEach, overwhelming a source system when many tables trigger at once
No schema-drift detection, letting new or renamed source columns silently fail or get dropped
keyPoints: Defines a control-table-driven design with one generic parameterized pipeline
Explains watermark-based incremental load logic correctly
Ties watermark advancement to confirmed success, not optimistic completion
Includes audit/logging and schema-drift detection as first-class concerns
Shows how onboarding a new source avoids new pipeline code

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Produces a sound control-table schema
Correctly explains the generic parameterized pipeline pattern
Gets watermark advancement/failure handling correct
Addresses schema drift and operational visibility

questions.title: Design Unity Catalog Grants for Row- and Column-Level Security
questions.prompt: A finance analytics table in Unity Catalog must let regional controllers see only their own region's rows, mask the SSN column for everyone except the payroll role, and give data scientists full column access but only to an anonymized row sample. Write the SQL you'd use to implement this.
questions.modelAnswer: This design uses three distinct Unity Catalog mechanisms for three distinct requirements, deliberately not conflated into one. Row-level security is implemented with a SQL row-filter function attached via ALTER TABLE ... SET ROW FILTER, which Unity Catalog evaluates for every query against the table regardless of whether the caller is Databricks SQL, a notebook, or a BI tool connecting through the same catalog — the function itself checks group membership first (so payroll admins see everything) and falls back to a region match against a current_user_region() lookup function, which in practice resolves the caller's region from a mapping table keyed on their principal, not from a client-supplied parameter that a user could spoof. Column masking for the SSN uses SET MASK with a function that again checks group membership and returns either the real value or a redacted format — the critical property is that this mask is enforced at the table level once and applies no matter which tool or query touches the column, so there's no way to bypass it by querying from a different client. For data scientists, rather than trying to build row/column security rules that produce 'anonymized but still analytically useful' data on the fly, I expose a separate, physically distinct sampled view (TABLESAMPLE) and grant access to that view only, which is simpler to reason about and avoids accidentally leaking a masking function's edge cases into a dataset meant for broader exploratory access. All three mechanisms are defined once, centrally, and enforced identically regardless of the querying tool, which is the entire point of doing this in Unity Catalog instead of per-tool application logic.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd implement each of these three requirements with the mechanism actually built for it rather than trying to force one general rule to do everything. Row-level security for regional controllers is a row filter function — I'd make sure it checks group membership for payroll admins first, and resolves the caller's region from a lookup table rather than trusting anything the client passes in, because a client-supplied region parameter is trivially spoofable. SSN masking is a column mask function with the same group-membership check, and the advantage of doing it this way instead of in application code is that it's enforced centrally no matter which tool queries the table — Databricks SQL, a notebook, Power BI through a Databricks connector, it doesn't matter. For the data scientist use case, I wouldn't try to get clever with a row filter that also anonymizes — I'd just expose a separate sampled view and grant access to that view specifically, because it's much easier to audit 'this role can see this view' than to reason about interacting row filters and masks producing an anonymized sample on the fly.
commonMistakes: Resolves the user's region from a client-supplied parameter instead of a server-side lookup, which is spoofable
Implements masking in application/BI-tool code instead of centrally in Unity Catalog, so it can be bypassed by another client
Tries to combine row filtering and anonymization into one function instead of a separate sampled view, making the logic hard to audit
Forgets that payroll_admin needs an explicit bypass in both the row filter and the mask functions
keyPoints: Uses Unity Catalog row filter functions correctly for region-based RLS
Uses column mask functions correctly for SSN redaction
Resolves user context server-side, not from a spoofable client parameter
Separates the anonymized-sample use case into its own view rather than overloading the masking logic
Recognizes enforcement is centralized regardless of querying tool

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct row-filter implementation for regional RLS
Correct column-mask implementation for SSN
Sound approach for the data-scientist anonymized-sample requirement
Addresses spoofing risk and centralized enforcement

questions.title: Write a Scoped SCD2 MERGE Against a Massive Delta Dimension
questions.prompt: Write the Delta MERGE statement that implements Type 2 history for a customer dimension with hundreds of millions of rows, structured so it only touches current-row files rather than rewriting the whole table's history.
questions.code:
MERGE INTO dim_customer AS target
USING (
  SELECT s.*, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP() AS load_ts
  FROM staging_customer s
) AS source
ON target.customer_key = source.customer_key
   AND target.is_current = true
WHEN MATCHED AND (
    target.email <> source.email OR
    target.address <> source.address OR
    target.tier <> source.tier
) THEN UPDATE SET
    target.is_current = false,
    target.effective_to = source.load_ts
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (
    customer_key, email, address, tier, effective_from, effective_to, is_current
) VALUES (
    source.customer_key, source.email, source.address, source.tier,
    source.load_ts, NULL, true
);

-- Second pass: insert the new current row for every customer just closed out
INSERT INTO dim_customer
SELECT s.customer_key, s.email, s.address, s.tier, s.load_ts, NULL, true
FROM staging_customer s
JOIN dim_customer d
  ON d.customer_key = s.customer_key AND d.is_current = false AND d.effective_to = s.load_ts;
questions.modelAnswer: The key design decision is the ON clause: by matching on both the natural key and is_current = true, Delta's merge planner can prune to only the files containing current rows for the keys present in the incoming batch, rather than scanning and potentially rewriting the entire historical table — this is what keeps the operation fast at hundreds of millions of rows as history accumulates over years. A single MERGE statement cannot both close out the old row and insert the new version of the same key in one pass, because MERGE applies at most one action per matched source row; the standard pattern is therefore two steps: the MERGE closes out the current row (setting is_current = false and effective_to) when a tracked attribute changed, and inserts genuinely new customers outright, and a second INSERT statement — scoped only to the keys just closed out — adds the new current row for anyone whose attributes changed. For this to perform well at scale, the table should be partitioned or Z-ordered on a hash of customer_key combined with is_current, so both the merge's target-side lookup and the second insert's join are limited to a small slice of files rather than scanning the full history. I would also add a liquid-clustering or Z-order maintenance job on a schedule, since the current-row partition specifically churns with every run and will fragment into many small files without periodic OPTIMIZE.
questions.professionalAnswer: The thing I'd get right first is the ON clause — matching on the key plus is_current = true is what lets Delta prune to just the current-row files instead of touching the whole multi-hundred-million-row history on every run. I'd also flag immediately that you can't do the full Type 2 flip in one MERGE statement, because a single MERGE only applies one action per source row — so I split it into the MERGE that closes out changed rows and inserts brand-new customers, followed by a second, narrowly-scoped INSERT that adds the new current version for exactly the customers that just got closed out. At this scale I wouldn't skip table maintenance either — the current-row slice churns every single run, so without a regular OPTIMIZE or liquid clustering pass it fragments into a huge number of small files and the merge gets slower every month even though the logic hasn't changed.
commonMistakes: Matches only on the natural key without is_current, forcing a full-history scan on every merge
Tries to close out the old row and insert the new version in a single MERGE statement, which isn't possible
No partitioning/clustering strategy, letting the current-row slice fragment into many small files over time
Compares all columns generically instead of only the attributes that should trigger a new historical version
keyPoints: Scopes the MERGE's ON clause to prune to current-row files
Correctly splits close-out and new-row-insert into two steps
Compares only the attributes meant to trigger a new version
Addresses partitioning/clustering and ongoing file maintenance at scale

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct, scoped MERGE logic for Type 2 close-out
Correctly handles the two-step close-out/insert pattern
Addresses performance at scale (pruning, clustering)
Addresses ongoing file maintenance (OPTIMIZE/liquid clustering)

questions.title: Write a Reusable dbt Macro for a Governed Metric
questions.prompt: Multiple dbt models need the same 'net revenue' calculation (gross minus returns minus discounts, excluding internal test accounts), and three different analysts have already implemented slightly different versions of it in separate models. Write a dbt macro that becomes the single implementation, and show how a model would call it.
questions.code:
-- macros/net_revenue.sql
{% macro net_revenue(gross_col, returns_col, discount_col, is_test_col) %}
    case
        when {{ is_test_col }} = true then 0
        else coalesce({{ gross_col }}, 0)
             - coalesce({{ returns_col }}, 0)
             - coalesce({{ discount_col }}, 0)
    end
{% endmacro %}

-- models/marts/fct_order_revenue.sql
select
    order_id,
    order_date,
    {{ net_revenue('gross_amount', 'returns_amount', 'discount_amount', 'is_test_account') }} as net_revenue
from {{ ref('stg_orders') }}
questions.modelAnswer: The macro parameterizes the column names rather than hardcoding a table's specific columns, which means it can be reused across every model that has a gross/returns/discount/is-test shape without copy-pasting the CASE logic, and critically it becomes the one place the business rule lives — if 'exclude test accounts' or the discount treatment changes, it changes in exactly one file and every downstream model picks it up on the next run. Beyond just writing the macro, the governance step that actually prevents drift is enforcing its use: I would add a dbt test (a custom singular test or a check against the compiled SQL) that fails CI if a model computes a revenue-shaped column without calling this macro, and I'd document the macro's business definition directly in its schema.yml description so it shows up in the dbt docs site as the authoritative definition analysts can discover instead of reinventing. For this specific scenario — three analysts already shipped divergent versions — the migration isn't just 'write the macro,' it's auditing each existing model's CASE logic against the new macro's output on historical data, reconciling any difference (which usually surfaces a real disagreement about how discounts or test accounts should be handled that needs a business decision, not just a technical merge), and then replacing all three with calls to the macro in the same PR so there's no window where four versions coexist.
questions.professionalAnswer: Writing the macro is the easy part — parameterize the column names so it's reusable, put the actual business logic in exactly one place. The harder and more important part is what happens next: with three analysts already having shipped slightly different versions, I wouldn't just add the macro and call it done, because now there are four implementations floating around. I'd pull the historical output of all three existing versions, diff them against what the new macro produces, and treat any difference as a real business question to resolve — maybe one version was actually right about something the others missed — rather than just picking the newest one and overwriting silently. Once that's resolved, I replace all three models to call the macro in the same change, and I'd add a lightweight CI check that flags any new model computing something that looks like revenue without going through this macro, because otherwise we're back here again in six months.
commonMistakes: Hardcodes column names in the macro instead of parameterizing it, limiting reuse
Adds the macro but doesn't migrate or reconcile the three existing divergent implementations
Treats reconciling the three versions as a pure merge instead of surfacing real business disagreements for a decision
No CI/governance mechanism to prevent a fourth divergent implementation from appearing later
keyPoints: Writes a properly parameterized, reusable macro
Documents the macro as the authoritative business definition in dbt docs
Proposes reconciling existing divergent implementations against the new macro's output
Treats discrepancies as business decisions, not silent overwrites
Proposes a governance mechanism to prevent future drift

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Writes a correct, reusable dbt macro
Proposes a sound migration/reconciliation plan for existing versions
Treats discrepancies as business decisions requiring judgment
Proposes an ongoing governance mechanism

questions.title: Design a Snowflake Secure Data Share for a Partner
questions.prompt: A retail partner needs read access to a curated subset of your sales data, refreshed daily, without you giving them a copy of the data or a login to your account. Write the Snowflake objects you'd create to do this via Secure Data Sharing, and explain why it's architecturally different from exporting a file.
questions.modelAnswer: Secure Data Sharing exposes a live, read-only pointer to Snowflake's own storage metadata to the consumer's account, rather than copying any bytes — the partner's account creates a database from the share and queries it directly against the same underlying micro-partitions my account owns, so there is no export file, no staging bucket, no ETL job moving data between organizations, and critically no stale copy sitting in the partner's environment the day after I update the source table. This is architecturally different from a file export in three ways that matter for an architect: freshness (the partner always sees the current state of the secure view, with zero replication lag, versus a file that's stale the moment it's written), cost (the partner's queries against the share consume their own compute warehouse credits, not mine, so I'm not paying to serve their analytical workload), and revocation (I can drop the share or revoke the grant instantly and their access disappears immediately, versus a file export where they already have a copy I can never truly take back). The secure view is the governance boundary — I never grant the share direct access to the base table, only to a view that's explicitly scoped to that partner's rows and the specific columns I'm willing to expose, and because it's a secure view (not a standard view), Snowflake prevents the partner from reverse-engineering the underlying query logic or seeing more than the filtered result set even through query profiling.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain the core difference up front: a data share isn't a copy of data, it's a live, read-only pointer into my account's storage that their account can query directly. That changes the whole conversation with the partner, in a good way — they're always seeing current data, there's no nightly export job for me to maintain and no stale file sitting in their S3 bucket. I'd always put a secure view between the share and the base table, scoped to exactly their partner_id and the columns I actually want them to see, never grant the share on the base table directly — and I'd use a secure view specifically, not a regular view, because a regular view can leak query plan details that let a sophisticated consumer infer more about the underlying table than I intended. The other thing I'd flag to the business: their queries run on their own warehouse, so I'm not footing the compute bill for their analytics, and if the relationship ever ends, I drop the share and their access is gone immediately — nothing like trying to claw back a CSV that already left the building.
questions.example: If the partner needs their own custom transformations on top of the shared data without me building each one, Snowflake's secure views can also be layered: the partner creates their own views on top of the shared database in their own account, with zero additional work on my side.
commonMistakes: Grants the share access directly on the base table instead of through a scoped secure view
Uses a standard view instead of a secure view, risking query-plan leakage of underlying logic
Describes data sharing as equivalent to an export/copy rather than a live pointer to the same storage
Ignores that the consumer's queries run on their own compute, not the sharer's
keyPoints: Correctly explains Secure Data Sharing as a live pointer, not a copy
Uses a secure view as the governance boundary, scoped to the partner
Explains freshness, cost, and revocation advantages over a file export
Notes the consumer bears their own compute cost
Uses the correct Snowflake share/grant syntax

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct Snowflake share/secure-view SQL
Explains the live-pointer vs. copy distinction accurately

Uses secure view correctly as the governance boundary

questions.title: Design a Partitioning and Clustering Strategy for a Multi-TB Delta Table
questions.prompt: A fact table of IoT sensor readings grows by roughly 2 billion rows a day and is queried mostly by device_id over a recent date range, but occasionally by analysts scanning a full year across all devices. Write the table design and maintenance commands you'd use, and justify the partitioning choice.
questions.modelAnswer: Partitioning by reading_date, not device_id, is the correct choice here even though device_id is the more common filter in isolation, because date-based partitioning aligns with how the data is actually written (append-only, time-ordered, ingested daily) and how it ages out — at 2 billion rows a day, device_id partitioning would produce an enormous number of small partitions per device per day and would not help the yearly full-scan queries at all, while date partitioning keeps each partition a reasonable size and lets both query patterns benefit: the device-filtered recent-range queries prune to a handful of date partitions, and the yearly full-scans at least scan a bounded, predictable set of partitions rather than an explosion of tiny device-level ones. For the device_id filtering within a partition, liquid clustering (CLUSTER BY) rather than Z-ORDER is the better fit for a table that's actively and continuously being written to, because liquid clustering incrementally maintains clustering as new data lands without requiring a full table rewrite the way Z-ORDER via OPTIMIZE does — it's designed specifically for high-ingest-rate tables like this one. The weekly OPTIMIZE job is scoped to only the most recent partitions, because older partitions are already well-compacted and re-optimizing them is wasted compute at this scale; VACUUM with a retention window balances storage cost against the ability to time-travel or recover from an accidental bad write, and extending deletedFileRetentionDuration slightly past the default protects against a concurrent long-running query being invalidated by VACUUM removing files it's still reading.
questions.professionalAnswer: My instinct would be to partition by device_id since that's the more common single-query filter, but at this ingest rate that's actually the wrong call — 2 billion rows a day partitioned by device would create a huge number of tiny partitions and wouldn't help the full-year scans at all. Partitioning by reading_date matches how the data is actually written and ages, and it still helps the device-filtered queries because they prune to a handful of recent date partitions. For the device_id access pattern within a partition, I'd use liquid clustering instead of a traditional Z-ORDER OPTIMIZE, specifically because this table is being written to continuously — liquid clustering keeps itself maintained incrementally without needing a full rewrite, which matters a lot once you're talking multi-terabyte scale. And I'd scope my OPTIMIZE job to just the last week of partitions, because re-optimizing a year of already-compacted history every run is pure wasted compute.
commonMistakes: Partitions by device_id, producing an excessive number of small partitions at this ingest rate
Uses Z-ORDER/OPTIMIZE on the full table history repeatedly instead of liquid clustering or a scoped recent-partition OPTIMIZE
Runs VACUUM with an aggressive retention window that risks invalidating long-running concurrent queries
Ignores that the yearly full-scan query pattern should also factor into the partitioning decision, not just the device filter
keyPoints: Correctly chooses date-based partitioning over device_id at this scale/ingest rate
Uses liquid clustering appropriately for a continuously-written table
Scopes OPTIMIZE to recent partitions rather than the full table
Sets a sensible VACUUM retention balancing cost and safety
Justifies the design against both stated query patterns, not just one

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct partitioning choice with sound justification
Correct clustering approach (liquid clustering vs. Z-ORDER) for this workload
Sound OPTIMIZE/VACUUM maintenance strategy
Addresses both stated query patterns

questions.title: Write a T-SQL Window Function for an Enterprise Cohort Report
questions.prompt: Write a T-SQL query that produces a monthly customer-retention cohort report (percentage of each signup month's customers still active in each subsequent month) directly against an enterprise OLTP-replica table, optimized so it doesn't require a full table scan on every run.
questions.code:
WITH cohorts AS (
    SELECT
        customer_id,
        DATEFROMPARTS(YEAR(signup_date), MONTH(signup_date), 1) AS cohort_month
    FROM dbo.customers
),
activity AS (
    SELECT
        customer_id,
        DATEFROMPARTS(YEAR(activity_date), MONTH(activity_date), 1) AS active_month
    FROM dbo.customer_activity
    WHERE activity_date >= DATEADD(MONTH, -24, GETDATE())
)
SELECT
    c.cohort_month,
    DATEDIFF(MONTH, c.cohort_month, a.active_month) AS months_since_signup,
    COUNT(DISTINCT a.customer_id) AS active_customers,
    COUNT(DISTINCT a.customer_id) * 1.0
      / FIRST_VALUE(COUNT(DISTINCT a.customer_id)) OVER (
            PARTITION BY c.cohort_month
            ORDER BY DATEDIFF(MONTH, c.cohort_month, a.active_month)
        ) AS retention_pct
FROM cohorts c
JOIN activity a ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id
GROUP BY c.cohort_month, DATEDIFF(MONTH, c.cohort_month, a.active_month)
ORDER BY c.cohort_month, months_since_signup;
questions.modelAnswer: The performance-critical decision here is bounding the activity CTE to a rolling 24-month window with a predicate on activity_date before any join or aggregation happens, rather than joining the full history and filtering afterward — on an enterprise OLTP replica, this is the difference between an index seek against a reasonably sized range and a full scan of years of activity data on every run. The FIRST_VALUE window function, partitioned by cohort_month and ordered by months-since-signup, retrieves month-zero's active count as the denominator for every row in that cohort's partition without a self-join back to a separately aggregated month-zero table, which both simplifies the query and avoids an extra scan. For this to actually perform well in production rather than just read cleanly, I'd want a covering nonclustered index on customer_activity(activity_date) INCLUDE (customer_id) so the date-bounded CTE can seek rather than scan, and I'd push this to run against a reporting replica or snapshot-isolated connection rather than the live OLTP primary, since a cohort report scanning two years of activity data is exactly the kind of analytical workload that shouldn't compete for locks with order-entry transactions. At true enterprise scale I would also consider pre-aggregating this into a small monthly cohort summary table refreshed nightly, since recomputing the full 24-month window on every dashboard refresh is unnecessary work once the historical months are no longer changing.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd fix before anyone even looks at the window function is the join pattern — I'd bound the activity data to a rolling window with a date predicate before the join, not after, because otherwise this scans years of activity history every single run. For the retention percentage itself, I like using FIRST_VALUE partitioned by cohort month instead of a self-join back to a separately computed month-zero table — it's cleaner and it's one less scan. But honestly, the bigger architectural point I'd make in an interview is that I wouldn't want this running live against two years of raw activity data on every dashboard refresh forever — I'd push for a small nightly-refreshed cohort summary table once historical months stop changing, and I'd make sure whatever does run live against the OLTP replica is actually hitting a reporting replica or snapshot isolation, not competing for locks with order-entry transactions.

Uses a self-join back to a separately aggregated month-zero table instead of a window function
Runs the report directly against the OLTP primary without considering replica/snapshot isolation
Recomputes the entire multi-year window on every run instead of considering pre-aggregation for stable historical months

Uses FIRST_VALUE correctly as the cohort denominator without an extra self-join

questions.title: Design CI/CD for a Multi-Team dbt Monorepo
questions.prompt: A dbt monorepo now has six teams contributing models, and a full `dbt build` takes 90 minutes, making every PR slow to validate. Write the CI pipeline structure you'd implement to keep validation fast and safe as the project continues to grow.
questions.code:
# .github/workflows/dbt_ci.yml (conceptual structure)
jobs:
  slim_ci:
    steps:
      - run: dbt deps
      - run: >
          dbt build
          --select state:modified+
          --defer --state ./prod-manifest
          --target ci

  full_nightly:
    if: github.event_name == 'schedule'
    steps:
      - run: dbt build --target ci

  code_quality:
    steps:
      - run: sqlfluff lint models/
      - run: dbt test --select source:*,tag:contract
questions.modelAnswer: The core technique is dbt's slim CI pattern: instead of running the full build on every PR, CI compares the PR's manifest against a stored manifest from the last successful production run and builds only the modified models plus everything downstream of them (state:modified+), using --defer so unmodified upstream models resolve against production's existing tables rather than needing to be rebuilt in the CI environment. This turns a 90-minute full build into a build scoped to whatever one team's PR actually touched, typically a small fraction of the DAG, and it scales as more teams contribute because a team's PR only ever pays the cost of its own change plus true downstream dependents, not the entire monorepo. Alongside slim CI, a full `dbt build` still needs to run on a schedule (nightly) against the CI target, independent of any PR, to catch cross-team integration issues that slim CI's dependency-based selection might miss — for example a model that silently relies on undeclared behavior from another team's table that isn't expressed as a formal ref() dependency. For a six-team monorepo specifically, I would also add model-ownership metadata (a meta.owner tag per model or per directory) so CI can route notifications and required-reviewer rules to the right team automatically, and I'd add a lightweight linting and contract-test stage (sqlfluff, dbt's model contracts, source freshness checks) that runs fast and fails before the slower build stage even starts, so a trivial style or governance issue doesn't burn 20 minutes of build time before being caught.
questions.professionalAnswer: The fix here is dbt's slim CI pattern — instead of running everything, I diff the PR's manifest against the last successful production manifest and only build what's modified plus what's truly downstream of it, deferring unmodified upstream models to production's existing tables. That takes a 90-minute full build down to just whatever one team's change actually touched, and it keeps scaling reasonably as more teams join because each PR's CI cost is proportional to its own blast radius, not the whole monorepo. I wouldn't drop the full build entirely though — I'd keep a nightly scheduled full `dbt build` specifically to catch cross-team issues that slim selection can miss, like a model quietly depending on something that isn't expressed as a formal ref. And with six teams in one repo, I'd add ownership tags on models so CI can route the right reviewers automatically, plus a fast linting and contract-check stage that runs before the build stage, so a style issue gets caught in seconds instead of after a 20-minute partial build.

Drops the full nightly build entirely, missing cross-team integration issues slim selection can't catch
No model-ownership metadata, so CI can't route reviews/notifications as the team count grows
Puts slow build steps before fast lint/contract checks, wasting compute on PRs that fail for trivial reasons

Keeps a scheduled full build for cross-team integration safety
Proposes model-ownership metadata for a multi-team monorepo
Orders CI stages fast-checks-first for efficiency
Explains why this scales better as more teams contribute
