Retains a full-build safety net appropriately
Addresses multi-team ownership/routing needs
Sound CI stage ordering for efficiency

questions.title: Structure a Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline with Quarantine
questions.prompt: Write a Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline (formerly DLT) definition for a Bronze-to-Silver step that enforces data quality expectations on incoming order events, routing violations to an explicit quarantine table instead of silently dropping them.
questions.modelAnswer: The design pattern is to compute the quarantine table and the clean Silver table from the same Bronze source, with the quarantine table's filter being the logical inverse of the expectations applied to Silver, rather than relying only on expect_or_drop and losing the rejected rows entirely. expect_or_drop enforces a hard constraint and silently removes violating rows from the output stream, which is appropriate for genuinely invalid data (a null customer_id, a non-positive amount) but 'silently removes' is exactly the behavior the requirement explicitly rejects — so the quarantine table exists specifically to capture those same rejected rows in a queryable, auditable location rather than letting expect_or_drop's default behavior make them disappear. The future_order_date check is declared with plain expect rather than expect_or_drop because a dated order slightly ahead of ingest timestamp (clock skew between systems) might be a soft warning worth tracking in pipeline metrics rather than an automatic rejection — expect records the violation rate without dropping rows, which is the right enforcement level for a condition that's suspicious but not necessarily wrong. In production I would also add dlt.expect_all_or_fail for any invariant whose violation should halt the entire pipeline run rather than just the offending rows, reserved for conditions that indicate the upstream source itself is broken (for example, an entire batch missing a required column), since continuing to process a structurally broken batch and just dropping bad rows can itself produce a misleadingly clean-looking but incomplete Silver table.
questions.professionalAnswer: The pattern I'd use is to build the quarantine table as the logical inverse of the Silver expectations, both reading from the same Bronze stream — because expect_or_drop on its own will do exactly what the name says, drop the bad rows, and that's the opposite of what 'never reaches Gold silently' requires. I want those dropped rows sitting somewhere queryable, not gone. For something like a future order_date, I'd use a soft expect instead of expect_or_drop, because that's more likely clock skew between systems than genuinely bad data, and I'd rather track how often it happens than throw away otherwise-valid orders over it. And if I saw an entire batch missing a required column — not just a few bad rows but a structurally broken source — I'd want expect_all_or_fail to stop the whole run, because quietly dropping rows and producing a Silver table that looks clean but is actually missing a chunk of a batch is worse than failing loudly.
commonMistakes: Uses only expect_or_drop and loses visibility into what was actually rejected
Applies the same hard-fail enforcement level to every condition regardless of whether it indicates bad data or just upstream clock skew
No quarantine table, so there is no way to audit what was dropped and why
Doesn't consider expect_all_or_fail for conditions that indicate the whole batch/source is structurally broken
keyPoints: Builds an explicit, queryable quarantine table rather than relying on silent drops
Chooses the correct expectation strictness (expect vs. expect_or_drop vs. expect_all_or_fail) per condition
Explains why future order_date deserves soft enforcement given likely clock skew
Addresses when a structural batch failure should halt the whole pipeline

questions.title: OneLake Shortcut vs. Physical Copy: Making the Call in Config
questions.prompt: A Fabric workspace needs data that already lives in an Azure Data Lake Storage account owned by another team. Write the decision logic (as a short checklist plus the Fabric configuration) for when you'd use a OneLake shortcut versus physically copying the data into the workspace's own lakehouse.
questions.modelAnswer: The decision hinges on four questions, not a default preference for one approach. First, does my workspace need write access or heavy independent transformation of this data — if yes, a shortcut (which is read-oriented and reflects the source's own write cadence) is the wrong fit, and a physical copy I control is more appropriate. Second, does the source team already enforce the governance and quality bar I need, or do I need to apply my own transformations/cleansing before this is fit for my consumers — a shortcut inherits the source as-is, so if I need a materially different shape or quality bar, I need my own copy, typically built via a pipeline reading through the shortcut rather than skipping the shortcut layer entirely. Third, what's the acceptable staleness — a shortcut has effectively zero replication lag because it's a pointer to the same OneLake-addressable storage, not a copy, so if freshness matters and the source updates frequently, that's a strong point in favor of the shortcut. Fourth, cross-region or cross-cloud considerations — OneLake shortcuts to another cloud's storage can introduce egress costs or latency that a copy, ingested once, would amortize over many subsequent reads; for a dataset queried heavily and repeatedly, copying once may be cheaper over time than paying a per-query cross-boundary cost indefinitely. My default bias is to start with a shortcut because it avoids duplicating storage and avoids a synchronization problem entirely, and only materialize a physical copy when one of these four conditions clearly argues against it.
questions.professionalAnswer: I don't default to either option — I work through a short set of questions. Do I need to write to this data or transform it heavily for my own consumers? If so, a shortcut doesn't fit well because it's read-oriented and reflects the source as-is; I'd build a copy through a pipeline instead. Do I need freshness? A shortcut has essentially no replication lag since it's a pointer into the same OneLake storage, not a copy, so if the source changes frequently and I need to see that immediately, that's a point for the shortcut. Is this cross-cloud or cross-region? Then I'm weighing a shortcut's recurring cross-boundary query cost against a one-time copy cost, and for something queried constantly, a copy might actually be cheaper over time. My starting bias is toward the shortcut because it avoids duplicating storage and avoids a whole class of sync problems, and I only reach for a physical copy when one of those specific conditions argues against it.
commonMistakes: Defaults to physically copying data out of habit, duplicating storage and creating a sync problem unnecessarily
Uses a shortcut for a workload that needs heavy independent transformation or write access
Ignores cross-cloud/cross-region egress cost implications of a frequently-queried shortcut
Doesn't consider staleness/freshness requirements when choosing between the two
keyPoints: Frames the decision around write-access need, governance fit, freshness, and cross-boundary cost
Correctly explains OneLake shortcuts as pointers with near-zero replication lag, not copies
Identifies when a physical copy is genuinely the better fit
Addresses cross-cloud/cross-region cost tradeoffs
States a sensible default bias with clear exceptions

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains OneLake shortcut mechanics
Provides a sound, multi-factor decision framework
Addresses cross-cloud/cost implications

questions.title: Write a Cost-Governance Query Against Snowflake's Account Usage
questions.prompt: Finance wants a weekly report of which warehouses and which teams are driving Snowflake credit spend, with an alert threshold for any warehouse whose spend grew more than 25% week over week. Write the query against Snowflake's account usage views that produces this.
questions.code:
WITH weekly_credits AS (
    SELECT
        warehouse_name,
        DATE_TRUNC('week', start_time) AS usage_week,
        SUM(credits_used) AS credits_used
    FROM snowflake.account_usage.warehouse_metering_history
    WHERE start_time >= DATEADD(week, -8, CURRENT_DATE())
    GROUP BY warehouse_name, usage_week
),
wow AS (
    SELECT
        warehouse_name,
        usage_week,
        credits_used,
        LAG(credits_used) OVER (
            PARTITION BY warehouse_name ORDER BY usage_week
        ) AS prior_week_credits
    FROM weekly_credits
)
SELECT
    warehouse_name,
    usage_week,
    credits_used,
    prior_week_credits,
    ROUND(
      (credits_used - prior_week_credits) / prior_week_credits * 100, 1
    ) AS pct_change
FROM wow
WHERE prior_week_credits > 0
  AND (credits_used - prior_week_credits) / prior_week_credits > 0.25
ORDER BY pct_change DESC;
questions.modelAnswer: WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY in ACCOUNT_USAGE is the correct source for this because it's the view that actually reflects billed credit consumption per warehouse per hour, as opposed to QUERY_HISTORY which tells you execution time but not credits, and it's important to know ACCOUNT_USAGE views have inherent latency (up to a few hours) and a retention window (typically 365 days), so this isn't suitable for real-time alerting, only for the weekly reporting cadence actually requested here. The LAG window function partitioned by warehouse and ordered by week gives a clean week-over-week comparison without a self-join, and filtering on prior_week_credits > 0 avoids a division-by-zero/undefined-percentage case for a warehouse that didn't exist or wasn't used the prior week, which otherwise would either error or produce a misleading infinite percentage increase. Attributing spend to a specific team, which Finance will inevitably ask for next, requires either a warehouse-naming convention that encodes team ownership (common but fragile if not enforced) or joining through QUERY_HISTORY's warehouse_name and query_tag/role columns if teams tag their queries or use dedicated roles — I would push to establish resource tagging or dedicated per-team warehouses as a governance standard precisely so this attribution doesn't depend on a brittle naming convention, and I'd build the alert threshold as a scheduled task or a Snowflake alert object rather than a report someone has to remember to open.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd pull this from WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY specifically, since that's what actually reflects billed credits per warehouse, not QUERY_HISTORY, which only tells you about execution time. I'd use LAG partitioned by warehouse to get a clean week-over-week comparison, and I'd make sure to guard against dividing by a zero or null prior-week value, because a warehouse that just got spun up would otherwise show an undefined or misleading spike. The thing I'd flag back to Finance before shipping this: attributing spend to a specific team isn't really a query problem, it's a governance problem — if teams don't have dedicated warehouses or consistent query tagging, I can't reliably say whose spend this is, I can only guess from naming conventions, which breaks the moment someone doesn't follow them. I'd recommend fixing that attribution gap with tagging or per-team warehouses as a standard, and I'd turn the threshold check into an actual scheduled alert rather than a report someone has to remember to check weekly.
commonMistakes: Uses QUERY_HISTORY instead of WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY for credit/cost attribution
Doesn't guard against division by zero/null for a newly created warehouse
Assumes team attribution is solvable purely in SQL without addressing tagging/warehouse-ownership governance
Builds this as a one-off report instead of a scheduled alert matching the stated requirement
keyPoints: Uses the correct ACCOUNT_USAGE view for credit/cost data
Correctly implements week-over-week comparison with LAG
Guards against division-by-zero/undefined percentage cases
Flags the real governance gap behind team-level attribution
Proposes turning this into an actual scheduled alert

Correctly handles edge cases (zero/null prior week)

questions.title: Gold Layer Is Lagging Silver by Hours in a Medallion Pipeline
questions.prompt: An enterprise medallion architecture's Gold tables are showing data that's 4-6 hours stale relative to Silver, which used to be near-real-time. No single job is throwing an error. Walk through how you would diagnose this and the most likely root causes.
questions.modelAnswer:
Because nothing is erroring, this is almost always a throughput or scheduling problem, not a logic bug, so I'd start by instrumenting rather than guessing. First, I'd check whether this is a Silver-to-Gold job scheduling issue versus a genuine processing-time regression: has the trigger interval or batch cadence for the Silver-to-Gold step silently changed (someone switched a continuous trigger to a longer fixed interval, or a dependent orchestration job's schedule shifted), or is the job still running on the expected cadence but each run is simply taking longer than it used to? I'd pull the job run history and compare batch duration over the past weeks against data volume over the same period — if volume grew faster than the job's processing time scaled, the most common cause is Delta file fragmentation in the Silver table: without regular OPTIMIZE, a continuously-written Silver table accumulates many small files, and reading from it for the Gold aggregation gets progressively slower purely from file listing and open overhead, with no error, just creeping latency.

The second most likely cause is resource contention: if the cluster or SQL Warehouse running this job is shared with other growing workloads, autoscaling lag or insufficient max capacity means the job queues or runs with fewer resources than it used to, again producing slow-but-not-failing behavior. I'd check cluster/warehouse utilization metrics during the job's run window specifically, not just average utilization. Third, I'd check for a skewed partition or a hot key in the aggregation — if one dimension's cardinality grew disproportionately (one customer or region now dominates the Gold aggregation), a shuffle-heavy step can silently become the long pole without any error, visible only as one task in the Spark UI taking dramatically longer than its peers. I would not accept 'add more compute' as the first fix without identifying which of these three it actually is, because each has a different durable remedy.
questions.professionalAnswer: Since nothing's erroring, I treat this as a throughput problem and go straight to the job run history rather than guessing. First question: did the schedule or trigger actually change, or is the job still running on time but just taking longer each run? If it's taking longer, I immediately suspect file fragmentation in the Silver table — a continuously-written table without regular OPTIMIZE accumulates small files, and reads get slower and slower with zero errors, just creeping latency, which matches exactly what's described here. I'd also check whether the compute running this is shared with other workloads that have grown — autoscaling lag or a hard capacity ceiling produces the same silent slowdown. And I'd specifically look in the Spark UI for one skewed task dominating a stage, because a hot key in the aggregation can quietly become the long pole as data volume or cardinality shifts. I wouldn't throw more compute at this without knowing which of those three it actually is, because 'just scale up' fixes the symptom for one of them and does nothing for the other two.

Doesn't check whether the trigger/schedule itself silently changed before assuming a processing-time regression
Looks only at average cluster utilization instead of utilization specifically during the job's run window
Ignores Delta file fragmentation as a creeping, error-free cause of slowdown

questions.title: Fabric Capacity Throttling Across Competing Business Units
questions.prompt: Multiple business units share one Fabric capacity (F-SKU), and one team's heavy Spark notebook runs are causing another team's Power BI reports to throttle during business hours. Diagnose the cause and propose the fix.
questions.modelAnswer:
Fabric capacity is a single shared pool of compute units (CUs) across every workload type — Spark, Power BI rendering and refresh, Data Factory pipelines, warehouse queries — on that capacity, and Fabric's smoothing and throttling model means a sustained burst of consumption from one workload (the heavy Spark notebooks) directly reduces the CUs available to every other workload on the same capacity during that window, including Power BI report interactivity. The first diagnostic step is the Fabric Capacity Metrics app, which shows CU consumption broken down by workload and by item over time; I would confirm the throttling window correlates exactly with the Spark team's run schedule, rather than assuming it before checking, since it could also be a Power BI refresh storm, a runaway DAX query, or an actual capacity undersizing issue independent of the Spark jobs.

Once confirmed, the durable fixes are, in order of preference: first, schedule the heavy Spark workloads outside the business hours when the Power BI consumers are actually interactive, which is the cheapest fix if the Spark jobs don't have a genuine real-time requirement; second, if they do need to run during business hours, move them to a separate Fabric capacity dedicated to that team's engineering workloads, isolating the blast radius so one team's burst can't throttle another team's reports — this is the architecturally correct long-term fix once business units are genuinely contending rather than just occasionally overlapping; third, if a single shared capacity is a hard organizational requirement, Fabric's workload-level CU allocation and surge protection settings can be tuned, and the capacity can be scaled up (a bigger SKU), but scaling up without addressing the scheduling conflict just raises the ceiling at which the same contention recurs as both teams' workloads grow. I would present the separate-capacity option as the real fix and the scheduling change as the immediate stopgap while that's being set up, since billing and governance teams often prefer isolated capacities per business unit anyway for cost attribution.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start in the Fabric Capacity Metrics app before touching anything, because I want to actually confirm the throttling window lines up with the Spark team's run schedule rather than assuming it — it could just as easily be a runaway DAX query or a refresh storm on the Power BI side. Once that's confirmed, my first move is the cheapest one: can the Spark jobs just run outside business hours? If there's no real-time need, that alone solves it. If they genuinely need to run during the day, I'd push for giving that team their own dedicated capacity rather than tuning surge protection on a shared one, because one team's workload bursting into another team's report-interactivity budget is exactly the failure mode separate capacities are meant to prevent — and honestly, most finance teams want that separation anyway for clean cost attribution per business unit. Scaling the shared capacity up is a real option too, but I'd be upfront that it just raises the ceiling where this same conflict happens again as both teams grow, it doesn't actually remove the contention.

questions.title: Snowflake Credit Spend Spiked 300% Overnight
questions.prompt: A Snowflake account's daily credit consumption tripled overnight with no known deployment or data volume change. Describe your diagnostic sequence to find the cause before finance escalates it.
questions.modelAnswer:
I would not start by looking at individual queries; I'd start at WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY to identify which specific warehouse's credit consumption actually spiked, because a 300% account-wide increase almost always concentrates in one or two warehouses rather than being spread evenly, and that immediately narrows the search space. Once I know the warehouse, I'd check QUERY_HISTORY filtered to that warehouse and the spike window for three specific patterns: a query or job that started looping or retrying (a scheduled task or orchestration tool firing far more often than intended, often from a misconfigured cron or an infinite-retry bug), a warehouse auto-suspend setting that got changed or disabled (a warehouse left running idle burns credits every minute it's up with nothing to do, and this is a surprisingly common accidental-change cause), or a genuine change in query pattern — a new or modified query doing a full table scan where it used to use a selective filter, often from a changed WHERE clause or a dropped/corrupted index-equivalent clustering key.

I would also check whether warehouse auto-scaling (multi-cluster warehouses) kicked in more aggressively than before, which multiplies credit cost directly, and whether this correlates with a concurrency spike from an application or BI tool rather than a data pipeline. Practically, I'd pull the top 20 most expensive queries by estimated credits in the spike window from QUERY_HISTORY and look for a single outlier pattern rather than assuming it's evenly distributed load growth — in my experience this kind of overnight 300% spike is almost always one specific cause (a stuck job, a disabled auto-suspend, a bad query plan change) rather than organic growth, and organic growth doesn't triple overnight with 'no known deployment or data volume change.'
questions.professionalAnswer: A 300% overnight spike with no deployment change tells me this isn't organic growth, it's something specific and probably recent — so I go straight to WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY to find which warehouse is actually driving it, because it's almost never evenly spread across the whole account. From there I check three things in order: is a scheduled job looping or retrying far more than intended, did someone disable or change a warehouse's auto-suspend setting so it's sitting idle and billing anyway, or did a query's execution plan quietly get worse — a dropped clustering key or a changed filter that turned a selective query into something closer to a full scan. I'd pull the most expensive queries in that warehouse during the spike window and look for one dominant outlier, because in my experience this kind of sudden, large spike is almost always one specific root cause, not a dozen small ones adding up — and I'd rather find the one thing than spend a day auditing everything evenly.

questions.title: dbt CI Blows Through Its Time Budget on a Large Monorepo
questions.prompt: A dbt monorepo's CI build time has crept from 12 minutes to 70 minutes over a year of six teams adding models, and PRs are now routinely blocked waiting on CI. Diagnose the likely causes and the fix.
questions.modelAnswer:
The first thing I'd check is whether CI is actually running a full `dbt build` on every PR rather than a state-based selection — a monorepo that grew from a handful of models to hundreds over a year, with CI still running everything on every PR, is the single most common and most fixable cause of exactly this symptom, and it means CI time scales with the total size of the repository rather than with the size of any individual PR, which is obviously unsustainable as more teams contribute. If slim CI selection (state:modified+ with --defer) is already in place and the time has still crept up, the next suspects are: a small number of extremely expensive models (a non-incremental full-refresh model over a huge source table, rebuilt in full on every CI run because it has no incremental materialization) that dominate build time regardless of how well-scoped the selection is, or a growing number of singular/generic tests that run as separate queries and add up linearly even on a small model selection.

I'd pull CI run logs and sort by per-model/per-test duration to find the actual long pole rather than guessing — in my experience it's rarely evenly distributed, it's usually two or three specific models or tests responsible for a disproportionate share of the time. Fixes, roughly in order: confirm and fix slim CI selection if it's missing; convert the expensive full-refresh models to incremental materializations where the business logic allows it; move genuinely slow data-quality tests (ones that scan huge tables) to the nightly full build rather than every PR's CI run, keeping PR-time tests scoped to structural/contract checks that are fast; and if the CI compute itself is undersized, consider a larger CI warehouse/cluster specifically for the build step, though I'd only reach for more compute after confirming the selection and materialization issues are actually fixed, since more compute just masks an underlying scaling problem temporarily.
questions.professionalAnswer: First question I'd ask: is CI actually running a full build on every PR, or is it using state-based selection? Because a monorepo that's grown for a year while CI still builds everything every time is the classic, almost boring explanation for exactly this symptom — CI time scales with total repo size instead of PR size, which obviously doesn't hold up as more teams join. If slim CI is already in place and it's still crept up, I'd pull the CI logs and sort by duration per model and per test, because in my experience it's never evenly spread — it's usually one or two full-refresh models over huge tables, or a handful of expensive data-quality tests, eating most of the time. I'd fix those specifically — convert what can be incremental, move the genuinely slow tests to the nightly full build instead of every PR — before I'd even consider throwing more CI compute at it, because more compute just hides the real scaling problem for another few months.

Doesn't pull actual per-model/per-test duration data, guessing at the cause instead
Treats all tests as equally necessary at PR time instead of moving slow ones to a nightly run
Ignores non-incremental full-refresh models as a likely concentrated cause

questions.title: Unity Catalog Lineage Has a Gap Across Two Workspaces
questions.prompt: A compliance audit asks you to trace a specific Gold metric back to its original source table, but Unity Catalog's lineage graph shows a break between two workspaces that share the same metastore. Diagnose why lineage might be missing and how you'd fix it.
questions.modelAnswer:
Unity Catalog lineage is captured automatically for operations that run through Databricks compute attached to a Unity-Catalog-enabled workspace and recorded against the table/column objects in the shared metastore, but it has specific, well-known gaps that produce exactly this symptom. The most common cause is that some step in the chain runs outside Databricks compute entirely — a query or write executed through an external tool connecting directly to the table via JDBC/ODBC, a Fabric or ADF pipeline writing to the table through a connector rather than a Databricks notebook/job, or a manual COPY INTO run from a non-Databricks client — because lineage capture requires the operation to actually execute on Databricks compute, Unity Catalog cannot see or record what happened outside it. The second common cause is that the second workspace, despite sharing the metastore, is on an older runtime or cluster configuration that doesn't support lineage capture (certain cluster access modes or older DBR versions have incomplete lineage support), or the job writing the downstream table uses a SQL or API pattern lineage doesn't track as of the runtime in use (some dynamic SQL generation patterns and certain external-table operations have historically had incomplete column-level lineage support).

To fix it for this audit, I would first manually trace the actual pipeline code for that break point to document the missing link by hand (compliance deadlines don't wait for a tooling fix), then identify the root technical cause — if it's an external tool bypassing Databricks compute, the durable fix is routing that write through a Databricks job/notebook instead so it's captured automatically going forward, and if it's a runtime/configuration gap, upgrading the second workspace's cluster policy to a lineage-capable configuration. I would also flag this as a governance finding: any workspace or pipeline that writes to Unity-Catalog-governed tables without going through Databricks compute is a lineage blind spot that should be inventoried proactively, not discovered reactively during the next audit.
questions.professionalAnswer: Lineage only gets captured for operations that actually run through Databricks compute against the shared metastore, so my first suspicion is that somewhere in this chain, a write or a query happened outside Databricks entirely — an external tool connecting directly via JDBC, or a pipeline from another platform writing to the table through a connector rather than a Databricks job. That's invisible to Unity Catalog by design, not a bug. My second suspicion is a runtime or cluster configuration gap on that second workspace — older cluster versions or certain access modes have had incomplete lineage support. For the audit itself, I wouldn't wait on a tooling fix — I'd manually trace the actual code at that break point and document the link by hand so compliance has an answer now. Then I'd fix the root cause: route that external write through Databricks compute if that's the gap, or upgrade the workspace's cluster configuration if it's a runtime issue. And I'd flag this proactively as a governance finding, because any pipeline writing to a governed table outside Databricks compute is a lineage blind spot we should be inventorying, not discovering during the next audit.

Doesn't manually document the missing link for the immediate compliance deadline while pursuing the technical fix
Treats this as a one-off bug rather than inventorying other potential lineage blind spots proactively
Ignores cluster runtime/configuration version as a possible cause of incomplete lineage capture

questions.title: A Structured Streaming Job Is Falling Behind and Backlog Is Growing
questions.prompt: A Structured Streaming job reading from Event Hubs into Delta has a steadily growing input backlog — each micro-batch takes longer than the trigger interval. Walk through your diagnostic process and the levers you'd pull.
questions.modelAnswer:
A steadily growing backlog where each batch takes longer than the trigger interval is backpressure: the system is consuming slower than data arrives, and the fix depends on identifying whether the bottleneck is on the read side, the processing side, or the write side, which the Spark UI's streaming tab and the structured streaming query progress metrics (inputRowsPerSecond vs. processedRowsPerSecond) will show directly. If processedRowsPerSecond is consistently below inputRowsPerSecond, that confirms genuine backpressure rather than a one-time blip, and I'd look at the batch duration breakdown (addBatch time vs. getBatch/read time) to localize it.

On the read side, the most common cause is too few Event Hubs partitions relative to the consumer parallelism the cluster could otherwise support — Structured Streaming's parallelism for Event Hubs is bounded by partition count, so a cluster that's otherwise capable of much higher throughput is artificially capped; the fix is increasing Event Hubs partition count (a source-side change, sometimes requiring a new Event Hub if partition count can't be increased in place) or, short term, tuning maxEventsPerTrigger to process more per batch, which trades batch latency for throughput. On the processing side, a shuffle-heavy transformation (a stateful aggregation or a join against a large static table without broadcast) can dominate batch time, and the fix is either broadcasting the smaller side of the join explicitly or reconsidering whether the aggregation's state store is appropriately watermarked and bounded, since an unbounded state store grows and slows every batch over time. On the write side, writing into a Delta table with too many small files from frequent micro-batch commits compounds over time exactly like the medallion-lag scenario, and a less frequent but larger trigger interval, or enabling auto-compaction/optimized writes on the target table, addresses that directly. I would not simply add cluster nodes as the first move without localizing which of these three it actually is, because scaling the cluster only helps if the bottleneck is CPU/memory-bound processing, not partition-bound reads or small-file-bound writes.
questions.professionalAnswer: A growing backlog where batches consistently take longer than the trigger interval is backpressure, and I'd confirm that first by comparing inputRowsPerSecond against processedRowsPerSecond in the query progress metrics rather than assuming it from the symptom description alone. Then I localize it: is it slow on read, slow in processing, or slow on write? If it's read-bound, the usual suspect with Event Hubs is too few partitions capping how much parallelism Structured Streaming can actually use, no matter how big the cluster is — so I'd look at increasing partition count, or in the short term tune maxEventsPerTrigger as a stopgap. If it's processing-bound, I'm looking for a shuffle-heavy join or an unbounded stateful aggregation eating more time every batch — broadcasting the small side of a join, or properly watermarking the aggregation, usually fixes that. If it's write-bound, I'd suspect small-file buildup from frequent micro-batch commits into Delta, and I'd either widen the trigger interval or turn on auto-compaction. The one thing I wouldn't do first is just add cluster nodes, because that only helps if the bottleneck is actually compute-bound — if it's partition-capped reads or small-file writes, more nodes doesn't move the needle at all.

Doesn't check Event Hubs partition count as a hard cap on read-side parallelism
Ignores unbounded/unwatermarked stateful aggregations as a cause of batch time growing over time
Doesn't connect small-file write buildup in Delta to the same backpressure symptom
keyPoints: Confirms genuine backpressure via actual streaming metrics, not just the symptom
Correctly localizes the bottleneck to read, process, or write stage
Identifies Event Hubs partition count as a read-side cap
Identifies shuffle/unbounded state as a processing-side cause
Identifies small-file write buildup as a write-side cause
Avoids defaulting to more compute before localizing the cause

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly confirms and localizes the bottleneck using real metrics
Identifies read-side partition-count cap correctly
Identifies processing-side shuffle/state issues correctly
Identifies write-side small-file issue and avoids the compute-first trap

questions.title: A Composite Power BI Model Times Out Only for Enterprise-Wide Reports
questions.prompt: A Power BI composite model combining an Import-mode budget table with a DirectQuery fact table over a Fabric warehouse works fine for single-region reports but times out for the enterprise-wide rollup. Diagnose the cause.
questions.modelAnswer:
Composite models with a mix of Import and DirectQuery storage modes use a feature called dual/limited relationships and query folding back to the DirectQuery source, and the most common cause of this exact symptom — fine at small scope, times out at enterprise scope — is that the DAX engine is generating a query plan that pushes a cross-source join or a large IN-list filter down to the DirectQuery source once the filter context (region) is removed or widened, and the underlying Fabric warehouse query either can't execute that pushed-down query efficiently or the result set being pulled back into the Vertipaq engine to complete the join locally becomes enormous. At single-region scope, the filter naturally bounds the DirectQuery side to a small result set that completes fast regardless of the join strategy; at enterprise scope, the same query pattern has to pull or process orders of magnitude more rows, and if the composite model's relationship is many-to-many or lacks a proper limited relationship configuration, Power BI may fall back to a much less efficient join strategy at the engine level specifically when the row counts cross an internal threshold.

I would use Performance Analyzer to capture the actual DAX and the generated SQL sent to the DirectQuery source for the enterprise-wide report, and compare it against the single-region version's generated SQL — this almost always reveals either a missing predicate pushdown (the filter that bounded the fast case isn't present in the slow case's generated query) or a dramatically larger data pull. The fix is usually one of: ensuring the relationship between the Import and DirectQuery tables is a proper one-to-many on a well-indexed key rather than many-to-many, pre-aggregating the DirectQuery fact table so the enterprise rollup queries a much smaller pre-summarized table instead of the full-grain fact, or reconsidering whether the budget table actually needs to be Import mode at all versus making the whole model DirectQuery with aggregation tables, which avoids the composite-model cross-source join problem entirely for this specific symptom.
questions.professionalAnswer: This smells like a composite-model cross-source join problem the moment I hear 'works at narrow scope, times out at wide scope,' because that's exactly the pattern you get when the DAX engine's join strategy against the DirectQuery source stops being efficient once the filter context that used to bound the result set goes away. I'd go straight to Performance Analyzer and capture the actual SQL being generated against the Fabric warehouse for both the single-region and enterprise-wide versions of the report, and compare them directly rather than guessing — I want to see whether the enterprise version is missing a predicate that the narrow version has, or whether it's just pulling back a much bigger result set to finish the join locally in Vertipaq. Depending on what I find, I'd either fix the relationship to be a clean one-to-many instead of many-to-many, add a pre-aggregated version of the DirectQuery fact table so the enterprise rollup isn't hitting full grain, or reconsider whether that budget table even needs Import mode — sometimes the cleanest fix for this exact composite-model pain point is going fully DirectQuery with proper aggregation tables instead.
commonMistakes: Assumes it's a generic 'DirectQuery is slow' issue without comparing generated SQL between the fast and slow cases
Doesn't check whether the composite model's relationship is many-to-many instead of one-to-many
Jumps to increasing warehouse compute without confirming the query pattern itself is efficient
Doesn't consider pre-aggregation or a DirectQuery-only redesign as fixes to the underlying composite-model join cost

Uses Performance Analyzer to compare generated queries between fast and slow cases
Checks relationship cardinality (many-to-many vs. one-to-many) as a root cause
Proposes pre-aggregation as a concrete fix for the enterprise-wide scope
Considers a DirectQuery-only redesign as an alternative fix

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the composite-model join/pushdown mechanism
Proposes a sound diagnostic method (Performance Analyzer comparison)
Identifies relationship cardinality as a root cause

questions.title: A Metadata-Driven ADF Framework Breaks After Upstream Schema Drift
questions.prompt: The metadata-driven ADF pipeline framework you support failed overnight for 40 of its 200 source tables after an upstream ERP vendor pushed a schema change. Diagnose the failure pattern and propose both the immediate recovery and the durable fix.
questions.modelAnswer:
The first diagnostic step is to confirm whether the 40 failing tables share a common trait — most likely, they're all sourced from the same ERP connection or the same upstream module, which strongly suggests one coordinated schema change (a column rename, a type change, or new required columns on a shared base table or view) rather than 40 unrelated failures. I'd pull the actual error messages from the ADF activity run output for a sample of the failures, since 'schema drift' can mean several different concrete failures: a mapping data flow or copy activity with a schema-on-write validation that now sees an unexpected or missing column and fails hard, a sink table whose target schema doesn't match the new source shape, or a type-coercion failure where a column that used to be numeric is now a string.

For immediate recovery, since this is a metadata-driven framework, I would not want a blanket fix applied framework-wide without understanding the actual change, because the wrong fix (for example, globally relaxing schema enforcement) risks silently loading bad data for the other 160 unaffected tables too. Instead, I'd isolate the 40 affected control-table rows, pause them specifically (IsActive = 0) so they stop retrying and alerting while I investigate, and manually reconcile the new ERP schema against the target tables for just that subset. The durable fix has two parts: first, update the affected target table schemas and the control-table metadata (expected column list, type mapping) to match the new ERP shape, and redeploy those 40 rows; second, and more importantly for an architect, add an automated schema-comparison step to the framework itself — a preflight check that compares the source's current schema against the last-known schema cached per source before running the full load, and raises an explicit, actionable alert naming exactly which columns changed, rather than letting schema drift manifest only as a hard pipeline failure discovered the next morning. This turns the next vendor schema change from an overnight outage into a proactive, same-day heads-up.
questions.professionalAnswer: First thing I'd check is whether these 40 tables have something in common — almost certainly they're all coming through the same ERP connection, which tells me this is one coordinated upstream schema change, not 40 separate problems. I'd pull actual error messages for a handful of them, because 'schema drift' covers a few different concrete failures — a missing column, a type that flipped from numeric to string, a new required field — and I want to know which one I'm actually dealing with before I touch anything. For immediate recovery, since this is a metadata-driven framework, I specifically wouldn't apply a blanket fix across the whole thing — I'd pause just those 40 control-table rows so they stop retrying and alerting while I reconcile the new schema for that subset specifically, then update their target schemas and metadata and bring them back online. But the fix I actually care about long-term is adding a schema-preflight check into the framework itself, so the next time a vendor changes something, I get a same-day alert naming exactly which columns changed, instead of finding out from 40 overnight failures.

Isolates the affected subset for recovery instead of a blanket framework change

questions.title: A Data Quality Issue Reached the Executive Dashboard Before Anyone Noticed
questions.prompt: A unit-conversion bug in a Silver transformation caused a metric to be overstated by roughly 8% for three weeks, and it was first caught by a board member questioning a number, not by any internal process. Walk through your incident response and the architecture changes you'd make afterward.
questions.modelAnswer:
The immediate response has two tracks that run in parallel: containing and correcting the data, and understanding and communicating the blast radius, and I would not let the second wait for the first to be fully finished. First, confirm the exact root cause and the exact window affected (which runs, which tables, which downstream reports), then determine whether every downstream consumer of the bad metric can be identified — this is where good lineage (Unity Catalog, Purview, or dbt's own lineage) pays for itself, because without it, 'who else saw this wrong number' becomes a manual, incomplete, and slow investigation exactly when speed matters most. I would fix the transformation, backfill the affected Silver and Gold tables for the full three-week window (not just going forward, since historical reports and any decisions made off that data need the correction reflected), and explicitly notify every known downstream consumer — not just the board member who caught it — with the corrected numbers and the specific window affected, because silently fixing it going forward without acknowledging the historical misstatement is how trust actually gets damaged, not the original bug itself.

The architecture changes afterward target why this wasn't caught internally: a unit-conversion bug producing a plausible-looking 8% overstatement is exactly the kind of error a human reviewing dashboards doesn't reliably catch, so the fix isn't 'look harder,' it's automated data-quality checks on the specific class of thing that went wrong — a reasonableness/anomaly check comparing each day's key metrics against a trailing average with an alert threshold, and specifically a unit/dimensional-consistency test on any transformation involving a conversion, since that's a narrow, testable, recurring risk class. I would also add this metric specifically to a short list of 'load-bearing' metrics that get a stricter contract and more reviewer scrutiny on any PR touching their lineage, since not every metric needs that level of rigor, but the ones that reach executive dashboards do. Finally, I'd push for a lightweight metric-level changelog visible to consumers, so a board member or executive has a place to check 'has this number been affected by a known issue' without that information living only in an internal incident channel.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd run two things in parallel from the start, not one after the other: fixing and backfilling the data, and figuring out exactly who else was downstream of that bad number. The lineage question matters enormously here — if we have good lineage, I can tell leadership definitively which reports and which decisions were touched by this; if we don't, that becomes a slow, manual, and probably incomplete investigation, at exactly the moment I need to move fast and be precise. I'd fix the transformation, backfill the full three weeks, not just go-forward, and then proactively notify every consumer I can identify with the corrected numbers and the exact window — because the thing that actually damages trust long-term isn't that a bug happened, it's finding out later that it was quietly patched without anyone being told. Afterward, I wouldn't tell the team to 'review more carefully' — an 8% overstatement from a unit-conversion error looks completely plausible to a human glancing at a dashboard, so the real fix is an automated reasonableness check comparing each day's key metrics against trailing history, plus specific tests on any transformation that does a unit conversion, since that's a narrow and recurring risk. And I'd put this specific metric on a short list that gets stricter review going forward, because the handful of numbers that reach the board deserve more scrutiny than the rest of the warehouse.

questions.title: Tableau and Power BI Disagree on the Same KPI
questions.prompt: Finance reports the same 'gross margin' KPI from both a legacy Tableau workbook and a newer Power BI model, and the two have disagreed by 2-3 points for months without anyone noticing until an auditor flagged it. Diagnose the likely causes and the governance fix.
questions.modelAnswer:
A persistent, stable 2-3 point gap rather than an erratic one points to a consistent definitional difference, not a data-freshness or bug issue, and the most likely candidates are: a different treatment of what counts as 'cost' in the margin calculation (one tool's calculated field includes freight or returns allowance and the other doesn't), a different filter on what counts as a 'sale' (one excludes intercompany transactions or test accounts and the other doesn't), or the two tools reading from genuinely different source tables or snapshot timing (Tableau pointing at an older extract or a different warehouse layer than the Power BI model's semantic layer). I would get the actual calculated-field/DAX formula from both tools side by side rather than guessing, and reconcile them line by line against a shared raw dataset — pick one specific period, compute gross margin by hand from the raw transaction data using an agreed-upon definition, and see which tool's output matches, which immediately tells you which one has the bug or the divergent assumption and which one is actually correct, or whether both are wrong relative to a third, true definition.

The deeper governance fix is that this gap existing undetected for months is itself the real finding: there was no single authoritative definition of 'gross margin' that both tools were required to implement, and no reconciliation or anomaly check comparing the two outputs on an ongoing basis. I would push to define gross margin once, formally, ideally in the dbt Semantic Layer or a governed metrics layer both tools eventually consume, document the exact inclusions/exclusions in a metric glossary accessible to both teams, and in the interim — before the full semantic-layer migration is complete — add a scheduled automated check comparing the two tools' output for this and other shared KPIs, alerting if the gap exceeds a tolerance, so the next discrepancy is caught by monitoring rather than by an external auditor.
questions.professionalAnswer: A gap that's stable at 2-3 points for months, not erratic, tells me this is a definitional mismatch, not a bug that comes and goes — so I'd pull the actual formula from both tools side by side rather than guessing which one's right. My first move is picking one period and computing gross margin by hand from the raw transaction data using one agreed definition, then checking which tool's output actually matches that — that tells me definitively which tool has the wrong assumption, whether it's freight treatment, intercompany exclusions, or a different source snapshot. But honestly, the bigger problem here isn't the specific bug, it's that this went undetected for months with an external auditor catching it before we did — that tells me there's no single authoritative definition of this metric and no ongoing check comparing the two tools. I'd push to define gross margin once, formally, ideally in a governed semantic layer both tools eventually pull from, and in the meantime set up an automated comparison between the two tools' outputs with an alert threshold, so the next time there's a drift, it's caught by monitoring, not by someone outside the company.

questions.title: A Massive Delta Table's Small-File Problem Is Strangling Query Performance
questions.prompt: A Gold Delta table queried constantly by BI tools has degraded from sub-second queries to 20+ seconds over six months, and a `DESCRIBE DETAIL` shows millions of tiny files. Diagnose how this happened and fix it.
questions.modelAnswer:
Millions of tiny files accumulating over six months points directly to a write pattern that creates many small files faster than any compaction process removes them — the most common cause is a frequent micro-batch or streaming write (every few seconds or minutes) without optimized writes or auto-compaction enabled, where each micro-batch commits its own small set of files regardless of how little data it contains, and without regular OPTIMIZE, those files just accumulate indefinitely. A second common cause, often compounding the first, is over-partitioning: if the table is partitioned on a high-cardinality column (or a combination of columns) relative to its actual data volume, every write touches many thin partitions, each accumulating its own small files, multiplying the small-file count well beyond what a reasonably partitioned table would produce from the same write frequency.

To confirm which it is, I'd check the write job's trigger frequency and whether optimizedWrites and autoCompact table properties are enabled, and check the partition structure against actual row counts per partition — a partition with a few thousand rows spread across hundreds of files is a clear signal of write-frequency-driven fragmentation, while uniformly thin partitions across the board signal over-partitioning. The fix for existing fragmentation is a one-time OPTIMIZE (with Z-ORDER or converting to liquid clustering if the table is under active high-frequency writes) to compact the existing small files, which will take real time and compute proportional to the table's size and should be scheduled during a low-query-traffic window given it rewrites a large volume of data. The durable fix is preventing recurrence: enable delta.autoOptimize.optimizeWrite and delta.autoOptimize.autoCompact (or migrate to liquid clustering, which handles this incrementally and is the better long-term answer for a continuously-written table), reconsider the partitioning scheme if over-partitioning was a contributing factor, and schedule a recurring OPTIMIZE job on a cadence matched to the write frequency rather than relying only on auto-compaction, since auto-compaction operates per-write and doesn't always fully consolidate under sustained high-frequency writes.
questions.professionalAnswer: Millions of tiny files building up over six months tells me the write pattern is creating small files faster than anything is compacting them — my first check is whether this table is being written to frequently, in small micro-batches, without optimized writes or auto-compaction turned on, because that's the single most common cause. My second check is the partitioning scheme — if it's partitioned on something high-cardinality relative to the actual data volume, every write spreads thin across a lot of partitions and multiplies the small-file problem on top of the write-frequency issue. I'd confirm by looking at row counts per partition relative to file counts — a handful of rows spread across hundreds of files per partition is the fingerprint of this exact problem. For the immediate fix, I'd run a one-time OPTIMIZE to compact what's already there, scheduled during low-traffic hours since rewriting that much data takes real compute. But the fix I actually care about is preventing it from happening again — turning on auto-compaction and optimized writes, or better, moving this table to liquid clustering if it's under continuous high-frequency writes, because that handles compaction incrementally instead of letting it build up silently for another six months.

Doesn't consider liquid clustering as the better long-term answer for a continuously-written table

questions.title: A Tableau-to-Power-BI Cutover Went Wrong on Launch Day
questions.prompt: After a six-month migration, the planned cutover from Tableau to Power BI happened over a weekend, and on Monday morning 30% of business users couldn't find their reports, several migrated dashboards showed wrong numbers, and the rollback plan wasn't actually tested. Diagnose what likely went wrong in the migration approach and how you'd handle the Monday-morning crisis itself.
questions.modelAnswer:
The Monday-morning crisis needs to be handled first and separately from the retrospective on what went wrong architecturally, because users need a working path right now. I would immediately assess whether Tableau can be brought back up as a fallback for the specific dashboards showing wrong numbers — if the rollback plan wasn't actually tested, this is the moment that gap becomes painfully real, so I'd rather spend the first hour confirming whether rollback is even viable than assume it is. For the 30% who can't find their reports, that's very likely a permissions/discoverability gap, not a data problem — workspace access, app permissions, or a navigation/bookmarking habit that didn't carry over — and that's fixable fast with clear communication and a temporary 'where did my report go' index page, which buys time without needing to touch the data layer at all. For the dashboards showing wrong numbers, those need to be pulled from general circulation immediately (or clearly banner-flagged as under investigation) rather than left live while people make decisions off bad numbers, even if that's uncomfortable on launch day.

On what went wrong architecturally: a six-month migration that still produced wrong numbers and discoverability gaps on cutover weekend almost always means validation happened on a subset of dashboards or a subset of users, not the full population, and the cutover was a single hard switch rather than a parallel-run period. The fix for the next phase (and for any future migration) is running old and new side by side for a defined validation window — weeks, not a weekend — with a formal sign-off per business unit before their specific dashboards are cut over, rather than one global cutover date for everyone; a genuinely tested rollback plan, meaning someone has actually executed it in a dry run, not just written it down; and a discoverability/communication plan (where things live now, who to ask) treated as seriously as the technical migration itself, since user-facing navigation changes are a real part of the migration scope, not an afterthought.
questions.professionalAnswer: Monday morning, I'm handling the crisis and the retrospective completely separately — the retrospective can wait a day, the crisis can't. First thing I do is find out if rollback to Tableau is actually viable right now, because if the plan was never tested, I need to know that in the first hour, not discover it's broken while trying to use it. For the users who can't find their reports, that's almost certainly a permissions or navigation problem, not a data problem, so I'd get a simple 'here's where your reports live now' communication out immediately — that buys real time without touching anything risky. For the dashboards showing wrong numbers, I'm pulling those from circulation or banner-flagging them right away, because I'd rather have an uncomfortable launch day than have an executive make a decision off bad data. Once the fire's out, the retrospective is pretty clear to me: a six-month project that still has wrong numbers and discoverability gaps on cutover weekend means validation wasn't actually comprehensive and the cutover was one hard switch instead of a real parallel-run period with per-business-unit sign-off. Next time, old and new run side by side for weeks, rollback gets a real dry run, not just a document, and the communication plan gets the same seriousness as the technical migration.

Assumes the rollback plan works without confirming it in the moment
Treats user discoverability/communication as separate from 'the real migration' instead of core migration scope

questions.title: Row-Level Security Doesn't Match Between Unity Catalog and Power BI
questions.prompt: A regional manager reports they can see another region's sensitive sales data in a Power BI report that connects live to a Unity Catalog table with a row filter defined. Diagnose how this is possible given the row filter exists, and fix it.
questions.modelAnswer:
A Unity Catalog row filter being bypassed almost always comes down to one of three things: the connection Power BI is actually using isn't passing through the user's real identity to Unity Catalog (a shared service principal or a fixed personal access token embedded in the connection, rather than per-user OAuth pass-through), the report is in Import mode rather than DirectQuery/live connection, or the row filter function itself has a logic gap for this specific user's context. If Power BI is connecting via a service principal or a shared credential, Unity Catalog's row filter evaluates against that service principal's identity and group membership, not the actual report viewer's — so if the service principal has broad access (which it often does, since it's usually provisioned for the BI team's general use, not scoped per-region), every viewer effectively queries as that broad-access identity regardless of who's actually looking at the report, and the row filter's region check simply never applies the way it's intended to.

The first thing I'd check is exactly how the Power BI semantic model's data source credentials are configured — per-user Azure AD OAuth pass-through versus a fixed service principal — because this is almost always the actual cause of exactly this symptom. The second thing I'd check is whether the report or dataset is Import mode; if it is, the row filter was applied once at refresh time under whatever identity ran the refresh, and every subsequent viewer sees the same imported snapshot with no per-viewer filtering possible at all, which is a fundamentally different (and in this case, worse) problem than a credential misconfiguration — Import mode and per-viewer row-level security from the source system are incompatible unless Power BI's own RLS is layered on top, redundantly re-implementing the same filter. The fix, once identified, is either switching the semantic model's authentication to per-user pass-through for a live/DirectQuery connection, or if Import mode is required for performance reasons, implementing Power BI's own row-level security roles that mirror the Unity Catalog row filter's logic exactly, accepting the governance cost of maintaining the same rule in two places consistently.
questions.professionalAnswer: If a Unity Catalog row filter is defined and someone's still seeing data they shouldn't, my first question is how Power BI is actually authenticating to that table — because if it's going through a shared service principal or a fixed token instead of per-user identity pass-through, the row filter is evaluating against that service principal's access, not the actual viewer's, and that service principal usually has broad access by design since it's meant for the BI team generally. My second question is whether this is Import mode, because if it is, the filter only applied once at refresh time under whoever's identity ran that refresh — every viewer after that sees the same cached snapshot with zero per-viewer filtering happening at query time at all, which is actually a more serious version of the same underlying problem. Depending on which it is, the fix is either switching the model to per-user OAuth pass-through on a live connection, or, if Import mode has to stay for performance, building Power BI's own row-level security roles that mirror the Unity Catalog logic exactly — which I'd flag honestly isn't ideal, because now that rule has to be maintained correctly in two places instead of one.
commonMistakes: Assumes the row filter itself is broken without first checking the authentication/connection mode
Doesn't distinguish Import mode (filtered once at refresh) from live/DirectQuery (filtered per query) as fundamentally different failure modes
Proposes fixing this purely at the Power BI RLS layer without addressing the underlying Unity Catalog pass-through issue
Doesn't recognize that a shared service principal typically has broader access than any individual viewer should have
keyPoints: Correctly identifies authentication/credential pass-through as the most likely cause
Correctly distinguishes Import mode's refresh-time filtering from live-connection per-query filtering
Explains why a shared service principal defeats the intended row filter
Proposes the correct fix depending on which cause is confirmed
Acknowledges the governance cost of maintaining duplicate RLS logic if Import mode must stay

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the authentication/pass-through root cause
Correctly distinguishes Import vs. live-connection filtering behavior
Proposes correct, concrete fixes for both scenarios
Acknowledges the governance tradeoff of duplicate RLS logic

questions.title: A Kappa-Style Reprocessing Run Fails After a Schema Change
questions.prompt: A Kappa-architecture pipeline that replays its Bronze Delta log to rebuild Silver/Gold after a logic change starts failing partway through replay, several months into the historical window, because an upstream schema changed at that point in history. Diagnose and fix.
questions.modelAnswer:
This is the central operational risk of Kappa architectures that doesn't show up in the simple version of the pattern: replaying a long historical window means the replay job has to correctly handle every schema the source has ever had during that window, not just its current schema, because the Bronze log faithfully preserved whatever shape the data actually was in at each point in time. A replay job written against today's schema will fail or silently misinterpret data the moment it hits the historical point where a column was renamed, a type changed, or a field was added, because the transformation logic assumes a single static schema rather than a schema that evolved partway through the window being replayed.

The immediate fix is to identify exactly where in the historical timeline the schema changed (Delta's schema history, via DESCRIBE HISTORY on Bronze or examining the actual failing batch's data, will show this) and make the Silver transformation schema-version-aware — either branching the transformation logic on an effective-date boundary (read the old shape before date X with one mapping, the new shape after with another, normalizing both to the current target schema), or, if the schema changes were additive and backward-compatible, handling them with coalesce/default-value logic rather than hard column references that assume presence. For the durable fix, I would build an explicit schema-registry-style versioning into the Bronze layer itself going forward — recording which schema version was in effect for each batch as metadata — so a future replay doesn't require archaeology through DESCRIBE HISTORY to reconstruct what changed and when; this is the practical cost of Kappa's single-codebase benefit that has to be paid deliberately, by treating schema evolution as a first-class, versioned concern in the pipeline design, rather than assuming the replay logic will always match whatever the source happened to look like.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is the real cost of Kappa that people don't appreciate until they hit it — replaying history means your transformation logic has to correctly handle every schema the source has ever had during that window, not just the one it has today. My first step is pinning down exactly where in the timeline the schema actually changed, which Delta's history and the failing batch itself will show pretty clearly. Then I make the Silver transformation schema-version-aware rather than assuming one static shape — either branching the logic on an effective-date boundary so data before and after the change get mapped differently into the same target schema, or handling it with defensive coalesce logic if the change was additive. But the fix I'd actually push for afterward is building explicit schema versioning into Bronze itself going forward, recording which schema was in effect per batch as metadata, so the next time I need to replay history, I'm not doing archaeology through table history to figure out what changed and when — I already know.
commonMistakes: Writes replay logic against only the current schema, assuming history never changed shape
Doesn't pinpoint the exact historical boundary where the schema changed before attempting a fix
Treats this as a one-off patch instead of building schema versioning into the pipeline going forward
Doesn't recognize this as a known structural cost of Kappa architecture that needs deliberate design, not just a bug
keyPoints: Correctly identifies historical schema evolution as the root cause
Uses Delta's history/metadata to pinpoint the exact schema-change boundary
Proposes schema-version-aware (branching or defensive) transformation logic
Proposes building explicit schema versioning into Bronze for future replays
Recognizes this as an inherent Kappa-architecture cost requiring deliberate design

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses historical schema evolution as the root cause
Proposes a correct immediate fix for the failing replay
Proposes a durable schema-versioning mechanism
Articulates this as an inherent Kappa tradeoff requiring deliberate design

questions.title: Multi-Region Replication Lag Breaks a Consistency Guarantee
questions.prompt: A multi-region lakehouse setup replicates Delta tables from a primary region to a secondary region for disaster recovery, and an audit discovers the secondary region was silently 40 minutes behind for two weeks due to a stuck replication job, during which a failover drill would have served stale data as if it were current. Diagnose and fix the systemic gap.
questions.modelAnswer:
The specific stuck-job cause matters less here than the systemic gap it exposed: a replication lag of 40 minutes existing silently for two weeks means there was no active monitoring of replication lag itself, only an assumption that replication was working because no error was thrown — a stuck or slow replication job often doesn't error, it just falls behind, and without an explicit lag metric being tracked and alerted on, that's invisible until someone goes looking, which in this case was an audit rather than the monitoring system doing its job. I'd first find the actual technical cause of the stuck job (a transient network partition, a credential expiry, a resource constraint on the replication compute, or a conflict with a concurrent schema change on the source) so it can be fixed directly, but I would treat that as the less important half of the finding.

The systemic fix is building an explicit, continuously monitored replication-lag metric — comparing the latest committed version/timestamp on the primary against the latest applied version/timestamp on the secondary, on a short interval, with an alert threshold tied to the organization's actual RPO (recovery point objective) for this data, not an arbitrary number. If the RPO is 15 minutes, a lag approaching that should page someone well before it silently grows to 40 and stays there for two weeks. I would also use this incident to question whether failover drills were actually validating the secondary's freshness as part of the drill itself — a failover drill that doesn't check 'is the data we just failed over to actually current' isn't really testing disaster recovery, it's testing that failover mechanically works, which is a different and less important thing. Going forward, every DR drill should include an explicit lag/freshness check as a pass/fail criterion, not just confirm the failover completed.
questions.professionalAnswer: The specific cause of the stuck job matters, but it's not the real finding here — the real finding is that a 40-minute lag sat there silently for two weeks, which tells me there was no active monitoring of replication lag itself, just an assumption that no error meant it was working. Stuck or slow replication often doesn't throw an error, it just quietly falls behind, so without an explicit lag metric being tracked and alerted on, this is invisible until an audit happens to catch it, which is exactly what happened. I'd fix the specific stuck-job cause, sure, but what I'd actually push hardest on afterward is building a continuous lag metric tied to the org's real recovery point objective — if RPO is 15 minutes, I want a page well before the lag gets anywhere near that, not after it's been sitting at 40 minutes for two weeks. And I'd use this to question whether our DR drills were ever actually checking data freshness as part of the drill, because a failover drill that just confirms the mechanism works without checking whether the data you failed over to is actually current isn't really testing disaster recovery.
commonMistakes: Focuses only on fixing the specific stuck-job cause without addressing the missing monitoring systemically
Assumes 'no error thrown' is equivalent to 'replication is healthy'
Sets an arbitrary lag alert threshold instead of tying it to the organization's actual RPO
Doesn't question whether DR drills were validating data freshness as part of the drill itself
keyPoints: Correctly identifies the systemic monitoring gap as the real finding, not just the stuck job
Recognizes that stuck replication often fails silently rather than erroring
Proposes a continuous lag metric tied to the actual RPO
Proposes alerting well before the RPO threshold, not at it
Proposes adding freshness validation as a pass/fail criterion in DR drills

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the immediate technical cause
Correctly identifies the systemic monitoring gap as the real finding
Proposes a sound RPO-tied lag monitoring/alerting mechanism
Proposes improving DR drill validation to include freshness checks

questions.title: System Design: An Enterprise Data Platform From Scratch
questions.prompt: A $2B manufacturing company has 40 disconnected source systems (ERP, MES, CRM, IoT sensors on the factory floor), no central data platform, and leadership wants one 18-month program to deliver governed self-service reporting, a reliable financial close pipeline, and a foundation for future ML use cases. Design the end-to-end data architecture.
questions.modelAnswer:
I would land every source — ERP batch exports, MES/IoT streaming telemetry, CRM API pulls — into a single Bronze layer under one lakehouse (Databricks or Fabric, chosen based on the existing Azure/Microsoft investment and the team's skill profile) rather than building bespoke per-source pipelines, using a metadata-driven ingestion framework so the 40th and 41st source are configuration, not new code. Governance (Unity Catalog or an equivalent single catalog) gets established at the same time as Bronze, not bolted on afterward, because retrofitting access control and lineage onto 40 sources after the fact is dramatically more expensive than building it in from day one.

Silver enforces data quality and conformance — standardized dimensions (one customer, one product, one plant hierarchy) built once and reused, with explicit, auditable quarantine for violations rather than silent drops, since a financial close pipeline absolutely cannot tolerate silently dropped or misclassified transactions. Gold splits into domain-specific marts (finance, operations, sales) each owned by the relevant business function with the platform team providing the infrastructure, which sets up a lightweight data-mesh-style ownership model appropriate for an org this size without over-engineering a full mesh on day one. The semantic layer sits on top as a single source of truth for metric definitions, with Power BI (or the org's existing BI tool) consuming governed metrics rather than reimplementing them.

For the 18-month program specifically, I would sequence delivery so the financial close pipeline — the highest-stakes, most time-boxed requirement — gets dedicated focus and a stricter data contract from month one, self-service reporting rolls out domain by domain as each Gold mart stabilizes rather than all at once, and the ML foundation is satisfied simply by the Silver layer existing as clean, governed, feature-ready data — I would explicitly not build any bespoke ML infrastructure in this phase, since the real foundation for future ML is having trustworthy data, not a feature store nobody's ready to use yet.
questions.professionalAnswer: With 40 disconnected sources and three different stated goals, my instinct is to refuse to treat this as three separate projects — I'd build one lakehouse with one metadata-driven ingestion layer so onboarding source 41 next year is a config change, not a new pipeline. Governance gets built in from day one, not bolted on later, because retrofitting access control across 40 sources after they're already flowing is a much bigger, much riskier project than building it alongside ingestion. For the financial close pipeline specifically, I'd give that its own stricter data contract and dedicated attention starting month one, because that's the requirement with zero tolerance for being wrong or late. Self-service reporting I'd roll out domain by domain as each area's Gold layer actually stabilizes, not as one big-bang launch at month eighteen. And for the ML foundation — I'd be honest with leadership that the right investment right now isn't a feature store or an ML platform, it's just making sure the Silver layer is clean, governed, and trustworthy, because that's actually what unlocks ML later; building ML infrastructure before the data underneath it is solid is a classic way to waste a budget line.
questions.example: A concrete sequencing decision: MES/IoT streaming data from the factory floor gets its own Bronze ingestion path using Structured Streaming from month one (since sensor data volume and velocity won't wait), while several lower-priority CRM and vendor-management sources are deliberately deferred to month 10-14 because they don't block the financial close or core reporting deliverables.
