Treats governance as a later phase instead of building it alongside Bronze ingestion from day one
Builds ML infrastructure (feature store, model registry) prematurely instead of prioritizing clean, governed Silver data as the actual ML foundation
Attempts a single big-bang launch instead of sequencing delivery by domain and business criticality
Gives the financial close pipeline the same contract rigor as every other dataset instead of elevated, explicit rigor
keyPoints: Designs one unified, metadata-driven ingestion layer rather than per-source pipelines
Builds governance in from day one alongside Bronze, not retrofitted later
Enforces data quality with auditable quarantine, appropriate for a financial close pipeline
Proposes domain-owned Gold marts appropriate to the org's scale
Sequences the 18-month delivery by business criticality rather than attempting a big-bang launch
Correctly scopes the ML requirement to clean governed data, not premature ML tooling

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Designs a coherent, unified end-to-end architecture
Builds governance in from the start, appropriately scoped
Addresses the financial close pipeline's elevated rigor requirement
Proposes a realistic, risk-aware 18-month sequencing plan

deepDive.heading: Clarifying the real requirement
deepDive.content: Three stated goals — self-service reporting, a reliable financial close pipeline, and an ML foundation — are not three separate platforms; they are three consumers of the same underlying governed data, and treating them as separate initiatives is the single most common way this kind of program fragments into incompatible silos again. The financial close pipeline carries the highest consequence of being wrong (regulatory and audit exposure), so its data contract needs to be stricter than the rest even though it shares the same underlying platform.

deepDive.heading: Ingestion layer
deepDive.content: A metadata-driven framework (one control table describing each of the 40 sources' connection, load type, and watermark strategy) feeding a small number of generic, parameterized pipelines, so onboarding source 41 is a configuration row, not new pipeline code. ERP batch exports land via scheduled Copy/pipeline runs; MES and IoT sensor telemetry land via Structured Streaming given their volume and the operational desire for near-real-time plant visibility; CRM and other SaaS sources land via API-based connectors on a schedule appropriate to their change frequency.

deepDive.heading: Medallion structure and data quality
deepDive.content: Bronze is raw and append-only, partitioned by ingestion date, under one Unity-Catalog-governed metastore. Silver conforms dimensions once — a single customer, product, and plant hierarchy used by every downstream domain — and enforces data quality via pipeline expectations with an explicit, queryable quarantine table, which is non-negotiable for anything feeding the financial close. Gold is organized into domain-owned marts (finance, operations, sales) so each business function owns its own metric logic and SLA, with the platform team owning the shared infrastructure, dimensions, and governance standards underneath.

deepDive.heading: Governance
deepDive.content: Access control, lineage, and PII classification are established at the same time Bronze ingestion begins, not after. Column-level lineage lets the finance team prove, to an auditor, exactly which source transaction a Gold financial figure traces back to. Row/column security (row filters for plant- or region-scoped visibility, column masks for sensitive HR/payroll data flowing in from the ERP) is defined centrally once and enforced consistently regardless of which BI tool or query engine touches the data.

deepDive.heading: Semantic layer and serving
deepDive.content: A single governed semantic layer (dbt Semantic Layer, or the BI tool's own semantic model fed from governed Gold tables) defines business metrics once, so self-service reporting across domains doesn't reinvent 'gross margin' or 'on-time delivery rate' per business unit. The financial close pipeline gets its own dedicated, more tightly contracted Gold tables with a reconciliation step against the ERP's own ledger totals before being considered final, rather than relying on the same looser validation as general reporting marts.

deepDive.heading: Sequencing the 18 months
deepDive.content: Months 1-4: ingestion framework, governance foundation, and the highest-priority sources (ERP financial modules, core MES/IoT telemetry) land in Bronze/Silver. Months 3-8: the financial close pipeline gets dedicated build-out and parallel validation against the legacy close process before cutover. Months 5-14: self-service reporting rolls out domain by domain as each Gold mart stabilizes, prioritized by business value and source readiness, not launched all at once. Throughout: Silver's conformed, governed structure is explicitly the ML foundation delivered in this phase — no bespoke ML infrastructure is built until a concrete, funded ML use case exists.

deepDive.heading: Key risks and mitigations
deepDive.content: The biggest risk to an 18-month program this broad is scope creep from business units wanting their reporting first; a steering committee with an explicit, criticality-based prioritization (finance close first, by mandate) protects the sequencing. The second risk is 40 sources meaning 40 different data-quality surprises; the metadata-driven framework's schema-drift detection and the quarantine-based Silver layer are what keep one bad source from derailing the whole program rather than just one domain's delivery date.

questions.title: Snowflake vs. Databricks vs. Fabric: A Real Decision Framework
questions.prompt: A CTO asks you to settle an internal debate: should the company standardize on Snowflake, Databricks, or Microsoft Fabric as its primary data platform? Give a genuine decision framework rather than a single universal answer, and state what you'd actually recommend for a mid-size company that is heavily invested in Power BI and Microsoft 365, with a data science team that wants more Python/ML flexibility than its current warehouse gives it.
questions.modelAnswer:
There is no universally correct answer because the three platforms optimize for genuinely different center-of-gravity use cases, and pretending one is categorically 'best' is how this kind of decision ends up being re-litigated every two years. Snowflake's strength is SQL-first analytics at scale with minimal operational overhead — storage/compute separation, strong governance (RBAC, tagging, Secure Data Sharing), and a very mature, low-friction experience for analysts and BI teams, but it is comparatively less natural for teams doing heavy custom Python/ML work or wanting direct control over file formats and compute engines, even though Snowpark has narrowed that gap meaningfully. Databricks' strength is exactly the opposite center of gravity: it is the strongest choice for teams doing substantial data science, ML, and custom Spark/Python engineering, with Unity Catalog providing comparable governance to Snowflake's RBAC and Delta Lake as an open, portable storage format, but it asks more of the team operationally (cluster/job management, though serverless options have reduced this) and its SQL-analyst experience, while much improved via Databricks SQL, is still not as instantly frictionless for a pure BI audience as Snowflake's. Fabric's strength is deep, native integration with Power BI and the Microsoft 365 ecosystem under one OneLake storage layer and one capacity-based billing model, which removes a lot of integration friction for an organization already standardized on Microsoft tooling, but it is the youngest of the three platforms and has the most evolving feature set, which carries real roadmap risk for capabilities not yet fully mature.

For the specific company described — mid-size, heavily invested in Power BI and M365, with a data science team wanting more Python/ML flexibility than its current warehouse gives it — I would recommend Fabric as the primary platform specifically because of the existing Microsoft investment, with its Spark/notebook experience and OneLake-native lakehouse covering the data science team's flexibility need without introducing a second major platform and its own separate governance, billing, and integration surface. The caveat I would be explicit about: if the data science team's needs are not just 'more Python flexibility' but genuinely advanced, large-scale ML/MLOps work where Databricks' more mature ML tooling (MLflow, feature store maturity, broader open-source ecosystem fit) is a hard requirement, that's a real reason to run Databricks specifically for that workload with Fabric or the existing stack remaining the BI/reporting platform — a deliberate, limited polyglot choice rather than an uncontrolled one, which is a materially different situation from the uncoordinated multi-platform sprawl I'd otherwise be trying to avoid.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell the CTO directly that anyone giving a single universal answer here is selling something, because these three platforms genuinely optimize for different things. Snowflake is the best fit when you want SQL-first analytics with the least operational overhead and your team is mostly analysts and BI people. Databricks is the best fit when you've got real data science and ML engineering happening and you want an open storage format and deep Python/Spark flexibility, at the cost of a bit more operational ownership. Fabric is the best fit when you're already deeply invested in Power BI and Microsoft 365 and want one integrated storage layer and billing model, with the tradeoff that it's the newest of the three and some capabilities are still maturing. For this specific company, given how much they're already invested in Power BI and M365, I'd lean toward Fabric as the primary platform, because its native Spark and lakehouse experience under OneLake should cover the data science team's flexibility ask without taking on a second major platform's governance and integration surface. The one thing I'd flag honestly: if what the data science team actually needs is deep, mature MLOps tooling, not just 'more Python,' that's a legitimate reason to run Databricks specifically for that workload alongside Fabric for BI — a deliberate, scoped two-platform choice, which is a very different thing from accidental platform sprawl.

Ignores the existing organizational investment (Microsoft ecosystem) as a legitimate decision factor
Treats 'wants more Python/ML flexibility' as automatically requiring Databricks without checking whether Fabric's native Spark experience would satisfy it
Recommends running multiple platforms without framing it as a deliberate, scoped decision versus uncontrolled sprawl

Avoids declaring a single universally correct platform

deepDive.heading: Why there is no universal answer
deepDive.content: The three platforms differ most in their center of gravity, not in raw capability — all three can technically do SQL analytics and all three can technically run Python, but each is optimized for a different primary user and workload, and the 'right' choice depends on which user population and workload dominates the organization's actual needs.

deepDive.heading: Snowflake's fit
deepDive.content: Best when the dominant workload is SQL-first analytics and BI at scale, the team is mostly analysts rather than engineers, and minimizing operational overhead (no cluster management, transparent scaling) is a high priority. Governance via native RBAC, tagging, and masking policies is mature and well understood. The relative weak point is deep custom ML/engineering work, though Snowpark narrows this.

deepDive.heading: Databricks' fit
deepDive.content: Best when the dominant workload includes substantial data science, ML engineering, or custom Spark/Python pipeline work, and the organization values an open, portable storage format (Delta Lake, usable outside Databricks itself). Unity Catalog provides comparable governance maturity to Snowflake. The relative weak point is a steeper operational learning curve for pure SQL/BI users, though Databricks SQL has narrowed this considerably.

deepDive.heading: Fabric's fit
deepDive.content: Best when the organization is already deeply invested in Power BI and Microsoft 365, and the value of one integrated OneLake storage layer, one capacity-based billing model, and native Power BI integration outweighs the risk of adopting the newest and still-maturing of the three platforms. Its Spark/notebook experience can meaningfully serve data science needs without introducing a second platform, provided the ML requirements aren't at the deepest, most specialized end.

deepDive.heading: Applying it to this company
deepDive.content: Given heavy existing Power BI/M365 investment, Fabric is the recommended primary platform: it minimizes new integration surface and billing complexity, and its native lakehouse/Spark capability should satisfy a 'more Python/ML flexibility than our current warehouse' ask for most mid-size data science teams. The decision should be revisited specifically, and only, if the data science team's actual requirement turns out to need Databricks-grade MLOps maturity.

deepDive.heading: When a scoped second platform is legitimate
deepDive.content: If advanced ML/MLOps truly is a hard requirement, running Databricks specifically for that workload while Fabric remains the BI/reporting platform is a legitimate, deliberate architecture — the key discipline is keeping it scoped and governed (clear ownership of which workloads live where, consistent governance standards across both) rather than letting it become an unplanned, ungoverned second platform that duplicates effort.

questions.title: System Design: Migrating a Legacy On-Prem SQL Server Estate to the Cloud
questions.prompt: A 15-year-old on-prem SQL Server estate (200+ databases, nightly SSIS/SSRS reporting, dozens of brittle linked-server dependencies) needs to move to a cloud lakehouse platform over 12 months without a reporting outage the business would notice. Design the migration architecture and sequencing.
questions.modelAnswer:
The first architectural decision is explicitly rejecting a big-bang cutover: with 200+ databases and dozens of brittle linked-server dependencies that almost certainly aren't fully documented anywhere, a single cutover date guarantees discovering unknown dependencies in production during the cutover window, which is the worst possible time to discover them. The approach is a strangler-pattern migration: stand up the target cloud platform (Databricks or Fabric, depending on the org's broader direction) alongside the existing SQL Server estate, and migrate databases in dependency-ordered waves — starting with databases that have the fewest linked-server dependents, not the ones that are most valuable or most urgent, because migrating a heavily-depended-upon database first means carrying the burden of keeping dozens of consumers working against a moved target simultaneously.

Before any wave begins, I would invest real time in a dependency discovery pass — querying SQL Server's own DMVs and linked-server catalog views across the whole estate to build an actual dependency graph, since 15 years of accumulated linked-server references almost certainly includes connections nobody currently on the team knows exist, and migrating without this risks silently breaking a report or a downstream system that was never in the migration plan's awareness. For each wave, data replicates to the cloud platform and runs in parallel with the legacy source for a validation window (reconciling row counts and key aggregates between old and new), reports get repointed to the new source only after that validation passes and a business-owner sign-off is obtained for that specific domain, and the legacy SSIS/SSRS artifacts for that wave are decommissioned only after a full reporting cycle (including any month-end or quarter-end processes) has run successfully against the new platform — not immediately after a successful validation window, because some of the riskiest dependencies (a quarterly report, a year-end close process) only surface on their own cadence, not daily. Linked-server dependencies crossing wave boundaries (a database already migrated being queried via linked server from one not yet migrated) need an explicit bridging strategy — typically a view or a temporary data-sync job replicating just the needed slice back to the legacy environment — so no wave is blocked waiting for every dependent database to migrate simultaneously.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd kill is any plan involving a single cutover date — with 200-plus databases and a decade and a half of linked-server dependencies that are almost certainly not fully documented, a big-bang approach just guarantees we find out about an unknown dependency during the cutover window, which is the worst possible time. I'd run this as a strangler migration instead: stand the new platform up alongside the old one, and migrate in dependency-ordered waves starting with the databases that have the fewest things depending on them, not the ones that feel most urgent. Before wave one even starts, I'd spend real time querying SQL Server's own system views to actually map the linked-server dependency graph, because I guarantee there are connections in this estate nobody currently on the team knows about. For each wave, I run old and new in parallel, reconcile the numbers, get an explicit sign-off from the business owner for that domain, and — this is the part people skip — I don't decommission the old system for that wave until it's survived a full reporting cycle on the new platform, including whatever quarterly or year-end process touches it, because that's exactly the kind of dependency that only shows up once a quarter and would otherwise slip through a two-week validation window.
questions.example: A concrete bridging case: Database A (finance, migrated in wave 2) is still queried via linked server by Database B (operations, not scheduled to migrate until wave 6); rather than forcing B to migrate early or blocking A's cutover, a lightweight sync job replicates the specific tables B needs back into a legacy-compatible shape inside the on-prem SQL Server environment until wave 6 arrives.

deepDive.heading: Why big-bang is the wrong call here
deepDive.content: 200+ databases with 15 years of accumulated, likely-undocumented linked-server dependencies means the actual dependency graph is unknown at the start of the project. A single cutover date forces every unknown dependency to surface simultaneously, in production, at the moment of maximum risk — the only defensible approach is incremental, dependency-ordered migration that surfaces unknowns in small, recoverable batches.

deepDive.heading: Dependency discovery
deepDive.content: Before wave sequencing is finalized, query sys.sql_expression_dependencies, sys.servers (linked servers), and SSIS catalog execution logs across the full estate to build an actual, evidence-based dependency graph rather than relying on tribal knowledge or existing architecture diagrams, which are routinely stale on an estate this old.

deepDive.heading: Wave sequencing
deepDive.content: Databases with the fewest inbound dependencies migrate first, proving out the migration tooling and process on lower-risk targets before tackling the handful of heavily-depended-upon core databases later, by which point the team has a validated playbook rather than learning it on the highest-stakes system.

deepDive.heading: Parallel run and validation
deepDive.content: Each wave's data lands in the cloud lakehouse and runs alongside the legacy source for a defined window, with automated reconciliation (row counts, key financial/operational aggregates) comparing old and new outputs. Reports are repointed to the new source only after reconciliation passes and the responsible business owner explicitly signs off — not on the migration team's own assessment alone, since the business owner is the one who will notice a subtle discrepancy the reconciliation script might miss.

deepDive.heading: Decommissioning discipline
deepDive.content: Legacy SSIS/SSRS artifacts for a migrated wave are not decommissioned immediately after validation passes; they stay live until a full reporting cycle, including any quarterly or year-end process that touches that domain, has successfully completed against the new platform at least once, because the riskiest dependencies are often the ones that only run on a quarterly or annual cadence.

deepDive.heading: Cross-wave dependency bridging
deepDive.content: A linked-server dependency that crosses a wave boundary (a migrated database still being queried by a not-yet-migrated one) is handled with an explicit bridging mechanism — a compatibility view, or a small sync job replicating just the needed slice back into the legacy environment — so no wave is held hostage waiting for every dependent database across the entire estate to migrate in lockstep.

deepDive.heading: Communicating risk to the business
deepDive.content: Throughout the 12 months, the business needs visibility into which wave is in flight, what's been validated, and what the rollback option is for the current wave specifically — not just a single overall 'migration status' that hides which parts are actually de-risked versus still in parallel-run validation.

questions.title: System Design: Medallion Architecture Across Multiple Business Units
questions.prompt: A holding company with four largely autonomous business units (each with its own ERP and its own definition of 'customer') wants one consolidated lakehouse for executive reporting, while each business unit keeps full autonomy over its own operational systems. Design the medallion architecture and the governance model that makes consolidated reporting possible without forcing the business units onto one shared operational system.
questions.modelAnswer:
The architecture has to separate two things that are easy to conflate: operational system consolidation (which this holding company explicitly does not want) and reporting-layer consolidation (which it does want), and the medallion design should only touch the latter. Each business unit's ERP lands independently into its own Bronze tables under one shared lakehouse and catalog — same platform, same governance model, but each business unit's raw data stays structurally separate and is owned by that business unit, which respects their operational autonomy while still getting everyone onto one platform for the parts that actually need consolidating.

The hard problem is Silver: each business unit's 'customer' has a different definition, different ID scheme, and possibly genuinely different business meaning (a customer in a B2B unit versus a consumer customer in a retail unit), so a single global customer dimension built by simply unioning four ERPs' customer tables would either force an inappropriate conformance or silently misrepresent genuine business differences. The correct approach is a conformed 'enterprise customer' dimension built deliberately, as its own project, with each business unit's data steward involved in defining the actual match/merge/mapping rules — probably using a combination of deterministic keys where available (tax ID, a shared account number from an intercompany system) and fuzzy matching with a human review queue for ambiguous cases, with full transparency into which source each conformed customer record maps back to, so a business unit can always trace a consolidated number back to their own ERP without having to trust a black box. Gold layer for executive reporting then builds on this conformed dimension, with the consolidated metrics' definitions documented and agreed across all four business units before being presented at the holding-company level — because an executive comparing business units needs to actually be comparing the same calculation, not four different units' versions of 'revenue' and 'customer count' that happen to share a label. Each business unit keeps its own domain-level Gold marts for unit-specific reporting that don't need to go through the conformance exercise at all, since that level of rigor is only required for genuinely cross-unit comparisons.
questions.professionalAnswer: The key move here is separating two things that are easy to mix up: this company doesn't want to consolidate operational systems, but it does want consolidated reporting, and the medallion design should only touch the reporting side. Each business unit's ERP lands into its own Bronze tables on one shared platform — same governance, separate ownership, so nobody loses operational autonomy, they're just now on common infrastructure. The real work is at Silver, specifically building a conformed enterprise customer dimension, because four business units almost certainly have four genuinely different notions of what a customer even is, not just four different ID formats. I wouldn't try to solve that with a quick union-and-dedupe — I'd treat it as its own project with each business unit's data steward actually involved in defining the matching rules, using deterministic keys where they exist and a human review queue for the ambiguous cases, and I'd make sure every conformed record is traceable back to its source so a business unit can always verify a consolidated number against their own system rather than just trusting it. Gold for executive reporting builds on that conformed dimension with metric definitions agreed across all four units up front, because an executive comparing units needs to know they're actually comparing the same calculation. Below that, each unit keeps its own Gold marts for unit-specific reporting that never needed this level of conformance rigor in the first place.

deepDive.heading: Separating two different consolidations
deepDive.content: The holding company wants consolidated reporting, not consolidated operations — the architecture must respect that distinction explicitly, or the project will be perceived (correctly) as a backdoor attempt to standardize the business units' operational systems, which will generate political resistance that has nothing to do with the technical design.

deepDive.heading: Bronze layer
deepDive.content: Each business unit's ERP lands into its own Bronze tables, on shared infrastructure and under one catalog for governance consistency, but owned and structured independently per unit. No attempt is made to reconcile anything at this layer — Bronze simply reflects each source faithfully.

deepDive.heading: The conformed customer dimension
deepDive.content: This is the project's genuine hard problem, treated as its own deliberate workstream rather than an incidental step. Each business unit's data steward participates in defining match/merge rules: deterministic matching on shared identifiers where they exist (tax ID, an intercompany account number), probabilistic/fuzzy matching with a human review queue for ambiguous cases, and an explicit decision log for cases where two business units genuinely disagree about whether two records represent the same real-world customer.

deepDive.heading: Traceability and trust
deepDive.content: Every conformed customer record retains a mapping back to its source business unit and source ID, so any business unit can verify a consolidated figure against their own system rather than being asked to simply trust the holding company's number — this traceability is what makes the conformed dimension politically viable, not just technically correct.

deepDive.heading: Gold layer and metric governance
deepDive.content: Cross-unit executive metrics (consolidated revenue, consolidated customer count) are defined once, agreed by all four business units' finance leads before being published, and documented in a shared metric glossary. Unit-specific Gold marts for each business unit's own internal reporting remain separate and don't require this conformance overhead, since comparing a unit against only itself doesn't need the enterprise dimension at all.

deepDive.heading: Governance model
deepDive.content: Access control reflects the same autonomy principle: each business unit's leadership can see their own detailed data and the consolidated enterprise view, but not another business unit's unit-specific detail unless explicitly granted — row-level security scoped by business unit on the shared platform enforces this without requiring separate infrastructure per unit.

deepDive.heading: Where this can fail
deepDive.content: The most common failure mode is rushing the conformed-dimension workstream to hit a reporting deadline, producing a customer dimension that's technically complete but that business units don't trust because they weren't meaningfully involved in the matching rules — once a business unit catches one wrong conformance decision, they stop trusting the consolidated numbers entirely, which undoes the entire point of the project.

questions.title: System Design: Real-Time Fraud Monitoring — Lambda or Kappa, Concretely
questions.prompt: Design the architecture for a real-time fraud-monitoring system that must score transactions within 200ms, support same-day analyst investigation with full historical context, and allow monthly retraining of the scoring model against corrected (fraud-confirmed) labels that only become known weeks later. Decide explicitly between Lambda and Kappa and justify every major component.
questions.modelAnswer:
This system has three genuinely different latency and correctness requirements layered on the same data, and the architecture should be judged on how well it serves all three without three separate codebases. The 200ms scoring requirement needs a true low-latency path: transaction events flow through a streaming engine (Structured Streaming in continuous or very short micro-batch mode, or a dedicated feature-serving layer) that computes or looks up precomputed features and calls the model within the latency budget — this path cannot depend on a full Delta table scan or a slow join, so recent aggregated features (velocity counts, recent transaction patterns per account) need to be maintained in a low-latency store (a streaming state store or a fast key-value cache) updated incrementally as events arrive, not recomputed from scratch per transaction.

For same-day analyst investigation with full historical context, the same events that fed the scoring path also land, via the same ingestion, into a Bronze Delta table, giving analysts a durable, queryable, complete history to pull up a flagged account's full transaction pattern — this is the Kappa property doing real work: one ingestion path serves both the real-time scorer and the historical investigation view, rather than a separate batch ETL job that might lag behind what the real-time system just scored.

For monthly retraining against fraud-confirmed labels that only become known weeks later, this is where I'd deliberately introduce a batch-like step without calling the whole architecture Lambda: retraining reads the same Bronze/Silver Delta tables in batch mode, joined against the now-available confirmed-label table, to build a training set — using the identical feature computation logic as the real-time path (ideally the same feature definitions executed through a shared feature store or shared code library, not reimplemented separately for training versus serving) so there's no train/serve skew. I would characterize this overall design as Kappa for the ingestion and serving backbone (one event log, one real-time consumer, one historical-investigation consumer) with a batch retraining job layered on top that deliberately reuses the same feature logic — not a classic Lambda architecture, because there is no separate batch recomputation of the real-time scoring path's own output, only a separate consumer (retraining) reading the same underlying log on its own schedule, which is exactly what Kappa's replay-from-log model is meant to support.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd treat this as three different consumers of the same event stream rather than three different systems, and that framing is what drives the Lambda-versus-Kappa decision. For the 200ms scoring requirement, I need a genuinely low-latency path — features maintained incrementally in a fast state store or cache as events arrive, not recomputed from a table scan per transaction, feeding the model within budget. For same-day analyst investigation, I want the exact same ingested events landing in a durable Delta table, so analysts get full historical context without me running a separate, possibly-lagging batch ETL just for investigation — that's the real benefit of one shared log serving both needs. For monthly retraining against labels that only show up weeks later, I do introduce a batch step, but I'd be careful not to call this Lambda just because there's a batch job somewhere — the critical discipline is that retraining uses the identical feature computation logic as the real-time path, ideally through a shared feature store or shared code, specifically to avoid train/serve skew. So I'd describe this as a Kappa-style single event log serving multiple consumers — real-time scoring, historical investigation, and periodic retraining — rather than two independently-maintained Lambda pipelines that could quietly drift apart.

deepDive.heading: Reframing the problem as three consumers of one stream
deepDive.content: Rather than three separate systems, this is one event log (transaction events) with three consumers at three different latency/correctness tiers: a sub-200ms scorer, a same-day historical-investigation query surface, and a monthly batch retraining job. Designing from this framing is what makes a Kappa-leaning architecture the natural fit rather than three bespoke pipelines.

deepDive.heading: Real-time scoring path
deepDive.content: Transaction events are ingested via a streaming source (Kafka/Event Hubs) and processed with Structured Streaming maintaining incrementally-updated feature aggregates (velocity counts, recent category mix, geolocation deviation) in a low-latency state store or external fast cache, since recomputing these from a cold table scan per transaction cannot meet a 200ms budget. The model call itself needs to be co-located or network-close to the feature store to keep latency inside budget.

deepDive.heading: Historical investigation path
deepDive.content: The same ingested events land, via the same pipeline, into a Bronze Delta table with no additional ETL step specific to investigation — analysts query this directly (through a SQL interface) to pull a flagged account's full transaction history, which is both simpler to maintain and guaranteed to be consistent with what the real-time scorer actually saw, since it's literally the same data.

deepDive.heading: Retraining path and the skew problem
deepDive.content: Monthly retraining joins the Bronze/Silver event history against a confirmed-fraud-label table that only becomes available weeks later. The critical design discipline is that the features used in training are computed with the identical logic as the real-time feature store — via a shared feature store framework or a shared code library compiled for both streaming and batch execution — rather than a data scientist independently reimplementing 'transactions in the last 10 minutes' as a batch SQL query that subtly differs from the streaming version's window boundary handling.

deepDive.heading: Why this is Kappa, not Lambda
deepDive.content: Lambda would mean two independently-implemented pipelines producing the same real-time output through different code paths merged at serving time. Here there is exactly one real-time output path; the batch component is a separate consumer (retraining) reading the same log on its own schedule for a different purpose (building a training set), which is precisely what Kappa's single-log, multiple-consumer model supports, not a parallel reimplementation of the scoring logic itself.

deepDive.heading: Operational risks
deepDive.content: The state store backing real-time features needs its own disaster-recovery and rebuild strategy (rebuilding it by replaying recent Bronze history after an outage), and the feature-sharing mechanism between streaming and batch needs active governance — if the shared feature library drifts into two versions anyway because of a rushed change, the entire argument for this architecture's safety collapses, so this needs to be enforced via CI, not just convention.

questions.title: System Design: One Governance Model Across Unity Catalog, Purview, and Power BI
questions.prompt: A multi-business-unit enterprise runs Databricks (governed by Unity Catalog), has Microsoft Purview deployed for compliance cataloging, and distributes reporting through Power BI with row-level security. Design the end-to-end governance architecture — classification, access enforcement, lineage, and audit — that actually holds together across all three, and identify the one place this kind of design most commonly breaks down in practice.
questions.modelAnswer:
The design principle is to assign each tool the role it actually performs well and avoid asking any one of them to do a job it wasn't built for: Unity Catalog is the enforcement point for everything living in Databricks (tables, lineage for anything processed through Databricks compute, row filters and column masks), Purview is the cross-platform discovery and compliance-reporting layer that crawls Unity Catalog, Power BI, and other sources to present one searchable catalog and stitched lineage view for auditors and data stewards, and Power BI's own row-level security is the final-mile enforcement for the semantic model layer specifically. PII and sensitivity classification should be defined once — ideally as tags applied in Unity Catalog at the column level — and Purview should ingest and surface those tags rather than maintaining an independently-defined classification scheme, because two independently-maintained classification systems for the same columns is exactly the kind of drift that causes a compliance audit to fail.

Access enforcement happens at each platform's native layer: Unity Catalog grants and row/column policies control who sees what inside Databricks regardless of client tool, and Power BI's semantic model RLS should be built to mirror, not reinvent, the same business rules — ideally generated or at least validated against the same source-of-truth policy definitions rather than manually re-authored by a different team. Lineage is captured natively within Databricks by Unity Catalog for anything processed there, and Purview's role is to extend that lineage visually across to Power BI datasets and reports, giving an auditor one place to trace a specific report's number back through the semantic model, through the Gold table, back to the original Bronze ingestion — Purview itself does not enforce any of this, it visualizes and reports on what the native platforms already enforced. Audit logging similarly stays native to each platform (Databricks audit logs, Power BI activity logs) with Purview or a SIEM aggregating them for a unified compliance view rather than any single tool being asked to be the source of raw audit truth for all three.

The place this most commonly breaks down in practice is exactly the Power BI RLS mirroring step: a Databricks-native row filter gets updated when a business rule changes, but Power BI's separately-maintained RLS role definitions don't get updated in the same change, because they're owned by a different team and not covered by the same CI/CD or change-review process as the Unity Catalog policy. The durable fix is treating the semantic model's RLS definitions as code, versioned and reviewed alongside the Unity Catalog policy changes they're supposed to mirror, ideally with an automated test that periodically compares what a sample user sees through each layer and flags a mismatch — because without an active check, this drift is invisible until someone notices they can see data they shouldn't, which is the worst way to find out.
questions.professionalAnswer: My approach is to give each tool the job it's actually good at, instead of asking one tool to cover everyone's needs. Unity Catalog enforces access and captures lineage for anything inside Databricks. Purview is the cross-platform catalog and compliance view — it crawls Unity Catalog and Power BI and gives auditors one place to search and trace lineage, but it doesn't itself block a query. Power BI's own row-level security is the last-mile enforcement specifically for the semantic model. For classification, I'd define PII and sensitivity tags once, at the column level in Unity Catalog, and have Purview ingest those rather than maintaining its own separate classification — two independently-maintained classification schemes for the same data is a compliance audit waiting to fail. The part I'd flag as the actual weak point in this whole design, because I've seen it happen, is Power BI's RLS drifting out of sync with the underlying Unity Catalog row filter — someone updates the Databricks-side rule, and the Power BI RLS role, owned by a different team with a different release process, doesn't get updated in the same change. My fix for that is treating the Power BI RLS definitions as code, reviewed in the same change process as the Unity Catalog policy they're meant to mirror, and ideally backed by an automated check that periodically compares what a sample user actually sees through both layers.

Treats audit logging as something one tool should centrally own rather than natively capturing and aggregating per platform

deepDive.heading: Assigning roles correctly
deepDive.content: Unity Catalog: native enforcement and lineage for Databricks. Purview: cross-platform catalog, discovery, and compliance reporting, not enforcement. Power BI RLS: final-mile enforcement at the semantic-model layer. Every governance design problem in this scenario traces back to whether this role assignment was respected or whether one tool was asked to do a job it wasn't built for.

deepDive.heading: Classification as a single source of truth
deepDive.content: PII/sensitivity tags are defined once, at the column level, in Unity Catalog, and Purview's scanners ingest and surface those tags in its own catalog view rather than an independently-maintained Purview classification scheme for the same columns, which would otherwise drift the moment either system's tags are updated without the other.

deepDive.heading: Access enforcement layering
deepDive.content: Unity Catalog grants, row filters, and column masks enforce access for any client querying Databricks-native tables, regardless of tool. Power BI's semantic model layer needs its own RLS specifically because the semantic model's DAX-level filtering is a separate enforcement point from the underlying table — but it should be built to mirror the same business rule, not invent a new one.

deepDive.heading: Lineage: capture vs. visualization
deepDive.content: Unity Catalog captures lineage natively for anything executed on Databricks compute. Purview extends this visually, stitching Unity Catalog lineage together with Power BI dataset/report lineage so an auditor can trace one path end to end — but Purview is not itself capturing new lineage events independently; it's visualizing what the native platforms already recorded.

deepDive.heading: Audit logging
deepDive.content: Each platform's native audit log (Databricks audit logs, Power BI activity log) remains the authoritative raw record for that platform; a SIEM or Purview's compliance reporting aggregates these for a unified view, rather than any one tool being asked to generate audit truth for platforms it doesn't natively operate on.

deepDive.heading: The real breakdown point: RLS drift
deepDive.content: In practice, this design most commonly fails at the seam between Unity Catalog's row filter and Power BI's RLS role, because they're usually owned by different teams on different release cadences. A Databricks-side policy change ships without the corresponding Power BI RLS update, and the mismatch is invisible until someone notices incorrect visibility — which is the worst possible way to discover a governance gap.

deepDive.heading: Fixing the breakdown point
deepDive.content: Treat Power BI RLS role definitions as code, reviewed and deployed through the same change process as the Unity Catalog policy they mirror, and add an automated reconciliation check — periodically querying what a sample set of test users see through each layer and alerting on any mismatch — so drift is caught by monitoring within hours, not discovered by an affected user or an auditor months later.

questions.title: Designing Domain Ownership for a Data Mesh Rollout
questions.prompt: You've convinced leadership to adopt a data mesh model for a company with five product domains. Design the concrete architecture that makes domain-owned data products real rather than aspirational — what each domain actually has to produce, and what the central platform team actually provides.
questions.modelAnswer:
Each domain is responsible for publishing one or more 'data products': a Delta or Iceberg table (or a small set of tables) with a declared schema, an owner, an SLA for freshness and availability, and a registered entry in the shared catalog, built and maintained by engineers embedded in or dedicated to that domain, not by a central team on their behalf. This is the part that fails most often if skipped: domains need actual data engineering capacity assigned to them, not just a mandate to 'own their data,' or the model collapses back into the central team doing the work with extra bureaucracy layered on top. Concretely, each domain's data product is backed by its own CI/CD pipeline that runs schema/contract tests before publishing a new version, with breaking changes requiring an explicit version bump and a deprecation window for consumers, since other domains' data products may depend on it.

The central platform team's job shifts entirely: they provide and operate the shared infrastructure (the lakehouse platform itself, Unity Catalog or equivalent for cataloging and access control, the CI/CD templates domains build on top of rather than reinvent, observability/monitoring tooling) and define federated computational governance — a small set of enterprise-wide standards (naming conventions, PII handling requirements, interoperability format standards) that every domain's data product must comply with, enforced automatically where possible (a catalog registration check, an automated PII-scan gate in CI) rather than through a manual review board that becomes its own bottleneck. The platform team does not own any individual domain's transformation logic or business rules — that boundary has to be real, or domains will keep escalating ownership back to the central team the moment something gets hard, which defeats the entire point of the reorganization.
questions.professionalAnswer: The thing I'd insist on before calling this mesh instead of 'central team plus extra process' is that each domain actually has engineering capacity assigned to it — not just a mandate to own their data, but real people who can build and maintain a pipeline. Each domain publishes a data product: a table or small set of tables with a declared schema, an owner, an SLA, registered in a shared catalog, with its own CI pipeline enforcing schema contracts before anything new gets published, and a real deprecation process for breaking changes since other domains will depend on it. The central team's job completely changes under this model — they're not building domain pipelines anymore, they're building the shared platform everyone builds on top of, and defining a small set of enterprise-wide standards that get enforced automatically wherever possible, not through a manual review board that just becomes a new bottleneck with a different name. And I'd protect the boundary hard — the central team does not own any domain's actual business logic, because the moment they start absorbing that back, you've just reinvented the centralized model with more ceremony.
