Protects the ownership boundary against re-centralization

questions.title: Designing Multi-Tenant Fabric Capacity for a Holding Company
questions.prompt: A holding company wants one Microsoft Fabric tenant shared by six subsidiaries, each with its own budget and its own need to avoid being affected by another subsidiary's workload. Design the capacity architecture.
questions.modelAnswer:
The core design decision is one Fabric tenant for identity, governance, and cross-subsidiary discovery, but separate Fabric capacities (F-SKUs) per subsidiary, each provisioned and billed independently against that subsidiary's own budget — this directly addresses both stated requirements, since one tenant preserves the ability to govern consistently and allow approved cross-subsidiary data sharing via OneLake shortcuts, while separate capacities give each subsidiary's workloads their own CU pool, meaning one subsidiary's heavy Spark job or refresh storm cannot throttle another subsidiary's reports, because they're not drawing from the same pool of compute units at all.

Workspaces within the tenant are organized and assigned to each subsidiary's specific capacity, with workspace-level access control restricting who can create or move items, and a clear governance rule (enforced via tenant settings or Purview policy, not just a wiki page) that a workspace cannot be silently reassigned to a different capacity without a change-control step, since that's the most likely way this isolation gets accidentally broken later. For subsidiaries wanting to share specific curated data with each other (a common holding-company need even with separate operational autonomy), OneLake shortcuts let one subsidiary's workspace reference another's data without copying it and without needing to be on the same capacity, since shortcuts work across capacities within the same tenant. I would size each subsidiary's initial capacity based on an actual workload assessment (current report complexity, refresh frequency, expected Spark usage) rather than a uniform default, since a one-size allocation either overpays for a light subsidiary or undersizes a heavy one, and I'd set up per-capacity cost and utilization monitoring from day one so each subsidiary can see and be accountable for their own consumption against their own budget, which is also what actually makes separate billing meaningful rather than theoretical.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd do one tenant, separate capacities per subsidiary — that's the design that actually satisfies both requirements at once. One tenant keeps governance and identity consistent and still allows cross-subsidiary sharing through OneLake shortcuts when subsidiaries want it, while separate F-SKU capacities per subsidiary mean one subsidiary's heavy Spark workload literally cannot throttle another's reports, because they're not sharing a CU pool at all. I'd size each subsidiary's capacity based on an actual assessment of their current workload, not a uniform default, because a flat allocation either overpays for a light subsidiary or starves a heavy one. And I'd put real governance around capacity assignment — a workspace shouldn't be able to get silently moved to a different capacity without a change-control step, because that's exactly how this kind of isolation gets accidentally broken six months later by someone trying to solve an unrelated problem. Per-capacity cost monitoring from day one is what actually makes the separate-billing goal real instead of aspirational.
commonMistakes: Proposes one shared capacity for all subsidiaries, failing the isolation requirement entirely
Proposes fully separate tenants, losing governance consistency and cross-subsidiary sharing ability unnecessarily
Sizes all capacities uniformly instead of basing sizing on actual per-subsidiary workload assessment
No governance control preventing a workspace from being silently moved between capacities
keyPoints: Correctly proposes one tenant with separate per-subsidiary capacities
Explains why separate capacities genuinely isolate workload impact
Uses OneLake shortcuts for cross-capacity, cross-subsidiary sharing
Sizes capacity based on actual workload assessment, not a flat default
Adds governance controls preventing accidental cross-capacity reassignment

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct one-tenant/separate-capacities design
Correctly uses OneLake shortcuts for cross-subsidiary sharing
Sound, workload-based capacity sizing approach
Adds governance controls protecting the isolation over time

questions.title: Designing Disaster Recovery for a Lakehouse That Finance Depends On
questions.prompt: The finance team has declared a 4-hour RTO and a 15-minute RPO for the lakehouse's core financial tables. Design the disaster recovery architecture that actually meets this, and explain what you'd push back on if the current infrastructure can't realistically support it.
questions.modelAnswer:
A 15-minute RPO for the finance tables means replication to a secondary region has to run continuously with lag kept well under that threshold and actively monitored, not periodically checked — I would implement near-continuous replication of the specific finance-critical Delta tables (via Delta's own deep clone on a tight schedule, or a streaming CDC-based replication to the secondary region, depending on write volume) with an explicit, alerted lag metric tied directly to the 15-minute RPO, paging well before the lag approaches that threshold, not at it. Critically, this RPO and the replication mechanism should be scoped specifically to the finance-critical tables, not the entire lakehouse — applying continuous replication to every table in the platform is both unnecessary cost and a distraction from protecting what actually needs this guarantee.

The 4-hour RTO requires that failover — redirecting the finance team's queries and pipelines to the secondary region — is a rehearsed, largely automated procedure, not a manual runbook assembled under pressure during an actual incident; this means compute (SQL warehouses, Databricks workspaces) needs to exist and be quickly activatable in the secondary region already, not provisioned from scratch during the incident, and the failover procedure itself needs to have been executed in a drill, with the drill specifically validating data freshness post-failover (confirming the secondary's lag was genuinely within RPO at the failover point), not just confirming the mechanism completes. If the current infrastructure doesn't support near-continuous replication (for example, a batch-only nightly sync to the secondary region), I would push back directly and explicitly rather than quietly trying to make a 15-minute RPO work on top of nightly batch infrastructure — that combination is not actually achievable, and promising it anyway sets up a failure the business will discover during an actual disaster rather than during a budget conversation. The honest conversation is: achieving this RPO/RTO requires investment (continuous replication infrastructure, dedicated secondary-region compute kept warm, and regular tested drills), and the business needs to either fund that investment or consciously accept a less aggressive RPO/RTO for these specific tables.
questions.professionalAnswer: A 15-minute RPO means I need near-continuous replication with an actively monitored lag metric, not a periodic check — and I'd scope that specifically to the finance-critical tables, not the whole lakehouse, because applying that level of infrastructure everywhere is unnecessary cost and dilutes focus from the tables that actually need it. For the 4-hour RTO, failover has to be a rehearsed, largely automated procedure with compute already provisioned and warm in the secondary region, not something assembled under pressure during a real incident — and the drill needs to specifically check that the data we failed over to was actually within RPO at that moment, not just that the failover mechanism ran successfully. Here's the part I'd push back on directly if the current setup is nightly batch replication: a 15-minute RPO on top of nightly batch infrastructure is not achievable, full stop, and I wouldn't quietly try to make it look achievable on paper. I'd tell finance and leadership plainly — hitting this target requires real investment in continuous replication and warm standby compute, and either we fund that or we agree on a realistic RPO/RTO for these tables, because finding out the gap during an actual disaster is far worse than finding it out now.
commonMistakes: Proposes periodic/batch replication and calls it compliant with a 15-minute RPO without acknowledging the mismatch
Applies continuous replication to the entire lakehouse instead of scoping it to the finance-critical tables
Treats the failover runbook as sufficient without an actual tested drill validating post-failover data freshness
Avoids pushing back on an unachievable target instead of surfacing the gap and its cost honestly
keyPoints: Designs near-continuous, monitored replication scoped to the specific RPO-bearing tables
Designs a rehearsed, largely automated failover procedure for the RTO
Requires drills that validate actual post-failover data freshness, not just mechanism completion
Explicitly pushes back when current infrastructure cannot realistically meet the stated target
Frames the gap as an investment decision for the business, not a technical bluff

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Designs a sound replication architecture meeting the RPO
Designs a sound, rehearsed failover procedure meeting the RTO
Requires genuine freshness-validating drills
Explicitly and honestly pushes back when infrastructure can't support the target

questions.title: Designing a Semantic Layer Shared Across dbt and Power BI
questions.prompt: Leadership wants one governed set of business metrics usable both through the dbt Semantic Layer for ad-hoc analyst queries and through Power BI for executive dashboards. Design the architecture that makes this a single source of truth rather than two tools pointed at the same tables with separately written logic.
questions.modelAnswer:
The architecture has to make the dbt Semantic Layer's metric definitions (built on top of governed Gold dbt models, defined once in YAML with explicit dimensions, measures, and business logic) the single authoritative layer, with Power BI consuming those definitions rather than reimplementing them in DAX — the mechanism for this is either querying the dbt Semantic Layer's APIs directly from Power BI via DirectQuery/a supported connector where that integration is mature enough for the organization's latency needs, or, more commonly in practice today, generating the Power BI dataset's tables and measures from the same metric YAML definitions through a CI step, so the DAX measures are mechanically derived from the dbt metrics rather than hand-written a second time by a different team. Either path keeps one authoritative definition and one place business logic changes; the difference is whether Power BI queries live through to dbt's semantic layer or whether it imports a generated, synchronized snapshot — the import path is usually necessary today for performance reasons given Power BI's VertiPaq engine's strengths, and I would be upfront that this means there's a sync step that needs monitoring, not a truly live single query path, which is an honest tradeoff rather than a solved problem.

Governance-wise, metric changes should go through the same CI/CD and review process as any other dbt model change, since a metric is just as load-bearing as a table, and the generated Power BI assets should be regenerated and redeployed as part of that same pipeline, not as a manual follow-up step someone has to remember. I would also build an automated reconciliation check comparing a sample of dbt Semantic Layer query outputs against the corresponding Power BI measure outputs on a schedule, specifically because this architecture has a sync step that can silently break (a failed regeneration, a stale Power BI dataset refresh), and I want that caught by monitoring, not by an executive noticing a mismatch in next quarter's board deck.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd make the dbt Semantic Layer the one authoritative place metric logic lives, and get Power BI to consume that instead of reimplementing it in DAX. In practice today, that usually means generating the Power BI dataset's measures from the same metric YAML as part of a CI step, rather than Power BI querying dbt's semantic layer fully live — I'd be honest that this is a sync, not a single live query path, mostly because of how well Power BI's VertiPaq engine performs with imported data versus a live connection at this layer. The sync step is exactly where this kind of design can quietly break, so I'd treat metric changes with the same CI/CD rigor as any other model change, and I'd add an automated reconciliation job comparing sample outputs from dbt's semantic layer against the generated Power BI measures on a schedule — because I'd much rather catch a broken sync through monitoring than have an executive notice two numbers don't match in a board deck.
commonMistakes: Assumes a fully live query path from Power BI to dbt's semantic layer is already mature enough without checking actual latency/support
Treats the generated/synced Power BI assets as a one-time setup instead of part of the ongoing CI/CD pipeline
Doesn't add reconciliation monitoring to catch sync failures between the two layers
Applies a lighter review process to metric changes than to other dbt model changes
keyPoints: Makes the dbt Semantic Layer the single authoritative metric definition
Proposes a concrete, honest mechanism (live query or generated/synced measures) for Power BI consumption
Integrates metric changes into the same CI/CD rigor as other dbt changes
Adds automated reconciliation monitoring between the two layers
Is explicit about the tradeoff (sync vs. truly live single source)

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes a sound, concrete integration mechanism
Integrates metric governance into CI/CD appropriately
Adds reconciliation monitoring for the sync risk
Honestly frames the sync-vs-live tradeoff

questions.title: Build vs. Buy: An Orchestration Layer for a Growing Platform
questions.prompt: The platform team currently orchestrates everything with a patchwork of ADF pipelines and cron-triggered scripts, and it's becoming unmanageable. Decide between building a custom orchestration framework in-house versus adopting a managed tool (Azure Data Factory's own native orchestration at scale, Fabric Data Factory, or an open-source option like Airflow/Dagster run on the platform), and justify the decision framework you'd use.
questions.modelAnswer:
I would default strongly toward adopting an existing orchestration tool rather than building a custom framework, because orchestration — retries, dependency graphs, scheduling, alerting, backfills — is a genuinely hard, well-solved problem, and building a custom version means the platform team is now maintaining orchestration software instead of maintaining data pipelines, which is not the organization's core competency and provides no competitive differentiation. The decision framework I'd actually apply: does the organization's existing cloud investment already provide a capable option (ADF at scale, or Fabric Data Factory, if the org is Azure/Fabric-committed) that handles the complexity the team is actually facing, or does the team's specific need (complex cross-system dependency graphs, a strong need for pipelines-as-code with full testability, a multi-cloud or open ecosystem requirement) genuinely exceed what the native tool offers, in which case an open-source option like Airflow or Dagster, adopted rather than built from scratch, is the next step before ever considering a fully custom build.

For this specific situation — a patchwork of ADF pipelines and cron scripts becoming unmanageable — the root problem described isn't actually 'we need a different orchestration engine,' it's 'we never adopted a disciplined pattern for the engine we already have,' which is a process and architecture problem, not a tooling gap. I would first assess whether a metadata-driven framework built on top of the existing ADF/Fabric orchestration (consolidating the cron scripts into the same control-table-driven pattern, replacing ad hoc scripts with proper pipeline definitions) solves the actual pain before concluding a new tool is needed at all — migrating to Airflow or building something custom to solve a problem that's actually about pipeline design discipline just moves the same disorganization into a new, unfamiliar tool, at real migration cost and risk, without addressing the root cause.
questions.professionalAnswer: My default is strongly toward adopting an existing tool, not building custom orchestration — retries, dependency graphs, backfills, alerting, this is a genuinely hard problem that's already been solved well multiple times, and building our own version means we're now in the business of maintaining orchestration software instead of maintaining pipelines, which isn't what the organization is actually trying to be good at. But before I even get to 'which tool,' I'd push back on the framing here — a patchwork of ADF pipelines and cron scripts becoming unmanageable usually isn't actually an engine problem, it's a discipline problem. We never adopted a consistent pattern for the engine we already have. I'd want to try consolidating onto a proper metadata-driven framework on top of the existing ADF/Fabric orchestration first, because migrating to a new tool to solve a problem that's really about pipeline design discipline just relocates the same mess into unfamiliar territory, with real migration risk, and doesn't actually fix anything.
commonMistakes: Defaults to building a custom orchestration framework instead of adopting an existing tool
Jumps straight to recommending a new tool migration without diagnosing whether the real problem is design discipline, not the engine
Doesn't weigh the organization's existing cloud investment/skill profile in the tool decision
Ignores the real cost and risk of migrating to a new orchestration tool
keyPoints: Defaults to adopting rather than building custom orchestration, with sound reasoning
Correctly diagnoses that the described problem is pipeline-design discipline, not an engine gap
Proposes fixing the existing tool's usage pattern before considering migration
Weighs existing cloud investment and skill profile appropriately
Frames the decision with a genuine, reusable framework rather than a one-off opinion

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Sound build-vs-buy reasoning favoring adoption over custom build
Correctly diagnoses the root cause as discipline, not tooling
Weighs existing investment and realistic migration cost
Provides a reusable decision framework, not just a one-off opinion

questions.title: Designing Real-Time Intelligence for a Mission-Critical Monitoring Use Case
questions.prompt: A utility company needs real-time monitoring of grid sensor data with automatic alerting when readings cross safety thresholds, and the monitoring cannot have a blind spot longer than 30 seconds. Design this using Fabric Real-Time Intelligence or an equivalent streaming architecture, and justify the choice.
questions.modelAnswer:
A 30-second maximum blind spot is a genuine real-time requirement, not a reporting-freshness nicety, so this needs an actual event-processing path with alerting evaluated continuously against incoming data, not a dashboard refreshing on an interval. In a Fabric-based design, grid sensor events stream into an Eventstream, which can apply lightweight transformations and route to a KQL database (Fabric's Real-Time Intelligence engine, built for exactly this kind of high-velocity time-series ingestion and sub-second query), with threshold-crossing alerting implemented as a continuous query (a Fabric Data Activator rule or a KQL-based alert rule) evaluated against the live stream rather than computed by a scheduled job — a scheduled job inherently introduces a blind spot equal to its own interval, which directly conflicts with the 30-second requirement if the job runs any less frequently than that.

The alerting mechanism itself needs its own reliability design independent of the broader analytics pipeline: if the alert rule's evaluation engine or its notification delivery path goes down, that's a silent safety gap, so I would build an explicit heartbeat/dead-man's-switch check — a separate, simple monitor confirming the alerting pipeline itself is actively processing events within the last 30 seconds, alerting on its own absence of activity, because the worst failure mode for a safety system is not 'it alerted on something minor,' it's 'it silently stopped alerting at all and nobody knew.' For the historical/analytical side, the same Eventstream also lands in a Delta/lakehouse table for longer-term trend analysis and compliance reporting, reusing the same ingestion rather than running a separate pipeline, but that path is explicitly not on the safety-alerting critical path — it's downstream and can tolerate the kind of lag that the real-time alerting path cannot.
questions.professionalAnswer: A 30-second blind-spot limit means this is a genuine streaming-and-continuous-alerting problem, not a 'refresh the dashboard more often' problem, so I'd rule out anything scheduled from the start. I'd stream sensor events through a Fabric Eventstream into a KQL database, since that's specifically built for high-velocity time-series data with fast query response, and implement threshold alerting as a continuous rule evaluated against the live stream — a Data Activator rule or a KQL alert — rather than a periodic job, because a periodic job's own interval becomes the blind spot, and anything less frequent than 30 seconds already violates the requirement. The part I'd insist on that often gets skipped: the alerting pipeline needs its own watchdog, a simple heartbeat check confirming the alert engine itself processed something recently, because the actual worst-case failure for a safety system isn't a false alarm, it's the system silently going dark and nobody noticing. For historical analysis and compliance reporting, I'd reuse the same ingested stream into a lakehouse table, but I'd be explicit that path is downstream of the safety-critical alerting path, not part of it, so it's allowed to have very different latency characteristics.
commonMistakes: Designs alerting as a scheduled job without recognizing the job's own interval becomes the blind spot
Has no dead-man's-switch/heartbeat check on the alerting pipeline itself
Conflates the safety-critical alerting path with the historical/compliance reporting path, applying the same latency requirements to both unnecessarily
Chooses a general-purpose warehouse/table for the real-time query layer instead of a time-series-optimized engine
keyPoints: Designs continuous, stream-based alerting rather than a scheduled job
Uses an appropriate time-series-optimized engine (KQL database) for the real-time layer
Adds a dead-man's-switch/heartbeat check protecting against silent alerting failure
Correctly separates the safety-critical alerting path from the historical/reporting path
Reuses the same ingestion stream for both paths without conflating their latency requirements

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Designs genuinely continuous, sub-30-second alerting
Uses an appropriate real-time engine and justifies it
Adds a watchdog/heartbeat mechanism for the alerting pipeline itself
Correctly separates safety-critical path from historical/reporting path

questions.title: Governing a Polyglot Estate: T-SQL, Snowflake, and Databricks SQL Together
questions.prompt: Through acquisitions, the company now has a core OLTP estate on SQL Server, an analytics warehouse on Snowflake, and a newly acquired company's data science team running Databricks. Leadership doesn't want to force a consolidation onto one platform in the near term. Design the governance and interoperability architecture that lets this polyglot estate function coherently.
questions.modelAnswer:
Given an explicit decision not to consolidate platforms near-term, the architecture has to accept three real enforcement points (SQL Server's own security model, Snowflake's RBAC, Unity Catalog for Databricks) and build coherence at the layer above them rather than pretending one platform can govern the others. The practical mechanism is a shared, cross-platform catalog (Purview, or an open-source alternative like OpenMetadata) that crawls all three platforms and presents one searchable inventory of what data exists where, with consistent classification tags (PII, sensitivity level) applied as policy-as-code definitions that are implemented — not just documented — identically in each platform's own native mechanism: a SQL Server column-level security/masking policy, a Snowflake masking policy, and a Unity Catalog column mask, all expressing the same business rule for the same logical data, maintained from one shared source definition where feasible (a central policy repository that generates or at least validates each platform's native policy) rather than three independently-authored implementations that will drift.

For interoperability, data that needs to move between platforms (an aggregate feeding a Databricks ML model that originates in the SQL Server OLTP system, or a Snowflake-curated dataset the Databricks data science team needs) should move through a small number of well-defined, versioned interfaces — Delta Sharing or Snowflake Secure Data Sharing for read access where the platforms support it directly, or a thin, governed ELT layer landing a copy in whichever platform needs it, with a clear data contract on that interface — rather than ad hoc point-to-point connections multiplying as more cross-platform needs emerge. I would also establish a lightweight platform-selection governance process: new initiatives default to the platform best suited to the workload (OLTP stays SQL Server, BI-heavy analytics defaults to Snowflake, ML-heavy work defaults to Databricks) based on a documented decision framework, specifically to prevent this polyglot situation from silently expanding into an even less coherent four- or five-platform estate over the next few acquisitions, since the current state is the result of exactly that kind of ungoverned growth.
questions.professionalAnswer: Since leadership has explicitly ruled out near-term consolidation, I'm not going to pretend one platform can govern the other two — I'm accepting three real enforcement points and building coherence above them instead. That means a shared cross-platform catalog, Purview or something like it, crawling all three and giving everyone one place to search what data exists and where, with consistent classification tags implemented identically in each platform's own native policy mechanism rather than three teams independently deciding what 'PII' means for their platform. For data that genuinely needs to move between platforms, I'd push hard for a small number of well-defined, versioned interfaces — Delta Sharing or Snowflake's own secure sharing where that's a direct fit, or a thin governed ELT layer with an actual data contract — instead of letting point-to-point connections multiply every time someone needs something from another platform, because that's exactly how this kind of estate turns into an unmanageable mess. And since this company clearly grows by acquisition, I'd put a lightweight platform-selection framework in place now, so the next acquisition's data stack has a documented default instead of just adding a fourth platform to the pile by accident.
commonMistakes: Tries to force one platform's governance model to cover the other two despite the no-consolidation mandate
Allows classification/policy to be independently authored per platform without a shared source definition
Allows ad hoc point-to-point data movement between platforms instead of defined, versioned interfaces
Has no forward-looking governance for future acquisitions, risking further ungoverned platform sprawl
keyPoints: Accepts the three real enforcement points rather than forcing false consolidation
Builds a shared cross-platform catalog with consistently implemented classification
Defines a small number of governed, versioned interfaces for cross-platform data movement
Proposes a platform-selection governance framework to prevent further sprawl
Respects the explicit no-consolidation mandate while still delivering coherence

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly accepts and designs around three real enforcement points
Designs a sound shared-catalog/classification approach
Defines governed interfaces for cross-platform data movement
Proposes forward-looking governance preventing further sprawl

questions.title: Designing a Clean-Room Data Sharing Architecture Between Two Companies
questions.prompt: Two companies want to jointly analyze overlapping customer behavior to inform a co-marketing deal, without either side ever seeing the other's raw customer-level data. Design the clean-room architecture that makes this possible.
questions.modelAnswer:
A data clean room's defining property is that both parties' raw data stays within each party's own controlled environment, and only pre-approved, aggregated, or specifically-permissioned query results ever leave that environment — this is categorically different from a data share, where one party exposes read access to specific curated data, because in a clean room neither party ever gets row-level access to the other's data at all, only the output of jointly-agreed computations. I would implement this using the native clean-room capability of whichever platform both parties already use if there's overlap (Snowflake's Secure Data Clean Rooms, or a Databricks-based approach using Delta Sharing combined with restricted compute and query templates), or, if the two companies are on different platforms, a neutral third-party clean room provider — the architecture in either case centers on pre-approved query templates (not ad hoc SQL access) that both parties agree to in advance, executed against each side's data in place, returning only the aggregate result (overlap counts, cohort-level statistics) above a minimum aggregation threshold specifically to prevent re-identification of individuals through a narrowly-scoped query.

The governance work that actually matters here happens before any technical implementation: both companies' legal and privacy teams need to agree on exactly what queries are permitted, what minimum aggregation threshold prevents re-identification (a query returning results for a group of 3 people is not meaningfully anonymized even if no raw rows were shared), and an audit log of every query executed and every result returned, reviewable by both parties, since the technical guarantee of 'no raw data crossed the boundary' only holds if the query templates themselves were actually vetted to not leak individual-level information through clever aggregation or repeated querying (an attacker can sometimes reconstruct individual records by running many overlapping aggregate queries and differencing the results, which is why query templates need to be fixed and reviewed, not an open query interface).
questions.professionalAnswer: The property I'd anchor the whole design on is that neither company ever gets row-level access to the other's data, only the output of jointly pre-approved computations — that's what actually distinguishes a clean room from a regular data share. I'd use whichever platform's native clean-room capability fits if both companies happen to be on compatible platforms, or a neutral third-party clean room if they're not, but either way the core mechanism is the same: fixed, pre-agreed query templates, not open SQL access, executed against each side's data where it already lives, returning only aggregated results above a minimum group-size threshold. The part I'd spend the most time on isn't actually the technology — it's getting both companies' legal and privacy teams to agree up front on exactly which queries are allowed and what aggregation threshold is enough to prevent someone from being re-identified, because a result for a group of three people isn't meaningfully anonymous even though no raw row ever crossed the boundary. And I'd insist on query templates being fixed and reviewed rather than an open interface, because a sufficiently motivated party can sometimes reconstruct individual-level information by running many overlapping aggregate queries and comparing the differences.
commonMistakes: Describes this as a data share rather than correctly distinguishing the clean room's no-row-level-access property
Allows open/ad hoc SQL access instead of fixed, pre-approved query templates
Ignores minimum aggregation thresholds, allowing small-group results that risk re-identification
Doesn't account for the differencing-attack risk from repeated overlapping aggregate queries
Treats this as primarily a technology implementation rather than a legal/privacy governance exercise first
keyPoints: Correctly distinguishes a clean room's no-row-level-access property from a data share
Uses fixed, pre-approved query templates rather than open query access
Enforces a minimum aggregation threshold to prevent re-identification
Accounts for differencing-attack risk from repeated queries
Treats legal/privacy agreement as the real governance work, ahead of the technical build

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines and designs the clean-room property
Uses fixed query templates with an appropriate aggregation threshold
Accounts for re-identification/differencing-attack risk
Correctly prioritizes legal/privacy governance work

questions.title: Designing Enterprise-Wide Cost Governance Across a Multi-Platform Estate
questions.prompt: Leadership wants a single, trustworthy monthly report of data platform spend across Snowflake, Databricks, and Fabric, broken down by business unit, with automatic alerts before any single unit significantly overshoots its budget. Design the cost-governance architecture.
questions.modelAnswer:
Each platform exposes its own native cost/usage data (Snowflake's ACCOUNT_USAGE views, Databricks' system tables for cluster/job cost, Fabric's Capacity Metrics app and admin APIs), and the architecture has to pull all three into one normalized cost model rather than presenting three separately-formatted reports and asking leadership to mentally reconcile them. I would build a small dedicated pipeline that extracts usage/cost data from each platform's native source on a daily cadence, normalizes it into a common schema (platform, business unit, workload type, cost, usage date), and lands it in a governed Gold table that the monthly report and any alerting is built on top of — this pipeline itself needs to be treated with the same rigor as any other financial data pipeline, since 'data platform spend' is itself going to be reviewed by finance.

The business-unit attribution step is the part that actually requires organizational work, not just a query: each platform needs a consistent tagging or resource-naming convention that maps a warehouse, cluster, or capacity back to the business unit responsible for it — Snowflake resource tags or warehouse-per-team conventions, Databricks cluster/job tags, Fabric capacity-per-business-unit assignment (which, if already designed that way architecturally, makes this attribution nearly free) — and without this convention being enforced (ideally at provisioning time, blocking a new warehouse/cluster/capacity from being created without a required business-unit tag), cost attribution degrades into guesswork. For alerting, I would implement a budget threshold per business unit per platform (and a combined total), checked on at least a daily cadence against actual spend-to-date projected against the full month's trend, alerting at a leading-indicator threshold (e.g., projected to exceed budget by more than 15%, based on current trend) rather than only alerting after the budget is already blown, since the entire point of 'automatic alerts before a significant overshoot' is to give the business unit time to react before the month closes, not just a postmortem explanation of what happened.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd build one small, dedicated pipeline that pulls native usage/cost data out of all three platforms — Snowflake's account usage views, Databricks' system tables, Fabric's capacity metrics — normalizes it into one common schema, and lands it in a governed table that both the monthly report and the alerting logic read from, rather than asking leadership to mentally reconcile three differently-formatted reports every month. The part that's actually hard isn't the pipeline, it's business-unit attribution — that requires a real tagging or naming convention enforced at provisioning time on each platform, ideally blocking a new warehouse or cluster from even being created without a business-unit tag, because without that enforcement, cost attribution just turns into guesswork from naming patterns. For the alerting, I wouldn't wait until a budget is already blown — I'd project each business unit's spend trend against their budget on a daily basis and alert at a leading-indicator threshold, something like 'on track to exceed by more than 15%,' because the whole point of asking for alerts before an overshoot is giving someone time to actually react, not just documenting after the fact what already happened.
commonMistakes: Presents three separately-formatted platform reports instead of one normalized cross-platform cost model
Treats business-unit attribution as a reporting-layer problem instead of requiring enforced tagging/naming at provisioning time
Alerts only after a budget is already exceeded instead of on a leading-indicator trend projection
Doesn't treat the cost-governance pipeline itself with the rigor appropriate to financial data
keyPoints: Normalizes cost/usage data from all three platforms into one common model
Requires enforced tagging/naming conventions for business-unit attribution
Treats the cost pipeline with appropriate financial-data rigor
Designs leading-indicator trend-based alerting, not after-the-fact alerting
Builds one unified report rather than three separate platform reports

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Designs a sound normalized cross-platform cost pipeline
Requires enforced business-unit attribution, not guesswork
Designs genuine leading-indicator alerting
Treats the pipeline with appropriate rigor as financial data

questions.title: Zero-Copy Architecture: When OneLake Shortcuts Become a Liability
questions.prompt: A Fabric estate has grown to rely heavily on OneLake shortcuts, with some Gold tables now being virtual chains of shortcuts three or four layers deep across different workspaces. Design the architectural guardrails you'd put in place before this becomes unmanageable.
questions.modelAnswer:
Shortcuts avoiding data duplication is a genuine architectural benefit, but a chain of shortcuts three or four layers deep across workspaces creates exactly the kind of fragile, hard-to-reason-about dependency graph that a well-designed metadata-driven ingestion framework is supposed to prevent — if workspace D's Gold table is a shortcut to workspace C's table, which shortcuts to workspace B's, which shortcuts to workspace A's actual physical data, nobody looking at workspace D can tell, without active investigation, how many hops away the real data is, who owns each hop, or what happens if any single workspace in that chain is deleted, has its access revoked, or has its underlying data change shape. This is functionally the same problem as the spaghetti of linked-server dependencies in a legacy SQL Server estate, just implemented with a modern zero-copy primitive instead of an old one — the technology changed, the governance discipline didn't, and the failure mode is the same.

The guardrails I would put in place: first, cap the practical shortcut-chain depth as an explicit architectural standard (for example, a Gold table may shortcut directly to a Silver table, but not to another Gold table that is itself a shortcut chain), enforced through a periodic automated scan of the OneLake shortcut graph across workspaces rather than relying on individual engineers remembering the rule; second, require every shortcut crossing a workspace/business-unit boundary to be registered with an explicit owner and purpose in the catalog, since an undocumented shortcut is the OneLake equivalent of an undocumented linked server; third, build and maintain an actual dependency graph visualization (either via Purview's lineage capability extended across Fabric items, or a custom scan of the Fabric API) so anyone can see, before deleting or restructuring a workspace, exactly what currently shortcuts into it. I would treat discovering this pattern as a signal to do a structural cleanup now — materializing the one or two most heavily-chained paths into actual physical Gold tables where the cost of re-computation is reasonable — rather than letting the chain grow another layer deeper before addressing it.
questions.professionalAnswer: A shortcut chain three or four layers deep across workspaces is the same failure pattern as a legacy linked-server spaghetti mess, just built with a newer zero-copy primitive — nobody looking at the end of the chain can easily tell how many hops away the real data actually is, or what breaks if one workspace in the middle gets deleted or has its access changed. I'd treat discovering this as a signal to act now, not later. My first guardrail is an explicit depth limit as an actual architectural standard — Gold can shortcut to Silver, but not to another Gold table that's itself a shortcut chain — enforced by a periodic automated scan of the shortcut graph, not by hoping everyone remembers the rule. Second, any shortcut crossing a workspace or business-unit boundary needs an owner and a registered purpose in the catalog, because an undocumented cross-boundary shortcut is exactly as dangerous as an undocumented linked server used to be. And I'd actually build a visual dependency map across the Fabric estate so before anyone deletes or restructures a workspace, they can see what currently depends on it. For the one or two paths that are already chained the deepest, I'd just materialize those into real physical tables now, because the cost of recomputing them is reasonable and it's much cheaper to fix two paths today than to fix a tangled mess after it's grown another layer.
commonMistakes: Treats shortcut chaining as purely a technical convenience with no governance implications
Doesn't recognize the structural similarity to legacy linked-server dependency sprawl
Proposes no depth limit or enforcement mechanism, relying on individual discipline
Doesn't build an actual dependency visualization, leaving impact analysis manual and error-prone
Doesn't recommend materializing the most deeply-chained paths proactively
keyPoints: Correctly identifies the structural risk of deep cross-workspace shortcut chains
Draws the correct analogy to legacy linked-server dependency sprawl
Proposes an enforced depth limit as an architectural standard
Requires ownership/registration for cross-boundary shortcuts
Proposes a real dependency visualization and proactive materialization of the worst chains

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies and explains the structural risk
Proposes an enforced depth-limit standard
Requires ownership/registration governance for cross-boundary shortcuts
Proposes dependency visualization and proactive remediation

questions.title: Designing CI/CD Maturity for a Combined dbt and Databricks Estate
questions.prompt: The organization runs dbt models on top of Databricks SQL warehouses alongside Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines doing upstream Bronze-to-Silver work, maintained by overlapping but not identical teams. Design the CI/CD architecture that gives this combined estate real deployment safety without each team needing to understand the other's full stack.
questions.modelAnswer:
The design principle is that each layer (Lakeflow pipelines producing Silver, dbt models consuming Silver to produce Gold) gets its own CI/CD pipeline appropriate to its own tooling, with a well-defined, versioned contract at the boundary between them, rather than one monolithic pipeline that requires understanding both stacks to safely change either side. The Lakeflow pipelines' CI validates pipeline syntax, runs expectations against a test dataset, and on merge deploys to a staging environment where it runs against representative data before promoting to production — critically, its contract with downstream dbt models is the Silver table schema itself, which should be covered by a schema/contract test that fails the Lakeflow CI if a change would break that contract without an explicit, coordinated version bump.

dbt's CI uses slim CI (state:modified+ with --defer) against its own manifest, and critically, dbt's CI should include a check that validates its assumptions about the Silver layer's schema actually still hold — a source freshness/schema test run against the real current Silver tables, not just mocked test fixtures — so a change on the Lakeflow side that breaks an assumption dbt was relying on gets caught in dbt's own CI the next time it runs, even if the Lakeflow team didn't realize the downstream impact. For genuine cross-team coordination on breaking changes (a Lakeflow Silver schema change that dbt models explicitly depend on), I would require the data contract itself to be a reviewed artifact — a schema definition file both teams' CI pipelines check against — with a deprecation window rather than an in-place breaking change, so the dbt team has a known window to update their models rather than discovering a break the morning after a Lakeflow deploy. This lets each team operate independently day to day while the explicit contract and cross-checking CI steps catch the genuine cross-boundary risk without requiring either team to deeply understand the other's full stack.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd give each layer its own CI/CD pipeline suited to its own tooling, with a real, versioned contract at the boundary between them — I don't want either team needing to deeply understand the other's full stack just to ship safely. Lakeflow's CI validates its own pipeline logic and expectations, and critically includes a schema/contract check on the Silver tables it produces, so it can't silently ship a breaking change to the thing dbt depends on without an explicit version bump. On the dbt side, I'd use slim CI for speed, but I'd also make sure dbt's CI validates its assumptions against the actual current Silver schema, not just mocked fixtures, so if something changed upstream that dbt didn't anticipate, dbt's own CI catches it the next run, even if the Lakeflow team had no idea it would matter downstream. For genuinely breaking changes to that boundary, I'd want the contract itself to be a reviewed artifact both pipelines check against, with a real deprecation window instead of an in-place change — that way the dbt team gets a heads-up and a window to adapt, instead of finding out the hard way the morning after someone else's deploy.
commonMistakes: Builds one monolithic CI pipeline requiring full cross-stack understanding to change either side safely
Doesn't define an explicit, versioned contract at the Lakeflow-to-dbt boundary
Runs dbt CI only against mocked fixtures without validating against real current upstream schema
Allows in-place breaking changes to the shared boundary instead of requiring a deprecation window
keyPoints: Gives each layer its own appropriately-scoped CI/CD pipeline
Defines an explicit, versioned contract at the Lakeflow-to-dbt boundary
Has each side's CI validate the shared contract, catching cross-boundary breaks early
Requires a deprecation window for genuine breaking changes
Avoids requiring either team to fully understand the other's stack

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Designs appropriately scoped, independent CI/CD per layer
Defines a concrete, versioned cross-boundary contract
Ensures both sides' CI actively validates the shared contract
Requires a deprecation process for breaking changes

questions.title: Designing a Governed Reverse-ETL Path Back to SaaS Tools
questions.prompt: Sales wants the governed customer-health score computed in the lakehouse pushed automatically into Salesforce so reps see it without leaving their CRM. Design the reverse-ETL architecture, including how you'd prevent it from becoming an ungoverned backdoor around the semantic layer.
questions.modelAnswer:
The reverse-ETL pipeline should read the customer-health score from the same governed Gold table or semantic-layer metric that any other consumer uses, never from an intermediate or ad hoc recomputation specific to the Salesforce push, because the entire value of having a governed metric evaporates the moment a second, slightly different implementation exists just for this one destination. Architecturally, a dedicated reverse-ETL tool (or a lightweight custom job, depending on scale and the organization's existing tooling) reads the Gold table on a defined schedule matched to how fresh Sales actually needs the score to be (hourly is usually sufficient for a health score; this almost never needs to be real-time), maps it to the correct Salesforce field via API, and — critically — writes only to a field clearly labeled and documented as system-generated/read-only from the sales rep's perspective, since a common governance failure in reverse-ETL designs is a well-meaning rep manually overwriting the pushed value in Salesforce, after which the 'governed' score silently diverges from its source of truth with no one noticing.

To prevent this from becoming a backdoor around the semantic layer, I would apply the same CI/review rigor to the reverse-ETL mapping as to any other consumer of the metric — a change to which Gold column feeds this field, or a change to the metric's underlying definition, should be visible in the same change-review process, not configured independently inside a reverse-ETL tool's UI by whoever set it up originally with no ongoing oversight. I would also add monitoring that compares the value actually sitting in Salesforce against the current Gold value for a sample of accounts on a schedule, specifically to catch the rep-overwrite problem and any silent reverse-ETL job failure, since 'the push job ran successfully' and 'the data in Salesforce is still correct' are two different claims, and only checking the first one is a common blind spot.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd make sure this pipeline reads from the exact same governed Gold table or semantic-layer metric every other consumer uses — the moment there's a separate recomputation just for the Salesforce push, the whole point of having one governed metric is gone. I'd use a dedicated reverse-ETL tool or a lightweight job on a schedule matched to how fresh sales actually needs this — usually hourly is plenty for a health score, this almost never needs to be real-time — and I'd make sure the destination field in Salesforce is clearly labeled as system-generated, because the failure mode I've actually seen is a rep manually overwriting the pushed value, after which it silently diverges from the real source and nobody notices until someone asks why the numbers don't match. To stop this from turning into a quiet backdoor around governance, I'd put the reverse-ETL mapping itself through the same change-review process as any other consumer of the metric, not let it live independently configured in a tool's UI by whoever set it up originally. And I'd add a monitoring check comparing what's actually sitting in Salesforce against the current Gold value for a sample of records, because 'the sync job ran successfully' and 'the data is still correct' are genuinely two different claims.
commonMistakes: Recomputes the metric specifically for the Salesforce push instead of reading the same governed source
Doesn't account for reps manually overwriting the pushed value, causing silent divergence
Treats the reverse-ETL mapping as a standalone config outside the normal change-review process
Only monitors job success instead of verifying the destination data is actually still correct
keyPoints: Reads from the same governed metric source as any other consumer
Schedules the push at a frequency matched to actual business need
Accounts for and guards against manual overwrite causing silent divergence
Applies the same change-review rigor to the reverse-ETL mapping as other consumers
Adds monitoring verifying destination correctness, not just job success

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly sources from the governed metric, preventing a parallel implementation
Guards against manual overwrite/silent divergence
Applies proper governance/change-review to the reverse-ETL mapping
Adds correctness monitoring beyond job-success checks

questions.title: Designing Data Retention and Right-to-Erasure for a Regulated Lakehouse
questions.prompt: A company subject to GDPR needs to support a 'right to erasure' request against customer data that's been flowing through a medallion lakehouse for years, including Delta time-travel history, Bronze archives, and downstream Gold aggregates. Design the architecture that makes this actually achievable, not just a policy on paper.
questions.modelAnswer:
The hard architectural truth to state upfront is that Delta's time-travel history and VACUUM-retained old file versions mean a simple DELETE statement does not actually erase a customer's data from disk immediately — the row disappears from the current table version, but the data still physically exists in older Parquet files referenced by the transaction log until those files are vacuumed past the retention window, so 'right to erasure' compliance requires explicit handling of this, not an assumption that DELETE is sufficient. The correct design deletes the record via DELETE/MERGE, then runs VACUUM with a retention period short enough to satisfy the erasure SLA (which may require temporarily reducing the table's normal retention window for the erasure operation, with the tradeoff of losing time-travel/audit capability for that window), and this needs to be a defined, tested, repeatable procedure, not an ad hoc script someone runs when a request comes in.

For Bronze, raw ingested data containing the customer's original records needs the same treatment, which is often harder because Bronze may be partitioned or structured in a way that wasn't designed with per-customer deletion in mind — I would design Bronze partitioning with eventual erasure in mind from the start (partitioning or at least indexing by customer ID or a consistent hashed identifier) specifically so a future erasure request doesn't require a full-table rewrite. For Gold aggregates, the question is different: an aggregate that already summed this customer's contribution into a larger number (a regional revenue total) doesn't need to be deleted, because the individual's identity isn't recoverable from the aggregate — but any Gold table that retains the customer at an identifiable grain needs the same cascading deletion. I would build this as a formal, cataloged erasure workflow: a single customer ID triggers a cascading job that identifies every table across Bronze/Silver/Gold where that customer appears at an identifiable grain (using the catalog's lineage to find them systematically rather than relying on a manually-maintained list that will miss tables added later), deletes/merges them out, and runs the appropriate VACUUM, with a completion certificate logged for audit purposes — because 'we deleted it' needs to be provable, not just asserted, when a regulator asks.
questions.professionalAnswer: The thing I'd be upfront about immediately is that a DELETE statement on a Delta table doesn't actually erase the data from disk right away — it removes the row from the current version, but the old file versions Delta's transaction log still references stick around until VACUUM clears them past the retention window. So real right-to-erasure compliance means DELETE followed by a VACUUM with a retention period short enough to meet the erasure SLA, and I'd be honest that this trades away time-travel and audit history for that window, which is a real tradeoff, not a free fix. For Bronze specifically, I'd want partitioning or at least indexing by customer ID designed in from the start, because trying to retrofit per-customer deletion onto a Bronze layer that wasn't built with that in mind usually means a painful full-table rewrite later. For Gold, I'd distinguish carefully — an aggregate that's already summed this person into a bigger number doesn't need deletion, their identity isn't recoverable from it, but anything that still has them at an identifiable grain does. And I'd build the whole thing as one formal, cataloged erasure workflow driven off lineage — one customer ID triggers a job that finds every table where they appear at an identifiable grain using the catalog, not a manually maintained list that's guaranteed to go stale — with a completion certificate logged, because when a regulator asks whether we actually erased something, I need to be able to prove it, not just assert it.
commonMistakes: Assumes a DELETE statement is sufficient without addressing Delta's time-travel/VACUUM retention of old files
Doesn't design Bronze for eventual per-customer erasure, risking a full-table rewrite later
Treats every Gold table identically instead of distinguishing identifiable-grain tables from true aggregates
Relies on a manually-maintained list of affected tables instead of using catalog lineage to find them systematically
Has no auditable proof of completion for an erasure request
keyPoints: Correctly explains Delta's time-travel/VACUUM retention as a real erasure obstacle
Designs Bronze with eventual erasure in mind (partitioning/indexing by customer ID)
Correctly distinguishes identifiable-grain Gold tables from true aggregates
Uses catalog lineage to systematically find all affected tables, not a manual list
Produces an auditable completion record for compliance

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly addresses Delta time-travel/VACUUM as a real erasure obstacle
Designs Bronze/Silver for practical per-customer erasure
Correctly distinguishes aggregates from identifiable-grain data
Builds a systematic, auditable, lineage-driven erasure workflow

questions.title: Capacity Planning for Power BI Premium/Fabric Across a Growing Organization
questions.prompt: An organization's Power BI Premium/Fabric capacity usage has grown 300% in a year with reports of intermittent slowness, and leadership wants a capacity plan for the next two years rather than reactive upgrades. Design the planning architecture and process.
questions.modelAnswer:
Reactive upgrades fail because they respond to symptoms (intermittent slowness) after they've already affected users, so the planning architecture needs a forward-looking model built on actual usage trend data rather than guessing at the next SKU size. I would start with the Fabric Capacity Metrics app's historical data, broken down by workload type (dataset refresh, report rendering/interactive queries, Spark/Dataflow usage if applicable) and by business unit if the tagging/workspace-to-capacity mapping supports it, to understand what's actually driving the 300% growth — new users, more complex models, more frequent refreshes, or a few specific expensive artifacts dominating consumption — because the right response differs materially depending on which of these is true: more users scales differently than a handful of badly-optimized datasets consuming disproportionate CU.

From that breakdown, I'd build a capacity forecast model projecting usage forward based on known organizational plans (headcount growth, planned new reporting initiatives, planned migrations onto the platform) rather than extrapolating the raw historical growth rate blindly, since a flat extrapolation of 300% growth for two more years is almost certainly not the right trajectory once you account for what's actually driving it and whether the drivers are one-time or ongoing. I would pair this quantitative forecast with specific, scheduled capacity reviews (quarterly) rather than a single two-year plan set once and left alone, since a two-year static plan in a fast-growing environment will be wrong by month six regardless of how carefully it was built — the actual deliverable isn't a static document, it's a living forecast model plus a governance process (a defined threshold that triggers a capacity review or scale decision before intermittent slowness recurs) that keeps the plan current as real usage data accumulates. I would also separately flag whether some of the slowness is actually fixable without more capacity at all — inefficient DAX, unoptimized composite models, or datasets that should be incremental-refresh and aren't — since adding capacity to cover for inefficient models just means paying more to mask a fixable problem.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't give leadership a single static two-year number, because in a fast-growing environment that number is wrong by month six no matter how carefully it's built. I'd start with the actual Fabric Capacity Metrics history, broken down by workload type and by business unit if possible, because I need to know what's actually driving this 300% growth before I can plan for it — more users scales very differently than a handful of badly optimized datasets eating a disproportionate share of CU. From there I'd build a forecast tied to known organizational plans — actual headcount growth, planned reporting initiatives — rather than just extrapolating the raw historical growth rate blindly, and I'd pair that forecast with a real quarterly review cadence instead of a one-time plan, because the deliverable leadership actually needs is a living model and a process, not a document that goes stale. And before recommending more capacity, I'd specifically check whether some of this slowness is actually a fixable efficiency problem — inefficient DAX, composite models that should be using aggregations, datasets that should be incremental refresh and aren't — because paying for more capacity to mask a fixable modeling problem is a bad use of the budget.
commonMistakes: Extrapolates the raw 300% growth rate blindly without diagnosing what's actually driving it
Delivers a single static two-year plan instead of a living forecast with a review cadence
Recommends a capacity upgrade without first checking for fixable model/query inefficiency
Doesn't break usage down by workload type or business unit before forecasting
keyPoints: Diagnoses the actual drivers of growth before forecasting, not a blind extrapolation
Builds a forecast tied to known organizational plans, not just historical trend
Proposes a living model with a regular review cadence instead of a static plan
Checks for fixable model/query inefficiency before recommending more capacity
Uses actual Fabric Capacity Metrics data as the evidence base

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses growth drivers using real usage data
Builds a sound, organization-aware forecast approach
Proposes a living process with review cadence, not a static plan
Checks for fixable inefficiency before recommending capacity increases

questions.title: Designing Event-Driven CDC Ingestion at Enterprise Scale
questions.prompt: The enterprise currently ingests OLTP data via nightly full-table extracts from a dozen core SQL Server systems, which is now too slow and too heavy on the source systems. Design a change-data-capture-based ingestion architecture to replace it, including how you'd roll it out without disrupting the existing reporting that depends on the nightly extracts.
questions.modelAnswer:
The target architecture replaces full-table extraction with CDC (SQL Server's native Change Data Capture or Change Tracking, captured via Debezium, Fivetran, or a native Fabric/ADF CDC connector) publishing row-level change events to a durable event stream, landing incrementally into Bronze Delta tables rather than being fully re-extracted and re-loaded every night — this both removes the heavy nightly extraction load from the source OLTP systems (which is itself a primary motivation, since a full-table extract against a live transactional system is exactly the kind of workload that competes for locks and I/O with the application) and gives Silver/Gold a path to near-real-time freshness if that's eventually wanted, even if it's not the immediate goal.

The rollout has to run CDC-based ingestion in parallel with the existing nightly extracts for a validation period per source system, not cut over all twelve simultaneously, because CDC correctness has specific failure modes that a nightly full extract doesn't (a missed or out-of-order change event, an initial-snapshot/backfill step that has to exactly reconcile with where CDC capture started, a schema change on the source needing explicit CDC-aware handling) that need to be proven correct against the same data the nightly process is already producing before anyone trusts it as the new source of truth. For each source system, I would validate by reconciling the CDC-fed Bronze/Silver tables against the nightly-extract-fed tables on an overlapping date range, require that reconciliation to pass for a full week (to catch any day-of-week-specific edge case) before retiring that source's nightly extract, and only decommission the nightly job once the downstream reports have been repointed and validated against the CDC-fed tables specifically — not assumed to work by inference because the underlying table is 'the same data.' I would roll this out source-by-source, prioritized by which systems' nightly extract load is causing the most actual pain for the OLTP system, rather than attempting all twelve in one coordinated cutover.
questions.professionalAnswer: The target state is CDC publishing row-level changes into a durable event stream, landing incrementally into Bronze instead of a full re-extract every night — that directly solves both problems, the nightly load on the source systems and the staleness, and sets up a path to near-real-time freshness later even if that's not the immediate ask. But I wouldn't cut over all twelve source systems at once, because CDC has its own specific failure modes a nightly full extract doesn't — missed or out-of-order events, an initial snapshot that has to reconcile exactly with where capture started, schema changes needing explicit handling — and those need to be proven correct against data people already trust before anyone relies on them. So I'd roll this out source by source, running CDC in parallel with the existing nightly extract, reconciling the two for at least a full week per source to catch any day-of-week edge cases, and only retire that source's nightly job after downstream reports have actually been repointed and validated against the CDC-fed tables specifically, not just assumed to be fine because it's technically the same underlying data. I'd prioritize which source migrates first based on which one's nightly load is actually causing the most pain on the OLTP side, since that's where the business case for doing this at all is strongest.
commonMistakes: Cuts over all source systems to CDC simultaneously instead of a source-by-source, validated rollout
Doesn't account for CDC-specific failure modes (missed events, initial-snapshot reconciliation, schema-change handling)
Assumes downstream reports work correctly on CDC-fed tables without explicit repointing and validation
Decommissions the nightly extract immediately after reconciliation passes instead of a sustained validation window
keyPoints: Correctly designs a CDC-based event-driven ingestion architecture
Identifies CDC-specific failure modes requiring explicit validation
Runs CDC in parallel with existing extracts per source for a validated reconciliation window
Prioritizes rollout order by actual OLTP load pain, not arbitrarily
Explicitly validates downstream reports against CDC-fed tables before decommissioning the old process

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Designs a sound CDC-based target architecture
Identifies and addresses CDC-specific failure modes
Proposes a safe, validated, source-by-source rollout
Requires explicit downstream report validation before decommissioning

questions.title: Decommissioning Legacy Tableau and Transferring Semantic Ownership
questions.prompt: The organization has decided to sunset a decade-old Tableau deployment in favor of a governed Power BI semantic layer, but dozens of business-critical Tableau workbooks encode undocumented business logic nobody fully remembers the rationale for. Design the architecture and process for this decommissioning without losing institutional knowledge embedded in those workbooks.
questions.modelAnswer:
The real risk in this decommissioning isn't the technical migration, it's that undocumented business logic embedded in calculated fields across dozens of workbooks represents real institutional knowledge about how the business actually defines its metrics — often including edge-case handling that exists for a historical reason nobody currently remembers, and simply rebuilding 'equivalent' measures in Power BI from scratch risks silently dropping that logic, which then surfaces months later as a confusing discrepancy nobody can explain. The architecture for preserving this starts with systematic extraction, not manual archaeology: Tableau workbooks' XML (.twb) format and the Tableau Server/Cloud metadata API can be programmatically scanned to extract every calculated field's formula across every workbook, producing an inventory of every distinct business calculation in use, which is both the raw material for migration and, just as importantly, the artifact that surfaces exactly how much undocumented logic actually exists before anyone starts rebuilding anything.

From that inventory, each distinct calculation needs to be triaged, not blanket-migrated: genuinely duplicate or near-duplicate calculations across workbooks should be consolidated into one governed definition, calculations that reveal a real, still-relevant business rule (a specific exclusion or adjustment that turns out to matter) get documented with their rationale (interviewing the business users who actually rely on that workbook, since they may remember why a rule exists even if it was never written down) and rebuilt deliberately in the Power BI semantic layer or ideally the dbt Semantic Layer as the new authoritative source, and calculations that turn out to be genuinely obsolete or superseded get explicitly retired with a documented decision, not silently dropped. I would run this with the same parallel-validation discipline as any other migration — old Tableau workbook and new Power BI report producing the same numbers for an agreed validation period, with the business owner of that specific workbook signing off — and I would not decommission a given Tableau workbook until its specific business owner has confirmed the new version, because the owner, not the migration team, is the only one who can actually confirm nothing important was lost.
questions.professionalAnswer: The technical migration isn't actually the hard part here — the hard part is that a decade of undocumented calculated-field logic across dozens of workbooks represents real institutional knowledge, and if I just rebuild 'equivalent' measures from scratch, I risk silently dropping something that exists for a reason nobody currently remembers, which then shows up as a confusing discrepancy months later with no one able to explain it. So before any rebuilding happens, I'd do a systematic extraction — Tableau's workbook XML and server metadata API can be scanned programmatically to pull out every calculated field's formula across every workbook, which gives me an actual inventory of every distinct business calculation in use, not a guess. Then I triage that inventory rather than blanket-migrating it: genuine duplicates get consolidated into one governed definition, calculations that turn out to encode a real still-relevant business rule get documented — including interviewing the business users who actually use that workbook, because they might remember the 'why' even if it was never written down anywhere — and rebuilt deliberately as the new authoritative version, and anything genuinely obsolete gets explicitly retired with a documented decision, not just quietly dropped. And I wouldn't decommission any specific workbook until its actual business owner has confirmed the new version matches, because they're the only one who can really tell me nothing important got lost in translation.
commonMistakes: Rebuilds 'equivalent' Power BI measures from scratch without systematically extracting the existing logic first
Blanket-migrates every calculation instead of triaging duplicates, still-relevant rules, and obsolete logic separately
Doesn't interview the actual business users who rely on each workbook to recover undocumented rationale
Decommissions workbooks based on the migration team's own validation instead of the actual business owner's sign-off
keyPoints: Systematically extracts existing calculated-field logic before rebuilding anything
Triages calculations into duplicates, still-relevant rules, and obsolete logic rather than blanket migration
Recovers undocumented rationale by interviewing actual business users
Rebuilds surviving logic deliberately in a governed semantic layer as the new authoritative source
Requires the specific business owner's sign-off before decommissioning each workbook

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes systematic extraction of existing logic before migration
Proposes a sound triage process for calculations
Recovers undocumented rationale through business-user engagement
Requires business-owner sign-off before decommissioning

questions.title: Defending an Unpopular Architecture Decision to Executives
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you recommended an architecture decision that was unpopular with executives because it cost more or took longer than they wanted, and you had to defend it. How did you make your case, and what happened?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer here does not lead with the technical justification; it leads with translating the architecture decision into the business risk or cost the executive actually cares about, because 'this is the more correct design' is not a sentence that wins a budget argument on its own. The structure that works: state the recommendation and the alternative being rejected in plain terms, quantify the real consequence of the cheaper/faster alternative in business language (downtime risk, compliance exposure, a specific future cost of rework), acknowledge honestly what the executive gives up by taking the more expensive path (a real timeline or budget cost, stated plainly, not minimized), and propose a way to de-risk their actual concern without abandoning the sound architecture — a phased approach that delivers something sooner while still building toward the right end state, for example.

The candidate should describe a real, specific instance: what the two options actually were, what evidence they brought (a cost model, a risk scenario, a comparable incident at another company or a past internal incident), how the conversation actually went including any pushback they got and how they responded to it, and the actual outcome, including if the outcome wasn't a clean win — maybe they got partial buy-in, or had to compromise on something, or the decision was reversed later and they had to manage that too. A red flag is a story where the executive simply deferred to the architect's authority without being given a real business-framed reason, because that's not persuasion, it's just hierarchy, and it doesn't demonstrate the actual skill being tested, which is making a technical case land with a non-technical audience under real pressure.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'll give you a specific one. I recommended we delay a reporting feature launch by six weeks to build proper row-level security into the data model instead of bolting it on with a workaround that would've shipped on the original date. The VP of Sales was not happy, because that date was already communicated to a major customer. I didn't lead with 'this is architecturally correct' — I led with what the workaround actually risked: a specific scenario where a sales rep could see another region's pipeline data, which given the customer we were trying to impress was exactly the kind of thing that would end the relationship if it ever happened, not just be embarrassing internally. I brought a one-page risk comparison, not a technical deep dive, and I was upfront that six weeks was a real cost, I wasn't going to pretend it wasn't. What actually got us to yes was proposing we ship a narrower version of the feature on the original date for the one customer group where the workaround genuinely wasn't a risk, and build the proper version for the broader rollout — so the VP didn't have to choose between 'ship nothing' and 'ship something risky,' there was a third option. The compromise meant extra work for my team short-term, but it protected the actual customer relationship and we didn't regret the architecture six months later when a second customer needed exactly that security model.
commonMistakes: Leads with technical justification instead of translating the decision into business risk/cost
Describes a story where the executive simply deferred to authority rather than being persuaded
Minimizes or hides the real cost/timeline tradeoff of the recommended path
Gives a vague, generic answer without a specific decision, specific pushback, and specific outcome
keyPoints: Translates the architecture decision into business-framed risk or cost
Honestly acknowledges what the executive gives up by taking the recommended path
Brings concrete evidence (cost model, risk scenario) rather than asserting correctness
Describes a specific real instance with real pushback and a real outcome
Shows willingness to find a de-risking compromise rather than an all-or-nothing stance

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Translates the technical decision into business-framed terms
Provides a specific, credible real instance with real stakes
